# Q16 - when have you gone beyond surface-level analysis?

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary); touches Insist on the Highest Standards.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - BOM parser edge-case analysis (PREP STORY 1, "The BOM Parser That Refused to Break"); a different deep-dive from Q11's classifier training.

## Core Answer

I built a tool that reconciles a Bill of Materials - the parts list for a circuit board - exported from SAP (Bosch's production-management software) against the PCB layout, the design file showing where every part goes, and flags components that are missing, extra, or mismatched. The reading part of the tool - the "parser," the code that opens and interprets the file - looked like the easy part, until real production files arrived. It handled many real BOMs, then broke, and every time it broke the first explanation was wrong.

The first break was total: every component reported missing. The surface read was "the file didn't parse." But the file opened fine and the layout matched clean - a dead parser doesn't fail that one-sided. I logged the raw cell values: every reference came back as "MP_R1" instead of "R1." A reference is the short code marking where a part sits on the board - R for resistor, C for capacitor. A manufacturing process code was glued on the front. The lazy fix - strip anything before an underscore - would have eaten legitimate test-point prefixes; a test point is a bare pad the factory probes with equipment, and its code can contain underscores So I audited the pattern across thousands of entries: the prefix was always two or three letters followed by a standard reference. I keyed the rule on that suffix, not on the underscore.

Second break: cells that looked empty. They showed fine in Excel - the data was there, my reader just couldn't see it. They were SAP hyperlink cells: the cell was a clickable link, not plain text, and the library hands you a link object where you expected a word. My test data had none, so I stopped trusting my own fixtures (the saved test files I'd built on) and wrote a recursive extractor - code that peels a cell's layers off one at a time until it finds text: a string if it is one, else the value field, else the link's display text.

Third: references like `R1||R2`. I'd been dropping them as invalid - but the layout always had a position at that spot, and garbage text doesn't get that consistent. So I asked the manufacturing engineer what the line meant: one position on the board, two possible parts depending on which version of the board is built - that's what the "variant notation" `R1||R2` spells. Each side became a valid match target; I split both separators and tested the whole matrix of combinations, malformed forms included.

Fourth, the subtlest: `DNP_R3` flagged as missing. Technically true, semantically wrong - DNP means "do-not-populate," i.e. the position is meant to be *empty* on purpose. False "missing" alerts - flagging something as wrong when it's actually fine - kill trust in an inspection tool.

What turned four patches into an actual dive was the audit around them: a regression suite - a kept set of real files the tool must pass after every single change, like re-taking the same exam - of 15 real production BOMs, grown every time production surfaced a new case, re-run after every change. That suite ran zero false positives and zero false negatives - on those files, nothing fine got flagged, and nothing actually wrong got missed - and in week one the tool caught three real mismatches manual review had missed.

What I took from it: surface analysis tells you what broke, not why. The references weren't the data; the conventions underneath them were.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: Parser worked on ~70% of real BOMs, then broke on production files - and each break's symptom hid a different root cause.
- Customer: The BOM-vs-layout reconciliation users - replacing a 20-30-minute-per-board manual cross-check (engineer-reported).
- Insight: The reference designators weren't the data; the manufacturing conventions underneath them were (MP_ prefix, hyperlink cells, variant separators, DNP semantics) - the unwritten factory rules hiding inside the files.
- Action (mine): Raw-cell logging; suffix-keyed prefix strip after auditing thousands of entries; recursive cell extractor after distrusting my own test fixtures; asked the manufacturing engineer what `||` meant, then built the splitter and test matrix; DNP detection; 15-BOM regression suite re-run on every change.
- Result: Zero false positives (nothing fine flagged) and zero false negatives (nothing wrong missed) across the 15-BOM suite; three real mismatches caught in week one.
- Learning: "Never normalize without understanding the semantics"; discovery was reactive - next time collect sample BOMs from the floor before writing code.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. How did you find the MP_ issue? - First real BOM run showed every component missing; I thought the file wasn't parsing at all. But a broken parser doesn't fail only on the BOM side - a file that truly wouldn't open would kill both sides of the comparison, not just one - so I logged raw cell values and saw "MP_R1" vs the layout's "R1." A naming convention, not a parsing failure - symptom vs cause. [SAFE]
2. What made you distrust each surface explanation? - Pattern: the output was too clean to be a crash. Total-but-one-sided misses -> data problem, not file problem. Cells visible in Excel but empty to the parser -> reader problem, not data problem. "Invalid" references that always had a real layout position -> my definition of valid was wrong, not the file. [SAFE]
3. Why regex and not positional/structured parsing? - A "regex" (regular expression) is a compact pattern describing text to look for, like "letters followed by digits." The BOM is semi-structured: references move between columns across exports. The text pattern (letters + digits) is the only reliable signal; a per-export column mapping - telling the tool which column holds what, each time - needs configuration, which defeats automation. [SAFE]
4. Walk through the recursive extractor. - "Recursive" means the code handles one layer of the cell, then hands the leftover to itself until it runs out of layers. String -> return it; else if it has a `v` value -> recurse into `v`; else if it has an `l` hyperlink -> take the link's display text. Priority-order property checks handled nested shapes I hadn't anticipated. [SAFE]
5. Why was DNP a false positive, not a real miss? - DNP = do-not-populate: the factory deliberately leaves that position empty. "Missing: DNP_R3" is technically true but semantically wrong - DNP means the position should be empty. Detected it case-insensitively (DNP, dnp, Dnp all caught), marked the position intentionally empty. False "missing" alerts - saying there's a problem when the emptiness is by design - erode trust in an inspection tool. [SAFE]
6. How did you know the strip wouldn't damage legitimate prefixes? - Audited instead of assumed: MP_ was consistently a 2-3-letter process code followed by a standard reference; "TP" test points - bare pads probed by testing equipment, with their own honest code style - have a different suffix pattern. Rule: unknown convention -> leave alone and flag, never guess. [SAFE]
7. Where did the `||` semantics come from? - From the manufacturing engineer, not the file. I had it filed as invalid; he explained it's one position, two candidate parts by board variant - the same board sold in versions, this spot gets part R1 on one version, R2 on the other. Both `||` and `/` split into valid match targets; matrix covered `R1||R2`, `R1/R2`, `R1||R2||R3`, and malformed `||R1` / `R1/`. [SAFE]
8. How solid is the 70%? - What it counts: roughly how many real files my early parser handled correctly. Where it came from: my own early trials against real files. How solid: a rough sense, not a measured corpus figure. It's there to size the gap, not as a statistic. [PARTIAL]
9. What does zero FP / zero FN actually cover? - Plain words first: a false positive is flagging something as wrong when it's actually fine; a false negative is a real problem the tool fails to report. What the zeros count: no fine things flagged and no real problems missed, across the 15 suite BOMs - that's the honest scope. I can't claim no edge cases exist in the wild; that's exactly why the suite grew with each new production find and re-ran on every change. [SAFE]
10. What's the manual baseline the tool replaced? - What it counts: an engineer eyeballing the parts list against the layout by hand, time per board. Where it came from and how solid: engineer-reported - cross-checking BOM against layout took 20-30 minutes per board; the report produces the same check in seconds. The 20-30 min figure is a team recollection, not instrumented. The three week-one catches are a story-bank record, not an audited count. [PARTIAL]
11. Performance? - What it counts: how long the tool takes to read a big parts list. A 2,000-component BOM parsed under 200 ms - a fifth of a second - against a sub-second success bar for 500-2,000 components; the scaling is linear O(n+m) - work grows in step with the size of both lists, so twice the parts is about twice the time, never a blow-up; unknown formats degrade gracefully rather than crash - they get flagged instead of taking the tool down. Where it came from and how solid: recorded figures, single-run - one measured timing, not a benchmark study. [PARTIAL]
12. Hardest part / what would you do differently? - Hardest: re-questioning my own test data after the hyperlink miss - the saved example files I'd trusted were the problem (my assumption failed, not the library). Differently: I found every case reactively via production failure - I'd collect sample BOMs from the manufacturing floor first. Accepted trade-off: the parser is tightly coupled to SAP export formats - it assumes Bosch's software lays files out a certain way. Surprise: DNP x variant interaction needed manufacturing intent, not text matching. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "Zero FP/zero FN across 15 BOMs" - defensible only with the scope attached; it counts nothing wrongly flagged and nothing missed *within the 15-file test suite*, not in the wild. Drop the "15" and it becomes an unbacked universal claim. Always say it with the suite. [SAFE as scoped]
2. 70% and the 200 ms figure - 70% is my feel from early trials, 200 ms is one recorded run; story-bank-recorded, estimate/single-run provenance, not surveyed or benchmarked. Label them that way under probing rather than defending precision. [PARTIAL]
3. "Three mismatches manual review missed" and the 20-30 min/board baseline - week-one story-bank record and engineer-reported recollection, not audited or instrumented; don't elaborate on how review missed them beyond what the record says. [PARTIAL]
4. "Garbage text doesn't get that consistent" distrust beat - a reasoning step, not a measured statistic; safe to say as my thinking, not as data. [SAFE]

# Q17 - tell me about a time when you had to implement a direction you didn't agree with

**LP:** Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit (primary; touches Are Right, A Lot, Earn Trust) - *the "disagrees with peers and supervisors" strength is a GAP; no lived imposed-direction event exists in the record*   **Story:** No superior-issued-direction event documented. Closest truths: full commit on the engineer's variant call (cross-ref Q6) and data-first pushback against the tool's pin-count rule (STORY 10) - each labeled for what it is and isn't

## Core Answer

I don't have a documented case of a manager handing me a direction I disagreed with and me executing it anyway. I built the inspection suite solo - it's a software tool that checks factory circuit boards against their design files - and there's no boss scene in my record, and I won't invent one.

What I do have is how I actually behave when a call that isn't mine stands in front of me. The clearest instance is the variant decision. My BOM parser treated `R1||R2` references as invalid and dropped them. (BOM = "bill of materials": the parts list for a circuit board, saying which component goes in which spot. `R1||R2` is shorthand meaning one spot on the board can take either of two interchangeable parts.) A manufacturing engineer told me they were valid - one position, either part. My first instinct was that my rule was right, because dropping them kept the comparison simple. But he had the domain intent and I didn't. Once I saw that, I didn't keep a piece of my old logic out of pride. I adopted his semantics completely - his meaning for the notation, not a half-measure of mine - and rewrote the splitter, the code that reads those references. That's the commit part, and it's real.

The disagree part is also real, just not aimed at a person. The reconciliation tool matched parts by comparing BOM pin count to layout pad count, literally. (Pins are the metal legs of a chip; pads are the solder spots on the board where those legs land.) I thought that rule was wrong - footprints legitimately carry more pads than the chip uses (a "footprint" is the physical solder pattern a part takes up on the board; some designs include solder spots nothing connects to), so it was raising false alarms - warnings on things that were actually fine - and the engineers stopped trusting the reports. I pushed back with data instead of opinion: twenty mismatched BOMs sorted into three cases. Larger footprint: flag for review, not mismatch. Smaller: genuine mismatch. Pin count stayed in the comparison because the requirement was to kill the false alarms without blinding the tool to wrong parts, so I made the signal discriminating - able to tell ordinary design quirks apart from real problems: component-type check (are the two parts even the same kind of part), configurable two-to-one threshold (the adjustable ratio the tool allows between extra solder spots and legs before it treats the difference as meaningful) - and shipped a debug view (a screen showing the raw values behind each warning) so an engineer can see the raw values and override the tool. False positives on mixed boards went from about 12% to under 2%. (Mixed boards = boards combining several different kinds of parts; what those percentages count and how solid they are is in the follow-ups below.)

So the honest shape of my answer: state the counter-argument once, with data; once the call stands, implement it fully, as if it were mine; if execution turns up a fact nobody saw, raise that once, then respect it. **[GAP]** - what's missing is a real time a person above me made the call against my view and I executed anyway. That example has to come from team experience, not from this record.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: the question demands a lived imposed-direction event - a boss's call you disagreed with but executed anyway; the record contains none - solo build, no supervisor appears anywhere
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers living with the false alarms (pin-count) - warnings on boards that were actually fine - and with wrong-part misses (variant) - real errors the tool could let through; a true direction-issuing superior is missing, not invented
- Insight: where I disagree it's against a rule or an assumption, never a person's call; where I adopt someone else's direction (the variant), the record ends in agreement - the disagree->still-commit tension the question probes is unevidenced
- Action (mine): adopted the engineer's `R1||R2` semantics completely and rewrote the splitter; categorized 20 BOMs into three footprint cases; kept pin count in and made it discriminating - review-vs-mismatch rule, component-type check, configurable 2:1 threshold, debug view with engineer override
- Result: multi-part references handled correctly (variant fix); false positives ~12% -> under 2% on mixed-component-type boards (pin-count rule change)
- Learning: counter once with data -> implement fully if the call stands -> raise new facts once; method proven on adjacent ground, but this exact case is a GAP I must fill with a real event, not a relabel

# Q18 - tell me about a time when you got negative feedback from a higher up

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary), Learn and Be Curious   **Story:** the five-day prototype and the one-hour team review (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md STORY 8); process lessons from STORY 10 and STORY 11

## Core Answer

My lead put my rough five-day prototype - a deliberately unfinished first version, made in five days just to draw reactions - in front of the manufacturing team, and within an hour they came back with three critical issues. That's the honest shape of the strongest negative feedback I got from above - the lead escalated it (passed it up for the team to review), the team delivered the critique, and no manager sat me down one-on-one. I won't inflate it past that.

Context in one line: engineers had wanted an automated PCB comparison tool for six months. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device; the tool was meant to automatically spot differences between two images of a board, and the "six months" is how long the request had sat, per the team's account.) It kept stalling because it was "too complex" to scope - too complicated to pin down exactly what to build. So instead of scoping, I built. Five days: one monolithic HTML file, inline JavaScript, no build system, no modules, no tests. (Plain words: a single web-page file that a browser opens, with all the program code written inside it - nothing split into separate parts, no tools that assemble the code automatically, and none of the automatic self-checks that catch coding mistakes.) It loaded two images, ran a basic pixel comparison - matching the images dot by dot on each dot's numeric brightness value - showed a result. It worked under clean conditions and was rough everywhere else - and I'd written its limitations down before the demo.

On day five I demoed to my lead. He shared it with the team right away. An hour later, the three. One: the pixel comparison broke under illumination changes - light levels - the same good board, photographed under different light, came back full of diffs, meaning the tool reported differences all over it. Two: no alignment at all - the tool couldn't line the two images up so the same points matched - unless the board was photographed at the exact same angle, the diff was meaningless. Three: no export - engineers couldn't save a result - no way to write it out to a file for use elsewhere; the tool only existed on screen.

I didn't defend it. I'd documented the limitations going in, so the feedback confirmed known gaps instead of exposing hidden ones. I told the team all three were real, and asked which order mattered for their work.

I ranked by impact and complaint frequency: alignment first - without it nothing else could work; illumination normalization second - fixing out the lighting differences so the same board doesn't look different - the most frequent complaint; export third - valuable but not a blocker. Nine days after the review the tool was production-ready - in use by the team for their actual work - two weeks total, five prototype plus nine of repair. That one hour taught me more about what to build than six months of scoping had. (Every number here - six months, five days, one hour, nine days, two weeks - counts calendar time spent on this work, from one source: my own telling of the story; these are self-reported durations, not figures a system logged.)

Two changes stuck. I started building observability in from day one instead of bolting it on after trust erodes - observability means the tool shows its own inner workings: what it decided and why. The BOM tool's debug view had been an afterthought (BOM = bill of materials, the parts list for a board; the debug view = a screen showing what the tool looked at and why it called what it called). And collecting failure cases, finding the pattern, fixing the root cause became my standard loop - failure cases being examples where the tool got the answer wrong, and the root cause being the underlying reason, not the surface symptom. I ran it on the Good Board tool's illumination, rotation, and scale problems - the board photographed under different light, at different angles, or at different zoom levels. The lesson wasn't "build better prototypes." I'd optimized for speed of feedback and underinvested in realism. The review cost me an hour of embarrassment and bought a roadmap that was actually right.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: six-month "too complex" stall on the PCB comparison request -> my counter-move: a deliberately rough 5-day prototype (unfinished-on-purpose build, made to be judged) with limitations documented upfront
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers who'd wanted the tool and issued the critique; my lead, who escalated rather than shielded (passed it up for review instead of protecting me from it)
- Insight: the prototype existed to collect exactly this feedback - all three hits landed on gaps I'd listed, so accepting them cost nothing I believed
- Action (mine): shipped rough on purpose; owned all three issues without defense (alignment = lining the images up; illumination = lighting; export = saving results to a file); ranked them myself by impact and complaint frequency (alignment -> illumination -> export); then made observability-from-day-one (the tool shows its own decision-making) and the failure-case loop (bad examples -> pattern -> underlying cause) permanent
- Result: production-ready at two weeks total (5 prototype + 9 repair); one hour of review beat six months of scoping
- Learning: optimized for speed of feedback, underinvested in realism - paid for with embarrassment once, converted into two process changes

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Was that really feedback "from a higher up"? - Honest answer: the critique came from the manufacturing team in a review my lead set up. What the lead himself did was share the build; no documented words of his criticizing it. The higher-up element is a senior reviewer escalating my rough work to real users, and it not surviving. I'd rather say that plainly than invent the one-on-one that didn't happen. [PARTIAL - premise labeled; never inflate]
2. What exactly did the lead say to you? - Nothing is on record beyond that he shared it immediately. I won't put words in his mouth. The three issues are documented as named by the team within the hour. [GAP - no quote exists]
3. How did you stay non-defensive? - I'd documented the prototype's limitations before the demo, so nothing the team hit was a surprise. Shipping a known limitation is different from shipping a bug, and the prototype's whole purpose was to learn what to build - defending it would have meant defending the wrong thing. [SAFE]
4. How did you pick the priority order? - Impact and frequency of complaint; my call, not the team's. Alignment gates every credible comparison on real re-shot photos (plain words: until the two images are lined up so the same point on each matches, any reported difference is unreliable). Illumination was the most frequent complaint; export is valuable but doesn't block inspection. [SAFE]
5. Is the timeline solid? - Two weeks total: 5 days prototype + 9 days refinement. One telling, one source, and the review happened on day 5 - so "production-ready nine days after the review" is the same fact stated carefully. In plain terms: these numbers count working days on the build, from my own account of the story - self-reported scheduling, not timestamps a system recorded. [SAFE]
6. Why does light break a pixel comparison? - Pixel diffing matches on raw values; global brightness shifts those values, so an unaligned board fires diffs everywhere. Plain words: a "pixel" is one dot of an image; the tool compares each dot's numeric brightness value, and turning the overall lighting up or down changes every one of those values at once - so the whole picture reads as different. That's the mechanism behind the documented illumination failure, stated as illustration - not an extra event. [PARTIAL - illustrative restatement]
7. What alternatives did you reject? - Going back to requirements gathering - asking users in detail what they need before building - it had already stalled six months - and defending scope ("it's just a prototype"), which dodges the feedback the prototype existed to collect. Both were rejected in favor of accepting the three hits and ordering them. [SAFE]
8. What went wrong / hardest part? - Handing over five days of work and watching an hour of review list three blockers - things that stop the tool from being usable. The embarrassment was the real cost. The alternative - polishing privately for months - was the failure that had already happened. [SAFE]
9. If a manager had said the whole approach was wrong? - Framework, not memory: ask for the specific failing case, not a verdict; reproduce it in the user's environment on the user's inputs; test the alternative against the cases that broke mine; commit to whichever survives the evidence. The record shows three specific issues, not a wholesale rejection. [GAP-labeled - framework]
10. What changed about how you take feedback now? - I ask for the failing case instead of the verdict, and reproduce it on the user's setup. And I make feedback cheap to give: the debug view exists so a user can show me which rule fired instead of just saying the answer looks wrong (the debug view = a screen inside the tool showing what it checked and why it decided what it decided; "which rule fired" = which of its checks triggered). [SAFE]
11. What would you do differently? - Build observability from day one instead of after trust erodes - the BOM tool's debug view was an afterthought, and from the start it would have caught edge cases - unusual situations outside the normal use - earlier. And run the collect-failures, analyze-patterns, fix-root-causes loop from the start - which I later did on the Good Board tool's illumination, rotation, and scale edge cases. [SAFE]
12. Who did the work? - Me. The PCB suite was a solo build - I was the only engineer. The prototype, the review response, and the two-week fix were all mine. No "we" in this story. [SAFE]

## Risk Check

1. Literal premise mismatch - a team critique escalated by my lead (passed up for review), not a superior's one-on-one. Status: defensible as labeled; it fails the moment it's inflated, so the honesty stays inside the spoken core, not just provenance (the source notes at the end of this file).
2. Attribution drift - any phrasing that makes the lead the critic (accidentally shifting who gave the critique) contradicts the record and re-opens the round-1 defect. Status: defensible; critique is attributed to the team in every telling, lead = escalator only.
3. The "same board, different light, full of diffs" line - mechanism illustration (explaining why the failure happened), not a new documented event. Status: PARTIAL; say "that's what the illumination failure looked like," never "this specific board."
4. All numbers (6 months, 5 days, 1 hour, 2 weeks, 5+9) - single telling, one source; conflicting tellings (150MB standalone; 4000+ line/21-module - other accounts of this same story describing it as a 150-megabyte single file, or as code over 4,000 lines split into 21 parts) excluded outright. Status: defensible.

# Q19 - tell me about a time when you had to make a difficult decision to meet a tight deadline

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary); Deliver Results; Are Right, A Lot.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the five-day first prototype (`AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md` STORY 8); the deadline-decision angle, distinct from Q13's quality-tradeoff and Q10's influence tellings of the same prototype.

## Core Answer

Start with the honest part: nobody handed me a date. The real problem was a stalemate. The manufacturing engineers wanted a PCB comparison tool - a PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device, and this tool checks a photo of a built board against its design drawing - and it had sat in the backlog, the team's parking list of work nobody has scheduled, for six months because it was "too complex to scope properly." (The six months is what I was told when I joined the thread - how long the idea had been parked, not something I tracked.) I decided the bottleneck was definition, not capability, so I set my own deadline: demo in five days. (Five days = calendar days from deciding to build to standing in front of the team.) Waiting for agreement would have meant waiting another six months.

The hard call was what to cut. The version I'd have been comfortable showing had image alignment (lining the photo and the design drawing up so identical parts sit on top of each other), illumination normalization (correcting brightness differences so the lighting doesn't read as a defect), and export (saving the result as a file an engineer can send elsewhere) - that version ended up taking two weeks. On day one I had three options: keep collecting requirements, build the trustworthy version and show up late, or cut to the smallest end-to-end slice (the tiniest version that walks the real job from start to finish) that answered the only question the demo had to answer - can this thing see a mismatch? - and show it on the date. I took the slice: upload, a pixel-level comparison (checking the two images point by point and marking where they look different), a visual result. I cut the three things that made the result trustworthy. That meant boards had to be photographed at the same angle in the same light, which almost never happens on a real line (a factory's production line, where lighting and camera angles wander). I knew that. I shipped it anyway.

What was at stake was credibility - mine and the tool's. A demo the team waved off would have sent the idea back to the backlog, this time on my work rather than on the fog around the problem. I judged that risk smaller than the risk of spending months building the wrong features. I drew one line: cut features, not correctness. The prototype was right about the conditions it claimed to support. I wrote the limitation down and said it out loud in the demo.

The lead shared it with the team immediately, and within an hour (the first hour after the live demo) they'd given me three problems: comparison failed under lighting changes, no alignment, no export. That was exactly what I'd bought five days for. I fixed them in impact order (biggest blocker first) - alignment first because nothing worked without it, illumination second, export last. Two weeks from the first line of code, the tool was production-ready. (The two weeks = 5 days to the demo plus 9 days of fixes, counted from my own work record, not a ticketing system; "production-ready" here means the engineers used the tool for real work - a milestone, not a measured quality score.) I'd hit the date I picked.

What I'd do differently: bring a couple of real board photos to the demo, so the team's hour went to next steps instead of rediscovering what I already knew. What I'd still defend: cutting scope to a named limit is how I met the deadline - not lowering the standard I could verify.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: PCB comparison tool the manufacturing engineers wanted; six months parked in the backlog as "too complex to scope properly."
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers; the engineering lead as the first demo audience.
- Insight: the bottleneck was definition, not capability - a working slice forces the opinions that six months of scoping could not.
- Action (mine): set my own five-day demo date; kept upload + pixel comparison + visual result; cut alignment, illumination normalization, export - with the limitation written down and stated out loud at the demo; ordered fixes by impact (alignment -> illumination -> export).
- Result: demoed on day five; lead shared it immediately; three concrete issues inside the first hour; production-ready two weeks from first keystroke (5 + 9); the date I set was met.
- Learning: meet a self-imposed deadline by cutting scope to a named limit, never by cutting the standard I can verify; bring real photos to the demo so feedback lands on next steps.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Was five days a real deadline? - Self-imposed, and I say so first. No external date existed; the real pressure was a six-month stalemate. I compressed on purpose to force a decision instead of another week of analysis. The "difficult decision" is the compression itself. [SAFE]
2. How did you pick what to keep versus cut? - The demo had to answer one question: can it see a mismatch at all. Upload, comparison, and a visible result answer that. Alignment, illumination handling, and export make the result *trustworthy* - they don't change whether the concept works. The trustworthy half was the deferrable half. [SAFE]
3. Isn't shipping a knowingly inaccurate tool a bad decision? - The cut was "works under real line conditions," not "works correctly." It was correct under the conditions it claimed to support, and the limitation was documented before the demo. A named limitation is a different act from a hidden defect. [SAFE]
4. Who did you consult before cutting scope? - Nobody, and that was the point. The only opinions available lived in the meetings that had produced six months of nothing. My consultation *was* the demo, scheduled early enough that the answer was still cheap. I bet on scope, not on permission - and I made the bet reviewable. [PARTIAL - honest limit on "consults when appropriate"]
5. What if the team had dismissed it? - There was no fallback artifact: export was one of the three cuts, so nothing could be saved out of it. The prior route was the engineers comparing board images by eye, and the prototype at least put both boards on one screen. The risk I was managing wasn't adoption - it was building the wrong features, and shipping early is what removed that. [SAFE]
6. How do you know the decision, not luck, produced the outcome? - The outcome was specific and directional: three concrete issues within the hour, that list became the priority order, production-ready followed in two weeks. I'm not claiming the tool was good on day five - only that cutting scope to a date is what produced the roadmap. [SAFE]
7. How reliable are the numbers? - All durations are my own work record, not instrumented: five days to prototype, nine more to production-ready. "Production-ready" is a milestone - the engineers used the tool - not a measured defect rate, and I don't upgrade it into one. [PARTIAL]
8. Did the speed create debt? - Yes, in two places. I broke the monolith (one big tangle of code in a single place) into modules (separate, self-contained pieces you can change without rewriting everything) after the first two weeks so the next feature wasn't a rewrite. And I later shipped a second tool by copying the first because I needed it working that week - that bought a deadline, then the copies drifted for months. Lesson: put a deadline on the copy too. [SAFE]
9. How big was the monolith, exactly? - I only say "modularized it." The record carries conflicting size tellings ("500 lines of JavaScript" and "4000+ lines / 21 modules" - those count lines of code in the program file and separate code files, i.e. the program's raw size, not anything about quality), and neither verifies against the actual code, so I quote neither. [GAP - generalize, don't number]
10. How did you order the fixes? - By impact and complaint frequency: illumination was the most frequent complaint, but alignment was the biggest capability gap - nothing worked without it - so alignment went first, illumination second, export third. My prioritization as the builder, not a negotiated call with the team. [SAFE]
11. Who disagreed with you on this? - Nobody, and I won't inflate it. The opposition in this story was a standing backlog conclusion - "too complex to scope" - not a person. [PARTIAL - stated plainly]
12. Bigger scale / where did this lead? - I built the suite solo, so the five-day call was mine alone. The prototype's pixel compare later became the aligned comparison engine - the part that decides whether a board matches its design and flags the differences. The accuracy figures for that fix live in my quality-compromise story, and I keep that single-told rather than restating it here. [PARTIAL - cross-ref Q13]
13. What would you do differently? - Collect a couple of real board photos before the demo, so the team's hour went to next steps instead of rediscovering the lighting and angle problems I already knew about. [SAFE]

# Q20 - a time when you needed to deep dive to solve a problem

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary); touches Are Right, A Lot and Insist on the Highest Standards.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the image-alignment pipeline (`AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md` STORY 2, canonical alignment telling; STORY 12/13 excluded).

## Core Answer

The problem looked small: alignment was off, so the PCB-versus-layout comparison tool started crying false alarms. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device; the "layout" is its design drawing; the tool lines the photo up over the drawing and flags every spot where the two disagree. A "false alarm" is the tool crying wolf - flagging a board that's actually fine because the two images aren't lined up. "Alignment" just means getting photo and drawing to land point-on-point.) The tool flags a mismatch at a ten-pixel photo-vs-layout disagreement - a pixel is one dot of the image, so ten dots apart fires a flag - if alignment drifts more than a few pixels, every result downstream is noise. The symptom was "alignment is bad." The deep dive was finding out *why*.

My first wrong assumption was the textbook one: match features, fit a transform - start with affine. (A "transform" is a math recipe for moving one image onto the other; "affine" is the simplest family of recipes.) Six numbers: rotation, scaling, translation, shear - turn, resize, shift, slant. It worked on flat boards shot straight-on and failed on real photos. So I asked - not "how do I fit it better?" but "why can't affine fit this at all?" The answer was in the camera model - the geometry of how a tilted photo flattens a real scene. Affine preserves parallel lines. Photograph a board at an angle and its parallel edges converge toward a vanishing point, like a straight road's edges meeting at the horizon. Perspective breaks parallelism, so no affine matrix can undo it. Wrong tool, not bad tuning. I switched to a homography fit with RANSAC - a perspective model that votes out outlier feature matches, so a few bad correspondences can't corrupt the matrix. (A homography is the warp recipe that includes camera tilt, letting parallel lines converge the way they do in a photo. RANSAC is a voting trick: rebuild the warp from a handful of matched points, many times over, and keep whichever version the most other points agree with - so wrong matches get voted out.)

That fixed the global case, but real photos still averaged fifteen to twenty pixels of misalignment - still 15-20 dots off, far past the ten-pixel flag rule. Second wrong assumption, mine: that any single global transform - one recipe applied identically to the whole image - was the end state. The physical detail that broke it - boards pass through a reflow oven (the oven that solders the parts down), and the heat bows them unevenly, the center differently from the edges. A global transform structurally can't fix a local bow. So I added a non-rigid stage - a warp that can bend different regions by different amounts. I compared elastic deformation, B-splines, and thin-plate splines (three bendable-warp families: one simulates real material bending, one is steered by an adjustable grid of points, one bends like a least-effort thin sheet), and picked TPS: it minimizes bending energy (the warp bends as little as its anchor points force - the smoothest fit possible), is deterministic given the control points (the anchor points where the warp is pinned; same anchors in, exactly the same warp out), needs no material constants that have no clear meaning for a board, and OpenCV's implementation is mature (OpenCV = the standard free image-processing toolbox). Control points came from template-matching known features - corners, fiducials, pads - (template matching = slide a small known picture across the photo and take where it overlaps best; fiducials = the reference dots the manufacturer prints on the board for machines to line up on; pads = the little solder dots where a component's legs attach) rejecting weak matches, because one bad point drags the whole warp.

Then I measured instead of eyeballing. My controlled test: twenty board images with markers at known positions - align each, measure the offsets afterward. (An exam I built for my own tool: I already knew each marker's true spot, so after alignment I could count exactly how many dots it landed off.) Average 2.1 pixels, standard deviation 0.8 - typical error about two dots, and the 0.8 spread means the errors clustered tightly: consistent, not one lucky run. The engineers overlaid the aligned photo on the layout and spot-checked pads - that caught cases where a good number hid a subtly wrong warp.

Far-edge misalignment came down from fifteen to twenty pixels to two or three - out at the board's edges, where the bowing bites hardest, the photo now landed within 2-3 dots of the drawing. And the false alarms stopped: with the images truly lined up, the tool quit flagging misalignment as if it were a defect. The lesson: "alignment is bad" was never one problem - it was two, each needing its own root cause.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: Comparison tool firing false alarms (flags on fine boards caused by sloppy photo-vs-drawing lining-up); symptom "alignment is bad"; the 10-pixel mismatch threshold (a 10-image-dot disagreement fires a flag) means alignment must land within a few pixels or every downstream result is noise.
- Customer: Manufacturing engineers using the PCB-vs-layout comparison on the factory floor.
- Insight: Two dropped assumptions, both on evidence - affine (the simplest warp math) structurally can't represent perspective (camera tilt: it preserves parallel lines), and a global transform (one stretch-and-shift for the whole image) structurally can't fix non-uniform reflow warping (uneven heat-bending from the soldering oven - physics, not tuning).
- Action (mine): Replaced affine with a RANSAC homography (tilt-aware warp with outlier voting) myself; added the TPS stage (least-bend flexible warp) after it; template-matched control points (corners, fiducials, pads) with similarity-threshold rejection (drop any match scoring below a minimum overlap); built the 20-image ground-truth test (markers whose true positions are the known answer key); kept engineers' overlay spot-checks as the safety net.
- Result: 15-20 px -> 2-3 px (far-edge photo-vs-drawing error before vs after, in image dots); 2.1 px avg / sd 0.8 on the 20-image test (my own measured exam; sd = spread around the average, so errors were tightly clustered); comparison accuracy ~85% -> >98% on moderate warping (how often the tool's right-or-wrong verdicts come out correct, before vs after - a documented outcome, not something I instrumented); pipeline handles up to ~30 deg off-perpendicular (camera tilt from straight overhead) and ~3 mm warp (how tall the board's bend is).
- Learning: Root-cause the symptom before reaching for a better fit; start with the simplest matching that works - board-outline contours (tracing just the board's outer edge) beat full SURF (a heavyweight landmark-matching algorithm) for most boards; name the boundary - beyond ~5 mm warp, TPS still fails.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Affine versus perspective, mathematically? - In plain words first: affine can turn, resize, shift and slant an image but always keeps parallel lines parallel; perspective additionally lets them converge, which is exactly what a tilted photo does. Affine maps (x,y) to (ax+by+e, cx+dy+f): linear plus translation, six parameters, preserves parallel lines. Perspective divides by (gx+hy+1): eight parameters, parallel lines can converge to a vanishing point - exactly what an angled photo does. [SAFE]
2. How does RANSAC work here, and why four points? - Randomly draw 4 point pairs, fit a homography, count how many other pairs agree within a pixel tolerance - the agreeing ones are the "inliers," points voting for this candidate warp - repeat thousands of times, keep the model with the most inliers. The homography has 8 unknowns and each pair gives 2 constraints, so 4 is the minimum - 3 is underdetermined (too few clues for a unique answer). I ran OpenCV's default 2000 iterations - 2000 random attempts; theory says ~370 suffice at a 50% outlier rate, i.e. if half the matches are bad - the extra cost on the order of 50 ms, a twentieth of a second, bought robustness insurance. [SAFE]
3. Why TPS over elastic deformation or B-splines? - In plain terms: elastic deformation simulates bending like a real material, B-splines steer a smooth surface with a grid of adjustable points, TPS bends like a least-effort thin sheet. Elastic needs physical constants I don't have and that have no clear meaning for a warped composite board. B-splines add a control-grid resolution - another knob. TPS minimizes bending energy - it bends as little as the anchors force - is deterministic given the control points (same anchors in, exactly the same warp out), and OpenCV's implementation is mature. [SAFE - wording locked; naming specific material parameters traces to the excluded telling]
4. How many control points, and what if one is badly matched? - A 2D warp needs at least 4 - four anchors is the bare minimum to pin down a flat stretch; with only 4 there's no redundancy to average out noise (no spare points for mistakes to cancel against), so in practice I typically found 15-30 spread across the board. A wrong point pulls the field - the bend-map - toward the wrong position - hence template matching on known features and rejecting matches below a similarity threshold, a minimum score for how closely the small picture must overlap the photo. [SAFE]
5. Why not a learned registration model? - A network predicting a displacement field (a map telling every pixel where to move) needs misaligned/aligned pairs with ground-truth correspondences - an answer key saying which spot in one image matches which in the other; I had no such data, and collecting it was its own project. TPS is classical - zero training data. With thousands of labeled pairs a learned model might win under extreme warp; real alternative, would revisit. [SAFE]
6. How were the numbers measured, and how much do you trust them? - The offsets are my own harness - a small test rig I built: 20 board images, markers at known positions, pixel offsets measured after alignment - average 2.1 px, sd 0.8 (the sd, standard deviation, is the spread around the average: errors clustered tightly around two dots). Small-n - only 20 samples - self-built, single-run: directional, not production telemetry (not data from real daily use). That's exactly why the engineers' overlay spot-checks stayed in - they caught a good-number-hides-a-subtly-wrong-warp case. The ~85% -> >98% comparison accuracy - how often the tool's verdicts come out right, both catching real problems and not crying wolf - is the documented before/after for the moderate-warping regime, the everyday-bend range this story covers; the per-image offsets are what I instrumented. [PARTIAL - offsets measured, accuracy documented outcome]
7. Where did the 2-3 pixel target come from? - Forced by the spec - the tool's own flag rule - not a wish: the comparison flags mismatches at a 10-pixel threshold, so alignment accuracy within a few pixels is the requirement before a single flag means anything (if the images still sit several dots out of line, a 10-pixel flag can't tell misalignment from a real defect). [SAFE]
8. What still fails? - Severe warping beyond roughly 5 mm - a visibly tall bend: control points can't capture that much deformation; that would need a more physically based model, and it's rare in production. Past about 45 deg the feature matching itself breaks - the software can't find enough correct landmark pairs to even start aligning - the shipped pipeline handled up to 30 deg off-perpendicular (tilt away from straight overhead) and ~3 mm of visible warp (how tall the board's bend is). I name the boundary rather than imply universality. [SAFE]
9. Any bug you found by auditing your own code? - Yes. I used a single element of the homography matrix as a proxy for local scale - only valid under translation and uniform scale, wrong under rotation or shear, which is precisely what a homography models. In plain words: I read "how much the image is zoomed at this spot" off one number of the warp matrix, which is only correct when the image was merely shifted or evenly resized - never when it's tilted. The correct local scale is the square root of the determinant of the Jacobian of the projective map at that point - the standard math for measuring stretch at a point on a warped map. I found it by reading my own code, not from output - the output looked fine. [SAFE]
10. What would you do differently? - I implemented full SURF feature matching - a heavyweight algorithm that finds distinctive landmarks across images - before discovering simple board-outline contour detection, just tracing the board's outer edge, was sufficient for most boards - more general, but costlier and harder to debug. Start simple, add complexity only when it buys accuracy. [SAFE]
11. Any stakeholder disagreement during the dive? - Honest answer: no person-vs-person dispute - I built the suite solo. The friction was internal: my metric gate - my own rule that the numbers had to hit the target before I'd ship - against the temptation to ship an alignment that "mostly worked." I won't inflate that into a stakeholder fight. [PARTIAL - none documented]
12. Wasn't the homography fix enough, since it solved the real perspective case? - No - because it fixed the geometry I'd assumed was the whole problem, the camera tilt, and real photos still sat at 15-20 px - still image dots, still far past the 10-px flag rule. "Fixed the global case" - one recipe for the whole image - is not fixed on the factory floor; I held it to the target the 10-pixel threshold demanded instead of stopping at the plausible answer. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. Headline numbers (15-20 px -> 2-3 px; 2.1 px / sd 0.8 on 20 images) - px = pixels, single dots of the image; sd = how tightly the errors cluster. Canonical STORY 2 record, identical to Q14's alignment figures; defensible as long as I lead with "a 20-image ground-truth set I built" - my own exam with known-answer marker positions - and never let it inflate into "validated in production." [defensible]

# Q21 - tell me about a time when you went out of your comfort zone

**LP:** Learn and Be Curious (primary); Invent and Simplify + Deliver Results (touch)   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - rebuilding CV into the browser with never-used tools after the known stack was locked out (PREP.md STORY 5, one telling only)

## Core Answer

The biggest move out of my comfort zone was rebuilding my inspection tool to run computer vision - a program that understands a photo well enough to spot problems in it - inside a browser, with tools I'd never opened, because everything I already knew how to build had just been ruled out.

I built the PCB inspection tools alone. A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device. The manufacturing engineers who used them sat on locked-down factory machines - no software installs. My stack was Python behind a small server; none of it could cross to that floor (Python being the language, and the server one shared computer on the network that each user's machine had to reach - which the locked machines couldn't do). If the tool didn't run in the browser, it didn't exist for them. So: image processing and a trained model - software that learned from example photos what a fault looks like - in JavaScript, on OpenCV.js and TensorFlow.js, neither of which I'd used. JavaScript is the language every browser runs, and those two are free browser libraries for image work and machine learning. And it wasn't a toy - the tool had to line up a photographed board that was physically bent against a flat reference (the board's flat design drawing), and run the defect model.

Before committing, I capped the risk: one day to prove the browser could do one real operation - load two images, find the edges (the outlines of the parts in each photo), show the difference (light up where the two don't match). It could. That day paid for the two weeks after it.

The first failure was mine and it was embarrassing. The model output was garbage, and I blamed the model for hours. What I'd actually done was feed it the image with the pixel array in the wrong order - to a model, a photo is just a stack of number-grids, and I stacked them in an order it didn't expect (the technical name is a wrong tensor shape) - no error thrown, just silently wrong output. Three hours to find what one line of checking would have caught in seconds. I now write the shape check before the inference code - "inference" meaning the moment the model actually makes its prediction.

The real climb was the bending. Straightening a warped photo needs a warping algorithm - digitally bending the photo so a curved board matches a flat drawing - and no JavaScript implementation of one existed to lean on. So I read the paper that defined it - Bookstein, 1989, the academic article that first laid out the maths for this kind of bend - and coded it step by step, checking my output against the worked examples in the paper. Reading a thirty-year-old paper to ship a feature you're building this week is the least comfortable I've been at work.

My rule the whole time: learn just enough to build the next feature, then build it.

What it left me able to do: ship to the factory floor with zero IT involvement, fast enough to feel interactive - about forty milliseconds per comparison once you click through boards. In plain terms: a millisecond is a thousandth of a second, so forty is a blink; that figure counts the time one photo comparison takes to finish, I read it off the developer tools built into the browser, and it's my own observation while working, not a formal benchmark. And I learned the pattern works, because I repeated it later with a vision-language API (an AI service that can look at pictures and answer in words, called from code): same unfamiliar ground, same method - list the real options, let the constraints I actually had pick.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: known stack (Python + Flask server - Flask being a simple tool for serving a Python program over a network) blocked from factory floor by install lockdown; the job required CV in a browser on two never-used libraries
- Customer: manufacturing engineers on locked-down factory machines - no installs, no IT bandwidth (no spare time from the IT department to help)
- Insight: bound the unknown cheaply - a one-day feasibility spike (a deliberately time-limited trial just to prove something can work) before committing; then learn just enough to build the next feature
- Action (mine): one-day minimal prototype (two images -> edges -> difference); ported the pipeline to OpenCV.js/TF.js; found and fixed the tensor-order bug (the wrong-order-of-numbers mistake from the core); implemented thin-plate-spline warping from the Bookstein 1989 paper (the specific 1989 bending maths), validated against its examples
- Result: browser-only tools, no IT approval, instant adoption; ~40 ms per comparison (console-timed personal observation, comparison step only - "console" being the timing tools built into every browser); alignment later canonically 15-20 px far-edge -> 2-3 px (px = dots on screen; how far the matched photo still sat off from the drawing at the board's far corners, 15-20 px before the fix, 2-3 px after); pattern repeated with the GPT-4o vision integration
- Learning: write the cheap invariant check (tensor shapes) before the code it protects - a one-line check that the numbers arrive in the order the model expects; when the literature already derived it, write the derivation down before coding, not after

## Follow-Up Bank

1. How did you actually learn the libraries? - Docs first for the API surface (the full list of commands the library offers), then the one-day minimal prototype, then incremental build: roughly two days on docs plus prototype, two weeks iterating the pipeline - my own recollection of how the learning time split, not logged hours. OpenCV.js mirrors the C++ API (C++ = the older compiled language the original OpenCV was written in), so general OpenCV knowledge transferred, but most docs and examples were C++ - I translated as I went. [SAFE]
2. What exactly was the tensor bug? - TF.js expects NHWC layout; I passed the CHW shape `[1, 3, 224, 224]` where the model wanted `[1, 224, 224, 3]`. In plain words: a tensor is the grid of numbers a photo turns into for the model, and those four numbers say how the grid is stacked - NHWC means one image, then height, then width, then the three red/green/blue channels last; CHW puts the colour channels before height and width. Both stackings hold the same picture - only the order differs - which is exactly why nothing crashed. No exception - just wrong scores. Three hours to isolate by printing shapes at each pipeline step (a pipeline = the chain of steps the image flows through; I had the code print the number-order it received at each step; that three hours is my recollection of the session, not a logged figure); now a shape assertion goes in before any inference code. [SAFE]
3. How did you validate a from-scratch warper with no reference implementation? - Two checks: the worked examples in the Bookstein paper itself, and my own small marked-grid test images (I drew grids with points at known positions, so I could predict exactly where each point should land) where I knew what the bend should look like - the warp had to pull each marked point onto its target. What it counts: whether my hand-written maths reproduced answers I could check by hand. Slow, boring verification, but it made the output trustworthy feature by feature. [PARTIAL - paper-examples validation is sourced; grid tests are my own ordinary harness, not instrumented]
4. Why that warping method over the alternatives? - The boards bent unevenly, so a flat perspective fix wasn't enough (a perspective fix = the simple correction for a photo taken at an angle, which assumes a flat surface); non-rigid was the actual requirement. I compared the standard non-rigid options (thin-plate spline, elastic, B-spline - three textbook ways of digitally bending an image) and the spline method needed only the marked control points the pipeline already produced (control points = spots, like component corners, that the matching step had already located on both images). [SAFE]
5. What if the one-day spike had failed? - Honest gap: no recorded fallback. The server option the network rules excluded would have been the only one left, so realistically I'd have had to reopen the IT conversation. The move wasn't "I had a plan B" - it was "I bounded the unknown before building on it." [GAP - stated plainly, not papered]
6. Where did the 40 ms come from, and does it clash with your "~45 ms CPU" figure? - Forty milliseconds is the image-comparison step in the browser (align + diff), timed in the browser console against routine board pairs on a factory-class laptop while developing - personal observation, not a benchmark suite. Plain line: it counts how long one photo-vs-design comparison takes to finish in the shipped tool; the source is timings I read off the developer tools built into every browser; the solidity is my own observation on ordinary boards, not a measured study. The ~45 ms figure is the classifier's inference on CPU in the server build (the classifier = the trained defect-spotting model; inference = one pass of it making a prediction; CPU = an ordinary processor rather than a graphics card). Different steps, different builds; I don't quote a browser inference time. [PARTIAL - honestly framed]
7. Was the unfamiliarity the language or the domain? - I already wrote the app's JavaScript; the discomfort was computer vision in a browser - a rendering-adjacent runtime doing numeric work I'd always done server-side in Python (a browser is built to draw pages, not to crunch numbers the way a server is). [SAFE]
8. The vision-LLM repeat - what did that involve? - Same comfort-zone shape: GPT-4o for reading mismatch reports, after weighing GPT-4V (slower, ~8 s vs ~3 s - seconds before each answer arrives), Claude 3 (less mature API - fewer tools for wiring software to call it), Gemini Pro Vision (weaker on small objects), and a local LLaVA (an open AI model I could run on my own hardware instead of online; needed >=8 GB VRAM the machines didn't have - VRAM is a graphics card's own memory). Picked on documented constraints, not my own bake-off. Reading a mismatch went from ~30 s manually to ~5 s (the human's zoom-and-decide time before, the AI's answer time after - not a stopwatch study), correct about 85% of the time by my own rough check - no held-out set (no batch of test examples the model had never seen, which is the fair way to score accuracy), and it ran only in the server build. [SAFE - canonical STORY 8 framing]
9. Did anyone push back? - No. Solo project; inventing a dissent would be the only false thing in this story. The debate I remember is with my own default that CV ships on a server (my instinct was that image tools must run on a central server - the argument was with that assumption). [GAP - stated, not papered]
10. What breaks at 10x the users? - Little, structurally: every user runs on their own machine, so more users load nothing I maintain (ten times as many people means no central system of mine gets busier - each just opens the same file locally). The ceilings are organizational - file distribution and per-machine labels - not compute (the limits are getting the file approved and onto locked machines, not processing power). [SAFE - reasoning, no scale claimed]
11. Do differently? - Shape assertion first (a one-line check that the numbers arrive in the order the model expects - three hours becomes a one-line failure), and start the warping work from a written derivation - I burned time re-deriving what the paper already established (working the maths out myself instead of taking it from the 1989 source). [SAFE]

## Risk Check

1. "40 ms in the browser vs the 45 ms CPU number elsewhere - which is a lie?" - Defensible as told: different pipeline steps in different builds, said exactly that in-core and in FU#6; never quote a browser inference time (the model's own prediction step in the browser - I have no number for it).
2. "'Implemented a 1989 algorithm from scratch' - whiteboard it." (whiteboard it = being asked to reproduce it live) - Needs comfort: I can explain conceptually (control points must land on targets, bending spread as evenly as possible) and show the paper examples I validated against, but I retired the formal matrix algebra from my prep - answer at the level FU#3 gives, don't bluff the derivation.
3. "If the spike failed, what then?" - GAP: no documented fallback; the honest "bounded the unknown" line is the answer - do not invent a plan B.
4. "You claim Learn and Be Curious - example of learning with no deliverable?" - GAP-adjacent: everything I learned here shipped; the one-day spike is the only no-output learning. Say that; don't stretch the Bookstein reading into curiosity-for-its-own-sake (it served a deadline). No feedback-seeking episode exists - never claim one.

# Q22 - tell me about a time you had a disagreement with your manager
**LP:** Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit  **Story:** [GAP] - no documented instance (framework only)

## Core Answer

I'll be honest up front: I don't have a real disagreement-with-my-manager story to tell, and I won't invent one. I built the PCB inspection suite solo, on an internship-led project, so there's no manager-blows-up scene in my record - the closest true things are stakeholder corrections I took well (an engineer telling me my BOM tool silently dropped `R1||R2` variants, and I owned that fix) and the times I committed fully to a decision I didn't pick. In plain words: the PCB inspection suite is software that photographs a finished circuit board - a PCB is the green board inside every electronic device - and checks it against the board's design file. A BOM (bill of materials) is the list of every part that belongs on a board, and my BOM tool read that list. `R1||R2` is how a design file writes "this one spot on the board can be built with either of two parts"; "silently dropped" means my tool just ignored those spots without telling anyone - an error, not a choice. A "stakeholder correction" is simply someone who uses the work telling me I got something wrong.

If you're asking how I'd handle a genuine one: I'd raise it privately, with data, once - explain the risk the way I see it and what it costs the customer - and separate the idea from the person. If the call still goes the other way, I commit to it in full and keep my mouth moving only toward making the chosen path work. "Have Backbone" and "Disagree and Commit" - the two Amazon principles this question targets - are the same coin: argue with evidence while the decision is open, then back the team's choice fully even if it wasn't yours. On this project the version I *can* speak to is the commit half: I proposed one way to parse component variants - that is, one set of rules for reading those "either/or" part notations out of the design file - got corrected on what the factory actually meant, adopted that decision completely, and then generalized past the single case they reported. That's the part I can defend for ten minutes. The part where a manager and I disagree head-to-head - I don't have a real example yet, and I'd rather say that than dress up a stakeholder correction as a boss confrontation.

# Q23 - tell me about a time where you took work outside your responsibility

**LP:** Ownership (primary; touches Deliver Results, Learn and Be Curious)   **Story:** AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 9 - the training-data collector, BGSW PCB inspection suite (solo build)

## Core Answer

Is about the half of the job that nobody wrote down.

I was the sole builder of the PCB inspection suite - the comparison engine and the defect classifier. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside almost every electronic device. The comparison engine is the part that photographs a finished board and finds where it differs from its design file; the defect classifier is a small AI that sorts each problem into a type - wrong part, backwards, missing.) The classifier was blocked on training data: about two thousand component images, none of them labeled. ("Training data" is the set of examples a model learns from; "labeling" means a person writing the correct answer on each image - "good" or which defect - so the model can go through *training*, the process of showing it enough examples that it learns the pattern on its own.) Building the tool to label them was part of my task. What was not part of anyone's task was making sure the labels could be trusted.

So, the tool first. A small Tkinter window (Tkinter is the plain pop-up-window toolkit that ships with the Python language - nothing extra to install): one image, a status bar, and the keyboard. G for good, one through four for the defect types, and it auto-advanced to the next image. A skip key, because an image too blurry to judge should not enter the dataset with a guessed label - skips went to a separate file for later. Sessions were resumable (close it and pick up exactly where you stopped), and the CSV output (CSV is just a plain-text spreadsheet, one row per image) matched the format the training pipeline already read (the software that runs the model's training already expected that file shape), so there was no conversion step. That took labeling from about thirty seconds an image to about three.

Then the part I'd actually call ownership. The task said label fast. It said nothing about trusting the result, and a dataset nobody checks quietly decides how good your model can be. So I labeled the entire set again, a week later, without looking at my first answers, and compared them. I agreed with myself 92 percent. (That number counts one thing only: how often my second, blind pass gave the same label as my first pass - a check that I'm consistent with myself, not proof the labels are right; it came from comparing my own two passes row by row, not any external test.) The eight percent were borderline, and I re-examined every one and picked the primary defect (when a part had more than one problem, the single main one to record), instead of leaving a coin-flip label to train on. I also plotted learning curves while training (a graph of how accurate the model got as it saw more images, which shows the point where extra data stops helping), which gave me a number for when to stop collecting data - the return was flattening, so I closed that round instead of chasing it.

What I took from it: the tool was the easy half, and believing its output is the job. And I assumed a mouse would feel more intuitive - it does, until you're on image five hundred. Keys won, and next time I'd add batch labeling for near-identical crops (batch labeling = labeling a whole group of look-alike images in one action; a "crop" is the cut-out close-up picture of a single part).

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: classifier blocked on ~2,000 unlabeled crops; tool was my task, label trust was nobody's
- Customer: the training pipeline waiting on data - and downstream, engineers trusting the suite's verdict
- Insight: "label fast" was the task; "trust the labels" was the responsibility
- Action (mine): built the Tkinter collector; did all 2,000 labels myself; re-labeled the full set a week later, blind; re-adjudicated every disagreement
- Result: ~30s -> ~3s/image; 92% self-agreement, 8% resolved
- Learning: a tool isn't the outcome - trustworthy data is; keyboard beats mouse at volume; batch labeling was the missing feature

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Was any of this actually outside your responsibility? - The labeling tool itself was on my task list, and I won't claim otherwise. The unassigned half was the trust: no one's task said verify the labels or decide when to stop collecting, and I took both.  [SAFE]
2. Why Tkinter, not a web tool? - Simplest thing that worked: ships with Python, no local server, no browser-compat work. UI polish was the trade-off, and it's fine for a one-person internal tool.  [SAFE]
3. How were the 30s and 3s measured? - 30s was my own stopwatch pass over a handful of images in the spreadsheet flow before I wrote the tool; the ~3s comes from timestamps in the tool's session CSVs. Rough personal timings, not instrumented throughput - the 30s->3s is the per-image speedup, and the ~10h manual figure was its own back-of-envelope I wrote down before building, not that baseline multiplied by 2,000 (that lands near 17h), so call the manual case somewhere around 10-17 hours by my rough estimate. Put the figures plainly: ~30s and ~3s are seconds *per image*, ~10-17 hours is my rough total for doing the whole ~2,000-image set the slow by-hand way, and by the same arithmetic the tool's ~3s over ~2,000 images is on the order of ~100 minutes for the whole set - a derived total from those two numbers, not a single stopwatch run I timed.  [PARTIAL - self-timed, not a study]
4. What does 92% agreement actually prove? - It measures label stability, not correctness (in plain words, "stability" means I'd give the same answer a second time, not that the answer is truly right): same person (me), a week apart, blind to the first pass, compared row-by-row. A consistent bias would survive it. A second labeler would have been the stronger check; there wasn't one on a solo project. The 8% disagreements were borderline and each was re-examined and assigned the primary defect.  [PARTIAL - honest limit]
5. Two defects on one image? - One label per image forces a primary-defect decision - a simplification, since a real component can have both. Genuinely ambiguous ones went to the skip file instead of a guessed label.  [SAFE]
6. Why CSV, not JSON? - Labels are flat: filename, label, timestamp, one row per image. CSV is simpler to write and inspect in Excel; JSON only pays if labels are nested. (In plain terms: CSV is a flat spreadsheet-style file, one row per item; JSON is a nested format meant for programmers - overkill here.)  [SAFE]
7. What did the learning curves say? - 2,000 images put the model at 94% (94% is the share of test images the model gets right, judged on examples it never trained on); doubling to about 4,000 was estimated at roughly 96%, marginal beyond - the number that said stop collecting.  [PARTIAL - curve-based estimate, not a measured sweep]
8. What would you improve? - Batch labeling for near-identical crops (a "crop" is the cut-out close-up picture of a single part): many images were the same component at slightly different angles, so a "label all similar" pass would cut the remaining time further.  [SAFE]
9. Hardest part? - Not the code. The grind: the whole set twice, then re-adjudicating roughly 160 borderline images (re-adjudicating = going back and deciding each one's label again) (~8% of 2,000, arithmetic not telemetry) without just confirming my own first guess.  [PARTIAL - 160 is derived]
10. Was there disagreement with anyone? - Solo builder, so no documented pushback to claim. The real disagreement was with my own first-pass labels on the borderline set.  [GAP - do not invent stakeholder conflict]
11. At larger scale, what breaks? - Self-agreement is the wrong audit with multiple annotators; I'd need inter-annotator agreement on a shared sample plus an adjudication rule before a second person touches the set. (Plain terms: "self-agreement" is whether I match my own earlier answers; "inter-annotator agreement" is whether two *different* people label the same images alike; an "adjudication rule" is a preset way to settle it when they don't.)  [SAFE - framed as what I'd do, not what happened]

# Q24 - tell me about a time you took on something outside your responsibilities

**LP:** Ownership (primary; touches Earn Trust, Customer Obsession) - *the "went beyond the assignment" claim is a GAP; the record frames the transparency work as assigned, not self-taken*   **Story:** No out-of-role event documented. Closest true ownership act: treating the engineers' distrust of the BOM tool (the parts-list checker) as my problem - the `?debug=true` view (a hidden page that shows how the tool reached each verdict) + reconciliation dashboard (a summary screen of mismatches) (STORY 11) - which my own source lists under the assigned Task. Distinct from Q23 (STORY 9 training-data collector)

## Core Answer

I'll start with the honest part: I don't have a documented case of picking up work that plainly wasn't mine. The story I keep reaching for is the transparency layer on the BOM reconciliation tool, and I want to tell it accurately. (BOM = bill of materials, the master parts list for a circuit board; the reconciliation tool is a program that cross-checks that list against the board's design drawing and the real board, then prints a match-or-mismatch verdict for every part.)

The problem was real. I built the reconciliation engine - the program that does that three-way comparison and prints a verdict per component. The engineers used it but didn't believe it. When it flagged a mismatch they couldn't see why, so for anything that mattered they re-checked by hand. I treated that distrust as mine to fix, not theirs to live with. So I built a debug view behind `?debug=true` - a hidden page you open by adding a short piece of text to the tool's web address, which shows the tool's inner workings exactly as it saw them: raw BOM text (the parts list as it was written), the reference after each parsing step (what the program understood at each stage), the layout match (which design item it paired with each part), the rules that fired, and a step-by-step decision tree (the chain of checks that produced the verdict). Plus a reconciliation dashboard with side-wise counters (mismatch tallies for each of the things being compared), status chips (small colored labels showing pass/fail), and severity ranking - ordering problems from worst to least - so clicking a row jumps to the component. In the first week the engineers used it to find two edge cases where my heuristic (rule-of-thumb matching logic) was wrong - both unusual naming conventions, and quick to diagnose because the view exposed the intermediate data. Those two are real events written up in the project record, not a measured rate. After that they stopped double-checking and relied on it for production verification.

That's genuine ownership of the adoption risk - the chance that people simply wouldn't trust or use the tool. But here's why I won't dress it as the answer to your question: my own project notes list the debug endpoint as part of the assigned task. The reflection calls it an afterthought - late, not out-of-scope. So the strongest true claim is "I owned more than the code," not "I took on something outside my responsibilities." **[GAP]** - the real outside-my-job example has to come from my team experience, and I'm bringing one rather than stretching this one.

- Action (mine): built the `?debug=true` per-component decision path (the hidden show-your-work page) and the reconciliation dashboard (221-line `reconciliation.js` - the file of code that powers the report; the line count is a plain code-size fact from my repo, not a performance figure - and `POST /debug`, a separate door other software can call to request the debug data); severity-ranked, click-to-navigate
- Result: two naming-convention edge cases found by engineers in week one (documented events, not a metric); they stopped manual re-checks and used it for production verification
- Learning: own the trust outcome, not just the feature - but label scope honestly; the out-of-role event is a GAP the candidate must fill with a real example
