# Q25 - tell me about a time where you gave someone wrong information

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary); touches Ownership.   **Story:** [GAP] - no documented personal event; honest bridge to documented tool-output behavior + labeled framework.

## Core Answer

[GAP: I have no documented moment where I personally handed someone wrong information, so I won't invent a scene. Here's what I actually have.]

My tools gave the manufacturing engineers - the people on the factory floor who use my software to check circuit boards - wrong information more than once, and that's a fair proxy for how I'd handle it happening in person.

The clearest case was the BOM reconciler. A BOM is the bill of materials: the exact parts list for one circuit board. It compared BOM pin counts (how many metal legs a part has) to layout pad counts (how many solder spots the board has ready for those legs) literally, so on boards with mixed component types it raised false alarms - it flagged a problem where there wasn't one - about 12% of the time: an engineer reading that report believed a part was wrong when it wasn't. That's wrong information in front of a user. I didn't blame the data. I pulled 20 problem BOMs, sorted them into three buckets - footprint (the board's solder pattern for that part) bigger than the part, smaller, or exact - and changed the rule so a bigger footprint became a "review," not a mismatch. False positives dropped under 2%. In plain terms: of 100 problems the tool reported, the ones that weren't real fell from about 12 to under 2 - and those figures are my own manual counts from reviewing the early reports, not something the software tracked automatically. I kept the pin-count signal and owned the leftover false-negative risk - the chance of missing a real problem - instead of deleting it to make the report look clean.

Two smaller patterns. The debug view - a mode that shows, step by step, how the tool read the parts list into the computer - showed raw parse output, so when the parser was wrong, meaning the tool misread the file - it happened twice in week one - the engineer saw exactly where, and I fixed it fast. And the AI analysis, right about 85% of the time, was labeled "AI Analysis" with a confidence number - a score for how sure the AI claims to be - and a correct/incorrect button. Never presented as a verdict.

So if I give someone wrong information directly, my pattern is: say so myself, immediately, before they act on it. Correct it concretely - the right fact and the impact, not a vague sorry. No blaming the tool or the question. Explain where my error came from so they can recalibrate trust - relearn how much to lean on each kind of answer from me. Fix the process so it doesn't recur, and ask them to flag me next time.

That's a real track record of owning wrong information my systems produced, and a stated plan for the interpersonal case I can't claim.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: tools put wrong information in front of engineers; no documented personal wrong-info event. [GAP]
- Customer: manufacturing engineers (factory-floor users) relying on reconciliation reports (parts-list-vs-board checks).
- Insight: wrong information is owned by fixing the rule and making the error visible, not by covering or trimming the signal.
- Action (mine): bucketed 20 false-mismatch BOMs (parts lists the tool flagged wrongly); changed pin-count rule to review-not-mismatch; built debug view; labeled VLM output (the image-reading AI) as suggestion with feedback button.
- Result: false positives ~12% -> under 2%; parsing errors visible instead of silent.
- Learning: transparency + process fix is how I make wrong information right - same steps apply to a personal mistake.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Did you actually give someone wrong information, or is this hypothetical? - No documented personal event; the record is about my tools' wrong output and my handling of it. The interpersonal half is a labeled framework, not a claimed scene. [GAP - acknowledged up front]
2. Why not just tell a story? - A fabricated scene collapses under Bar Raiser probing. Being straight about the gap and showing documented behavior is the Earn Trust answer. [GAP-tagged, defensible stance]
3. Closest real case? - Pin-count rule (comparing a part's metal legs to the board's solder spots): false alarms ~12% on boards with mixed component types; 20-BOM categorization into footprint-bigger / smaller / exact - that is, how the board's solder pattern compares in size to the part's own; rule changed; under 2%. [SAFE - STORY 10 documented]
4. Where do 12% and 2% come from? - From my own review of the mismatch reports in the first weeks - counts off the flagged boards (out of 100 flagged problems, the ones that weren't real dropped from ~12 to under 2), not a telemetry dashboard - software that would count this automatically. 5. How did you correct it with the engineers - apologize? - Made it about the data, not an apology: fixed the rule, shipped the debug view - the step-by-step view of how the tool reads the data - so they could verify reasoning themselves. [SAFE]

Fix the process, then make it observable. [SAFE]

The ~85% is a rough self-assessment, no held-out set - a held-out set is a batch of test examples the AI never saw before, kept back for a fair score; I didn't build one. # Q26 - a time when you had to finish a project quickly to meet a deadline

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary); Deliver Results.   **Story:** STORY 12 (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md) - three tools in production, the eight-week solo delivery.

## Core Answer

The deadline I'd point to is eight weeks to deliver the whole PCB inspection suite - three tools - on my own. (PCB = the green circuit board inside electronic devices; the "suite" = three programs that check a board for build mistakes; "eight weeks" = the calendar window from start to all three running.)

The factory needed three checks covered. Schematic vs EBOM: does the bill of materials match the schematic - the schematic is the design drawing of the circuit, and the bill of materials (BOM for short) is the list of parts the board is built from; this check asks whether the list and the drawing agree. PCB vs Layout: does the physical board match its design file - the blueprint of its physical structure. Good Board vs New Board: does a fresh board match a known-good reference - a board already confirmed perfect. Different inputs, different algorithms (step-by-step calculation rules), different failure modes (the ways each check typically goes wrong) - and I went in with incomplete information. I'd never parsed a Gerber file (Gerber = the standard manufacturing file that tells factory machines where the copper and parts go), and I hadn't used OpenCV.js or TensorFlow.js (a ready-made image-processing library and a ready-made AI-model library, both running inside a web browser).

So I sequenced by dependency and impact instead of designing one perfect unified engine - dependency meaning what has to exist before something else can work, impact meaning how much pain each tool removes. The BOM check went first - biggest pain point, no dependencies - with its parser (the program that reads and translates that file format), a debug endpoint (a small test address that shows what the parser read, so mistakes are visible), and a reconciliation dashboard (a screen listing what matches and what doesn't) out in the first two weeks. PCB vs Layout second, because that's where the hard unknown lived: reading the Gerber files and alignment (shifting a board's photo onto the design picture so matching points line up). Board-vs-board last, because it could stand on the plumbing the first two had already paid for - the shared code, like reading files and lining up images, that later tools reuse for free. Each shipped as a complete, usable slice: one tool engineers could actually use, not three unfinished ones. A half-built unified engine would have delivered nothing at week eight.

The risk I attacked early was Gerber parsing. The spec - the format's rulebook - runs 200-plus pages (counted in the published Gerber specification; a fact about the format, not my estimate), so instead of writing my own parser I found an open-source one - free, community-owned code anyone can use - and integrated it. That bought back weeks of calendar time (my estimate of what hand-writing it would have cost - the math is in follow-up 4) - the Bias for Action call I'd defend hardest, because I didn't need to prove I could write a parser; I needed the tools shipped.

I kept the UX identical across all three - UX meaning what the tool looks like and how you drive it: same drag-and-drop (you pull files into the window), same colors, same export (saving results as a file) - so engineers learned the workflow once and I didn't rebuild the interaction layer - the parts of the software a person touches and clicks - three times. The final two weeks went to the training pipeline (running sessions that taught the engineers to use the tools) and a single-file offline build (one self-contained file that opens in a browser with nothing installed), so the tools ran on factory machines with no network.

All three landed inside the eight weeks. Fifteen engineers across two sites use them - that count comes from who attended my training and got user accounts, remembered, not from a usage dashboard - and they tell me it saves the team around twenty hours a week: total working hours the engineers believed they saved across all three tools, their reported number, not something I instrumented (never measured by the software itself).

What I'd change: get the real Gerber files and sample BOMs (real-world parts lists) in front of me before I estimate. My first risk read was guesswork until I saw the actual formats.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: eight-week deadline (calendar window, stated in the story) for the full three-tool PCB inspection suite (three board-checking programs), solo, with incomplete information (no Gerber experience - the board manufacturing file format; new to OpenCV.js/TensorFlow.js - the browser image-processing and AI libraries).
- Customer: manufacturing engineers at two sites doing schematic/layout/board verification (checking the parts list, the design drawing, and built boards).
- Insight: ship ordered, complete slices by dependency + impact (what must exist first, and what hurts most); kill the biggest unknown early by reuse instead of building it.
- Action (mine): sequenced EBOM -> PCB vs Layout -> board-vs-board; integrated `gerber-parser` rather than writing one; identical UX across tools; training pipeline + standalone offline build last.
- Result: all three tools delivered inside eight weeks; 15 engineers / 2 sites using them (counted from training attendance and accounts, from memory); ~20 hrs/week savings (the engineers' own estimate of team time saved, engineer-reported, not measured).
- Learning: real artifacts before estimates; under deadline, reused beats proven.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Was eight weeks aggressive or padded? - Aggressive against the unknown: new file format (Gerber), two new libraries (OpenCV.js, TensorFlow.js). It landed only because of the sequencing plus reusing the Gerber parser - the original plan assumed I'd write it, which is what made the timeline look impossible. [SAFE]
2. How did you pick the order? - Dependency and impact - what must exist before the next thing works, and which check removes the most pain. BOM check: top pain, standalone. Layout check: steepest learning curve, so second while there was slack. Board-vs-board: heaviest algorithmically (the most calculation involved), but it rode the first two's infrastructure (their shared code). [SAFE]
3. What would you cut if you were going to miss? - PCB vs Layout: most complex, least used. Shipping the other two would have delivered most of the value in roughly half the time, and I'd have phased the third (delivered it later as its own round). "Most of the value in half the time" is my rough estimate, not a measurement. [PARTIAL - self-assessed 80/50-style split from STORY 12]
4. How sure are you about the parser saving weeks? - Estimate, and a counterfactual one - a guess about a road not taken, so no data could ever exist for it: a self-written parser against a 200-plus-page spec versus an existing one I integrated in days ("days" = my recollection of that integration's effort). I'd call it two to three weeks of the eight, but I can't prove the alternative. [PARTIAL - estimate]
5. Where does "twenty hours a week" come from? - Engineers' own recollection in training and follow-ups: per-board BOM cross-checks that took them 20-30 minutes now come back in seconds. To spell it out: the 20-30 minutes is their own estimate of one manual parts-list cross-check per board, and the "seconds" is how fast the tool produces its report; the ~20 hrs/week is their total across all three tools. I never built telemetry on time saved (the software never collected usage or timing data automatically), so I say "they tell me." [PARTIAL - engineer-reported, not instrumented]
6. How do you know 15 engineers at 2 sites? - Headcount from the training sessions I ran and the accounts I provisioned (the user logins I set up for people). It's recollection, not a dashboard. [PARTIAL - qualitative]
7. How did you know each tool was done, not demo-ready? - It passed real boards before hand-off. The BOM reconciler ran a 15-BOM regression suite - fifteen parts lists with known right/wrong answers, re-run to check the tool didn't misbehave - with zero false positives or negatives on first week's real usage (it cried wolf zero times and missed zero real differences across those fifteen), catching three genuine mismatches (real mistakes the tool found on live boards, not test cases); parse of a 2,000-component BOM came in under 200 ms - reading a very long parts list in a fifth of a second. Plain-provenance note: those figures come from my own test suite and first-week use - measured, but self-measured, not audited externally. Adoption is the harder evidence - a demo nobody uses isn't delivery. [SAFE - matches canonical BOM anchors]

Did the AI bits work in the offline build? - No. The GPT-4o component analysis (the AI model that can see images and explain a flagged spot) ran only in the server build (the version hosted on a company computer with network access); the standalone file works with the comparison pipeline alone (the engine that marks differences in red, without AI explanations). I treated the VLM (vision-language model - AI that looks at a picture and describes it in words) as optional so the deadline never depended on network or a third party. [SAFE - canonical STORY 8 anchor]
9. Hardest moment? - Gerber parsing was the risk from day one. If I'd discovered at week six that I couldn't read the format, the deadline was dead. Attacking it in week one with reuse is what I'd repeat. [SAFE]

# Q27 - Tell me about a time when you exceeded expectations.
**LP:** Deliver Results (primary); Insist on the Highest Standards.   **Story:** STORY 6 - the 4-signal PCB-vs-layout comparison engine; VLM kept server-only per STORY 8 anchors; engine numbers = canonical STORY 6 set.

## Core Answer

The tool compared a photographed PCB against its layout design. (PCB = the green circuit board inside electronic devices; the layout design = the drawing the board is built from.) The ask was simple: flag where the board doesn't match. My first version met it literally - grayscale both images (convert them to plain shades of black-and-white brightness), subtract, flag the differences. It caught the obvious defects, and on real boards it cried wolf about 15 percent of the time - almost all false alarms from lighting and sensor noise. (A "false positive" or "false alarm" = the tool points at a spot and calls it bad when the board there is actually fine. "Sensor noise" = random graininess from the camera.) Technically done. Useless on the floor: one bad flag in seven and engineers stop trusting the report and check everything by hand. Then the tool saves nothing.

So I set my own bar: cut the false alarms without losing real catches, and prove it on images where I knew the answer. Nobody asked me to. That gap is the expectation I exceeded.

I rebuilt the comparison as four signals, each one seeing what the others miss. (A "signal" here = one independent way of testing the two pictures against each other, like a different pair of glasses; the "4-signal engine" is just the name for the combination of four of these tests.) Raw grayscale difference catches gross mismatches. CLAHE normalizes local contrast (an automatic brightness-equalizer applied patch-by-patch over the image), so lighting stops registering as a defect and a wrong-value resistor starts to show. A histogram stretch exaggerates near-identical parts (it stretches the spread of light-vs-dark values apart so nearly-identical parts look visibly different). Canny edge maps are immune to brightness - my strongest signal for structural differences like a missing component. (An "edge map" = a black-and-white outline of every shape in the photo; outlines don't change when the lighting does.) Each signal votes; the votes combine into a weighted score (more trustworthy signals' votes count for more), and I left the threshold on a slider (a dial the engineer turns to decide how eager the tool is to cry "mismatch") because the engineer knows the board and I didn't.

Then the hard part: proving it. I built a ground-truth set - a hundred board images with known wrong, missing, and extra components - (a "ground-truth set" = a test collection where the right answers are already written down, so every flag the tool gives can be checked against a known fact) and grid-searched the signal weights against precision and recall (grid search = trying every combination of weights and keeping the best-scoring one; precision = when the tool flags something, how often it's really a defect - not crying wolf; recall = of the real defects, how many it caught - not missing any). False alarms went from about 15 percent to under 3, true catches stayed above 95 ("true catch" / true positive = a real defect the tool did catch), and the best threshold scored an F1 of 0.94. (F1 = one accuracy number that balances not-missing-a-real-defect against not-crying-wolf; 1.0 is perfect.)

I did consider generative AI for the detection itself - the server build of the tool uses a GPT-4o VLM to read mismatch reports. (VLM = vision-language model, an AI that can look at a picture and read it like a person.) But the factory tool ran offline on locked-down machines, and a detector that isn't reproducible can't be audited when a board gets rejected. ("Reproducible" = gives the identical answer every time on the same input; a read-the-picture AI can answer differently on a re-run, so you can't prove why a board was failed.) So the model stayed server-side, where it helps a human read, and the detection stayed classical CV (ordinary image-processing math, not AI - same input, same output, every time).

Two corrections. A fifth signal - frequency-domain via FFT - added compute and no accuracy, so I cut it. (FFT = a transform that views the image as repeating patterns and textures instead of pixels - a different pair of glasses, but it bought nothing here.) And I'd have started from the edge detection instead of the raw difference; that spent my early iterations fixing false alarms I never needed to own.

The ask was a comparison that works. I shipped one the engineers trusted, and the false-alarm rate is the evidence.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: Board-vs-layout comparison cried wolf ~15% of the time -> engineers re-checked everything -> tool saved nothing. (~15% = share of flags raised on boards that were actually fine.)
- Customer: PCB manufacturing engineers on a restricted-network factory floor (suite built solo).
- Insight: The ask was "works"; the actual requirement was "trusted" - false-alarm rate is the business metric.
- Action (mine): Four-signal voting comparison (raw / CLAHE / contrast-stretch / Canny edges); self-built 100-board ground-truth set (test images with the right answers already known); grid-searched weights; threshold left as engineer's slider; VLM kept server-side only.
- Result: False positives ~15% -> <3% at true positives >95% (false positive = flagging a good spot; true positive = catching a real defect); F1 0.94 (P 0.97 / R 0.91) on the 100-board set (P = precision = ~97 of every 100 flags are real problems; R = recall = ~91 of every 100 real problems caught; F1 = the one score balancing both).
- Learning: More signals != better (FFT cut); start from the most robust signal (edges), not the easiest.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What was actually expected of you? - "A comparison that flags mismatches. The one-signal version literally met that. I didn't accept it." [SAFE]
2. How is beating your own bar 'exceeding expectations'? - "The business expectation was inspection time saved. A 1-in-7 false-alarm tool saves zero - engineers verify by hand regardless. Trust was the real deliverable; the false-alarm drop is the proof." [SAFE]
3. Where did the 15% baseline come from? - "I ran the single grayscale-diff version over real photographed boards and counted flags with no defect behind them. Small personal harness - 15% is the order of magnitude that killed the design, not a lab figure." [PARTIAL - engineer-self-measured, small N] (Plain: what it counts = flags on actually-fine spots as a share of all flags; where from = my own hand count over real board photos; how solid = rough order-of-magnitude, not an instrumented study.)
4. How was the final number measured? - "A ground-truth set of 100 board images I prepared myself - known wrong, missing, or extra components. I ran the pipeline across threshold settings and computed precision, recall, F1: 0.97 / 0.91 / 0.94 at the best threshold." [SAFE - candidate's account, personal harness] (Plain: what they count - P 0.97 = about 97 of every 100 flags point at a genuine problem; R 0.91 = about 91 of every 100 planted real defects get caught; F1 0.94 = the single score balancing the two. Where from = my own hand-checked 100-board set. How solid = a real check, but small and self-built, so I present it as my test set, not an industry benchmark.)
5. Why four signals, not three or five? - "Each covers a category the others miss: gross mismatch, lighting-robust difference, subtle appearance difference, structural difference. Three leaves a category open. I tested a fifth - FFT frequency-domain - no measurable gain, so out. Signal quality beat signal quantity." [SAFE] (FFT = viewing the image as repeating texture patterns instead of shapes.)
6. How were the weights chosen? - "Started equal, grid-searched combinations summing to 1.0: raw 0.2, CLAHE 0.3, contrast 0.2, edge 0.3. Edge and CLAHE higher because they were the most reliable on the ground-truth set. Weights live in a config object." [SAFE] (Grid search = try every combination, one by one, keep the winner; the weights are just how much each signal's vote counts.)
7. Where did generative AI actually go? - "The server build uses a GPT-4o VLM to read mismatch reports - cut a ~30-second manual read per item to ~5 seconds, and it got the reading roughly 85% right by my own rough assessment, no held-out set, about a cent an analysis. The offline factory build ran no VLM at all." [PARTIAL - ~85% and 30s->5s are estimates/self-assessment; say so] (Plain: VLM = an AI that looks at a picture and reads it. ~30 s = how long a human took to interpret one flagged item by eye; ~5 s = the computer's reply time, not a human-time before/after. ~85% = how often its reading was right, per my rough tally - a "held-out set" (fresh examples kept back for a fair test) was never built, so it's a judgment, not a measurement. About a cent (~$0.01) = the fee charged per look by the paid AI service. All server-build only.)
8. Why not the VLM for detection? - "Locked-down factory network, and a non-reproducible detector can't be audited when a board is rejected. I made the AI part optional by design - it assists reading, never decides pass/fail." [SAFE] (Non-reproducible = it could answer differently to the same photo on a re-run, so a rejected board couldn't be defended.)
9. Hardest part? - "The ground-truth set. Every one of the 100 boards needed known defect locations, so I built it from controlled photographs with planted mismatches - wrong, missing, extra parts - before trusting any accuracy number." [PARTIAL - supporting account, defensible method] (In plain: I deliberately placed known mistakes on boards, photographed them, and used the answer key to score the tool - so every accuracy number traces back to a fact I set up on purpose.)
10. Disagreement? - "An engineer wanted a fixed strict default shipped. I shipped the slider instead - the right operating point moves with board and lighting, and they, not I, know which. Compromise: a conservative default they can loosen." [PARTIAL - engineer-reported recollection] (The "operating point" = where on the slider the tool sits between too jumpy and too relaxed.)
11. Was it fast enough on the floor? - "About 500 ms per typical board, in-browser, offline - interactive, no server round-trip." [SAFE] (Plain: half a second of computer time to produce the report for one board, on the machine itself - no waiting on any server.)
12. Scale / larger impact? - "It became the comparison core of the offline tool the floor used; time saved is engineer-reported recollection, not instrumented - I'd quote the false-alarm rate, not hours." [PARTIAL - deliberately no invented hours] (False-alarm rate is the one number with a checkable method behind it; hours saved is only what engineers told me.)
13. Do differently? - "Start from edge detection, and build the ground-truth set first - I validated last when I should have validated first." [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "100 images is a small validation set" - defensible as a personal, self-built harness for a solo tool; say so plainly, don't inflate N.
2. "Prove the grid search / show the code" - GAP: a code audit (answers/Q27.md provenance) found thresholds loosened for demo comfort and an unused weight-override path. Stay at the STORY 6 account level; do not offer code-level detail unprompted.
3. "Is the 15% baseline on the same data as the <3%?" - needs honesty: baseline was real photographed boards, the <3%/0.94 came from the 100-board ground-truth set; know this distinction cold or the numbers unravel. (Not the same images: the 15% counts bad flags in everyday use; the <3% and F1 0.94 are scores on my planted-defect test set.)
4. "'Exceeded expectations' = perfectionism?" - defensible: tied to a business consequence (trust -> no time saved), and the bar was set before the result existed.

# Q28 - a time when you had a complex problem where you needed to understand the details, who did you talk to for useful information, and how did you use it?

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary); Learn and Be Curious.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - BOM reconciliation parser, the manufacturing-engineer conversation (PREP STORY 1); spine here is the person consulted and how their input changed the design (Q5 told the trust angle, Q16 the edge-case tour).

## Core Answer

The complex problem was the BOM reconciliation parser in the PCB inspection suite. (PCB = the green circuit board inside every electronic device. Its BOM - Bill of Materials - is the shopping list of every part that belongs on it. The "parser" is the software that reads that list from the file, and "reconciliation" means checking the list against the board's design file.) The detail I couldn't reach on my own wasn't in the data - it was in a person's head on the manufacturing floor.

The tool I built reconciles a Bill of Materials exported from SAP (the business software factories use to run purchasing and production) against the PCB layout (the design file showing where each part sits) and flags components missing, extra, or mismatched - marks them as problems for a human to look at. It worked on most real BOMs I tried, then production files arrived and it broke. Some of the failures were pattern problems - a process-code prefix glued onto references (every part carries a label like R1 for "resistor number 1" - the designator; some files had an internal process code stuck in front of it instead of the bare label), or spreadsheet cells exported as hyperlinks (a cell that came out as a clickable link object instead of plain text, so the software read the wrong thing) - things I could diagnose from raw-cell logs (a dump of exactly what the program saw in each cell) and data audits.

The one I couldn't crack was `R1||R2`. And `R1/R2`. (Variant notation: two part labels joined by double-bars or a slash.) My parser treated them as invalid and silently dropped them - skipped them without any warning. I could see the text; I couldn't see the intent, and no amount of reading the file harder would tell me whether dropping them was right. So I went to the person who knew: a manufacturing engineer who used the tool and had done the cross-checking by hand before it existed.

He explained it plainly. One physical position, either part valid, depending on which board variant you're building (a variant = a version of the same board built with slightly different parts for different products or regions). So `R1||R2` in the BOM against a single layout position is not a mismatch and not malformed - it's a manufacturing instruction. What my parser called garbage was a legitimate assembly rule.

That rewrote that part of the design. I built a variant splitter that normalizes both separators, extracts the individual references, and treats each as a valid match target for the position. (The splitter is a small piece of code that breaks that either-or notation apart: it reads `||` and `/` as the same "either one" mark, pulls out each part label - R1 and R2 - and lets the checker accept either label for that position.) To make sure the fix matched what he actually told me - not what I half-remembered - I made a test matrix (a grid of deliberate cases to check, both valid and broken): `R1||R2`, `R1/R2`, `R1||R2||R3`, plus malformed shapes like `||R1` and `R1/`, checked against a regression suite of fifteen real production BOMs (a standing set of 15 real parts lists re-run after every code change, to catch anything a fix broke). That suite ran with zero false positives and zero false negatives - on that set, it flagged nothing that wasn't a real mismatch and missed no real mismatch - and the tool returned in seconds a report the engineers said took twenty-to-thirty minutes per board by hand (their estimate of their own old manual cross-check, not something I timed). In the first week it caught three real mismatches manual review had missed.

The lesson stuck: diving deep isn't only reading the artifact (the file itself) harder - some detail lives in the person who holds the intent, and one narrow question beats guessing. What I'd change: I found this reactively, after my wrong assumption had already dropped valid parts in production. Next time I sit with the engineers and collect real files before writing the parser.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: BOM-vs-layout (parts list vs design file) parser broke on production files; the hardest failure was semantic - about meaning - not a pattern bug.
- Customer: manufacturing engineers - the people the tool replaced (20-30 min/board manual cross-check, their reported figure - what they told me, not timed).
- Insight: `R1||R2` / `R1/R2` = variant notation meaning one physical position, either part valid by board variant - intent a file cannot show.
- Action (mine): went and asked the engineer; built the variant splitter (breaks either-or notation into the individual part labels, both separators treated alike) normalizing both separators; wrote the variant + malformed test matrix; ran it against the 15-BOM regression suite (the standing real-file test set re-run after every change).
- Result: zero false positives / zero false negatives on the 15-BOM suite (no false alarms, no missed real problems - on that set); report in seconds vs reported 20-30 min; three real mismatches caught week one.
- Learning: some detail lives in the person who holds the intent - ask narrow questions early; my discovery was reactive, next time collect real BOMs upfront.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Who exactly did you talk to, and why him? - A manufacturing engineer who used the BOM tool and had done the board cross-referencing by hand before it existed. He actually knew how variants (the different versions of the same board) get built, so he held the intent behind notation I could only see as text. [SAFE]
2. Why couldn't you work it out from the data alone? - The file gave me the string `R1||R2`, not its meaning. "One position accepts either part depending on variant" is a manufacturing convention - not inferable by pattern matching (checking text shapes against known formats), which is exactly why I needed a person. [SAFE]
3. How did you verify the fix matched what he said? - Test matrix (a deliberate grid of valid and broken cases): `R1||R2`, `R1/R2`, `R1||R2||R3`, and malformed `||R1` / `R1/`, each checked for extracting the right references (part labels) as valid match targets (labels the position is allowed to accept); re-run against the 15-BOM regression suite (the standing set of real parts lists re-checked after every code change) after every change. [SAFE]
4. How did you decide what to solve yourself versus ask about? - Deliberate split (a conscious dividing line between what I could fix from data and what needed a person): pattern problems (`MP_` prefix - a process code stuck in front of a part label; hyperlink cell objects - spreadsheet cells holding a clickable link instead of plain text) I could audit in the data and fix; semantic intent (variant references, what DNP means on the line - "Do Not Populate", the factory's way of marking a position left empty on this version of the board) only the engineers could tell me. [SAFE]
5. Why "either reference matches" instead of flagging variant positions for review? - Either-matches (accepting any of the listed parts as valid for the position) arrived as a stated requirement from the engineer; flagging every variant position would push work back onto the manual queue the tool existed to clear (the backlog of boards a person had to check by hand). Honest gap: my record doesn't show a formal comparison of that alternative. [PARTIAL]
6. What if no engineer had been available? - Default behavior skips anything not matching the standard reference pattern (the plain part-label format the software expects, a letter plus a number like R1), so it degrades instead of crashing - keeps running but quietly skips the odd entries - but that means silently dropping valid components, a worse failure than an error (a silent miss lets a wrong board pass; an error at least gets looked at). Part of why I'd interview users before writing the parser next time. [SAFE]
7. How solid is "worked on most real BOMs"? - Roughly 70% from my early trials against real files - that number counts the share of real parts lists I first tried that processed correctly, and it came from my own early usage, not a survey of a defined file set; a sense from usage, not a surveyed corpus figure. [PARTIAL]
8. How reliable are the result numbers? - All reported or recorded, none instrumented by me (nothing counted by a measuring system I built): the 20-30 min baseline is the engineers' recollection; the three week-one catches are a story-bank record, not an audited count; zero FP/FN is scoped to the 15-BOM suite, not a universal claim - on that one test set there were no false alarms and no missed real mismatches, nothing more. [PARTIAL]
9. Performance? - A 2,000-component BOM parsed in under 200 ms - a parts list for a board with 2,000 parts read and checked by the software in less than a fifth of a second; a recorded single-run figure against my sub-second bar (my own target of under one second), not a benchmark distribution (not a series of many timed runs with averages and worst cases). [PARTIAL]
10. What went wrong? - My own assumption: I'd filed `R1||R2` as garbage (invalid text) and the parser silently dropped valid parts in production (skipped them with no warning, so nobody looked at them). A customer correction caught my mistake - I would not have found it from the data alone. [SAFE]
11. Hardest part? - Admitting the file couldn't answer the question and going to ask, after I'd already shipped the wrong behavior. Also distrusting my own fixtures (the sample files I'd written my tests against) - my test data had no hyperlink cells. [SAFE]
12. Scale / do differently? - One team, one plant, one week of numbers - I won't pretend wider. Differently: collect sample BOMs from the floor and interview users before writing code, not after it breaks. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "How do you know the engineer's explanation was correct?" - defensible: the fix went through a targeted test matrix plus the 15-BOM regression suite with zero FP/FN (no false alarms, no missed real problems - on that set); keep the scope attached to the zero-zero claim.
2. 20-30 min baseline, three week-one catches - engineer-reported / story-recorded, never instrumented (never counted by a measuring system - what people told me and what my notes recorded). Say "reported, not measured" under probing; defensible with the label, GAP without it.
3. The variant splitter itself is not visible in the repo snapshot (the copy of the codebase as filed) - narrative only. GAP: never offer "I can show you the splitter"; talk about the semantics and the correction.
4. Scope: one team, one plant, one week - small. State it up front rather than let the interviewer discover it.

# Q29 - a time when you had a blocker in your work and how did you resolve that blocker?

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary); Deliver Results   **Story:** STORY 4 "The Standalone HTML That Replaced a Server" - the OpenCV.js / WebAssembly load blocker only; a different moment from Q7 (IE11 miss) and Q8 (solo ship) in the same project.

## Core Answer

The clearest blocker I hit was OpenCV.js refusing to boot inside my PCB inspection suite's single-file offline build. (OpenCV.js is the browser image library - a professional image-processing tool that runs inside the web browser instead of being installed on the computer - and "offline" meant the file had to work with no internet at all.) Without it, alignment and comparison - the actual product - never started.

The setup: manufacturing engineers needed the tool on factory-floor machines - no internet, no installs, minimal IT support. The original ran on a Flask server (a small program that hosts the tool on one machine while everyone else opens it over the network), and Python installs (Python being the programming language that server needs) were beyond what the team could do. So I was compiling everything into one HTML file they could double-click. The file built, the UI opened, and the pipeline just sat there dead.

The trouble was how WebAssembly loads. (WebAssembly is a way for a browser to run code written in older, compiled languages at near desktop-program speed - but first it has to receive a binary: a block of compiled machine code.) OpenCV.js is JavaScript plus a binary module, and the loader normally fetches that binary as a separate file - like any web page downloading its pieces from a dedicated file server while it opens, which is what a CDN is. A single offline file has nothing to fetch from. So I separated the two steps: the JavaScript loaded fine, instantiation failed - instantiation meaning the browser turning that block of code into a running module - and reading the loader showed me the fetch. The transport was the blocker, not the library. Shipping a folder of files was off the table - a second file that gets accidentally moved was the exact failure I was eliminating.

The fix removed the fetch. I embedded the binary inside the HTML as a base64-encoded copy - base64 is a way of rewriting any file as plain text so it can live inside a text file - then changed the loader to decode it at runtime into raw bytes and hand them straight to the WebAssembly engine. No network, no extra files: "embedded" meant everything ships inside the one file. Same trick for the machine-learning library - also a browser image/learning library - : inline the bundle, make the weights (the learned numbers inside a model) a constant instead of a sidecar file (a helper file that has to sit beside the main one).

The cost was real and taken deliberately: about 5 seconds to load on a factory machine, versus 2 for the server version. What those count: double-click to a working tool; where they come from: my typical observed startup noted on real machines - stopwatch-grade, not a formal benchmark. A slower cold start on a tool that works offline beats a fast tool that doesn't. And "it runs" wasn't the bar - I ran the same boards I knew through both builds and compared the outputs, by hand plus a small automated diff. By hand means I read the two result sets side by side; the small automated diff was a simple script I wrote to flag any place the two outputs disagreed. They matched, alignment within about a pixel - about one dot on screen - on what I checked.

The result was one file, about 25 megabytes - into the tens of megabytes, because every image and learning part now lives inside it. Engineers double-clicked it - no Python, no server, no IT ticket (no help-desk request) - distributed by email and USB.

The lesson: when a deliverable is blocked, question the delivery mechanism - mine was a transport assumption, not code. And one limitation I accepted too quietly: the file was big enough to hit email attachment caps; compressing the embedded libraries (shrinking the files with standard compression) would have fixed that.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: standalone single-file build shipped with a dead pipeline - OpenCV.js's WASM binary had nothing to fetch from offline, so alignment/comparison (the product) never initialized
- Customer: manufacturing engineers on factory-floor machines - no internet, no installs, minimal IT support
- Insight: split library load from module instantiation - the JS loaded, the binary failed; the transport, not the library, was the blocker
- Action (mine): embedded the WASM binary as a base64 data URL inside the HTML and modified the loader to decode it to an ArrayBuffer at runtime; same pattern for TF.js (inlined bundle, weights as a JS constant); verified by re-running the same known boards through both builds and comparing outputs - by hand plus a small automated diff
- Result: ~25 MB double-click file, no server/install/IT ticket; distributed by email and USB; outputs matched the server build on the known boards re-run through both builds
- Learning: when blocked, question the delivery mechanism before the code; took a slower cold start deliberately; accepted the file-size/distribution limit too quietly

## Follow-Up Bank

1. What exactly was the blocker? - OpenCV.js is a WebAssembly module: its binary loads separately, normally fetched at runtime (the browser downloads the block of compiled machine code when the tool starts, from a file server - the CDN-style fetch a normal web page also relies on). In the single offline file there was nothing to fetch from, so instantiation failed and the alignment/comparison pipeline couldn't start. [SAFE]
2. How did you diagnose it? - Separated the JavaScript load from the WASM instantiation: JS succeeded, instantiation failed. Reading the loader showed it requesting the `.wasm` file over the network. That moved the problem from "broken library" to "missing transport" - from "the tool is broken" to "the tool is fine, it just had no way to receive one of its parts." [SAFE]
3. Why base64 instead of sidecar files or a service worker? - Sidecar files (helper files that must stay next to the main one) break the one-file rule - move one file and the tool dies, the exact failure I was removing. A service worker (a small background program a web page can install in the browser to serve files locally) needs HTTPS (encrypted web traffic) to register and adds compatibility risk on the floor machines. Base64 costs ~33% size overhead (the text version of a binary is bigger than the original) but removes every external dependency. [SAFE]
4. What did the fix cost, exactly? - ~2 seconds of runtime base64 decode on startup (re-translating the text-embedded code back into machine code each time the tool opens); ~12.5 MB of embedded libraries inflating to the ~25 MB file (OpenCV.js alone ~8 MB) - the rest is the machine-learning libraries, the model weights, and the app itself, which together push the single file into the tens of megabytes; recompile takes ~10 seconds (my build script re-assembling the file after a change), mostly the OpenCV file. Recorded figures, not benchmarks - my own notes while building, not instrumented measurements. [SAFE - label on probing]
5. How did you verify the standalone matched the server build? - By hand: I ran the same known boards through both builds and compared the outputs, reading the two result sets side by side, with a small automated diff flagging score mismatches - a simple script I wrote pointing out every place the two outputs disagreed; alignment within about a pixel - roughly one dot on screen - on what I checked. The known-board set wasn't a measured sample, so I quote no parity percentage. [SAFE]
6. Why not escalate to IT for network access? - The blocker sat in my own build pipeline; the offline constraint was the product requirement, not a ticket. Escalating would have added delay without changing the constraint. [SAFE]
7. Can you show me the offline file? - Honest line: it's built from source by my compile script, and the size/load figures are my recorded account of the offline build - my own notes from real use, not instrumented measurements - so I don't offer to open it on the spot. [PARTIAL - artifact can't be produced in the room]
8. Did it run on every machine? - It needed a WebAssembly-capable browser - one new enough to support the browser's fast compiled-code feature - and machines without it got a clear startup error instead of a half-working tool. The environment-assumption miss there is a separate failure story - one cross-reference, no retelling. [SAFE]
9. Hardest part / what almost went wrong? - Resisting the urge to swap libraries. The failure read like an OpenCV bug; the fix was nearly the wrong rewrite. Patience to isolate load vs instantiate - asking "can the browser read the file?" and "can it start the compiled code?" as two separate questions - found the real cause. [SAFE]
10. Do differently? - Compress the embedded libraries from the start: at ~25 MB the file ran into 20 MB email attachment caps (most email services refuse bigger files); gzip on the embedded libs (a standard file-compression method) could have brought it near 15 MB - a distribution problem I accepted when I didn't have to. [SAFE]

## Risk Check

1. "Produce the 25 MB offline file - how do I know it existed?" - PARTIAL: the numbers are the candidate's recorded account of the build (canonical STORY 4 account per bank rules), not an instrumented benchmark, and the artifact isn't shown in the room. Hold scope to "built it, tested it, shipped it"; never upgrade to measured-precision claims.
2. "5s vs 2s - measured how?" - Defensible with label: typical observed startup on factory machines vs the server build, stopwatch-grade, not a distribution. State it exactly once as "about," then move on.
3. "Is 'within a pixel' the tool's accuracy claim?" - No: it's the tolerance of my by-hand, both-builds comparison - the same known boards re-run through each build, outputs checked with a small automated diff - on the boards I checked, not a measured benchmark set. The alignment accuracy story is a different tale. Keep the two numbers in their separate stories.
4. "Why accept a worse load time instead of solving it?" - Defensible: cost was one-time per session against a constraint that blocked the entire deliverable; compression was triaged as "can wait" - and the one thing I'd undo is leaving it there.

## Core Answer

What I can say my record shows work I added, not work I took from someone else.

Built-in example, labeled: I was assigned the offline single-file build of the inspection suite. ("Inspection suite" = my set of tools that check factory circuit boards; "offline single-file build" = a version that runs entirely from one file in a machine's web browser, with no company server and nothing to install.) On my own initiative I added save-failure protection against the browser storage cap, and I personally got the file onto the factory machines by email and USB. (A browser only lets a tool save a small amount of data on one computer; when that space fills up, saving fails quietly. My protection made the tool notice and handle that, so results weren't lost without anyone seeing.) Nobody told me to do those parts. But nobody had them either - the docs never show a responsibility line I stepped over, so I won't call it "outside my role." Volunteering inside your own deliverable is a different, weaker claim, and I'd rather say that plainly than have it fall apart when someone asks the obvious question: whose job was it before you?

A real answer to this question needs one event with a boundary in it: the role line as it actually stood -> the gap I saw - unowned, or owned by someone else -> why I took it anyway -> what it cost me -> what happened -> what I learned about where my line should sit.

If I can't produce that event, the spoken answer is the concession above - the honest admission that the event doesn't exist - then ask whether the volunteered-extras pattern satisfies what they're probing. Ownership LP (Amazon's "Ownership" leadership principle: going beyond the job description without being asked) can still register on that honesty; an invented boundary-crossing will not survive ten minutes of questioning (the deep follow-up an Amazon Bar Raiser interviewer applies).

# Q31 - tell me about a time when you had to finish a project quickly to meet a deadline

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary - removed the schedule-threatening manual step fast, small right tool over a perfect one); Deliver Results (secondary - final milestone landed inside the eight-week window).   **Story:** STORY 15 "Compiling a Full Stack into a Single File" (build turnaround under deadline), artifact facts from STORY 4; distinct from Q26 (eight-week scope) and the five-day prototype (Q13/Q18/Q19).

## Core Answer

The deadline was the last milestone of an eight-week solo project: ship my PCB inspection suite as one standalone HTML file - no server, no network - that factory machines could just open. Weeks seven and eight. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside electronic devices; the suite is my browser-based tool that checks a made board against its design files. "HTML file" is the ordinary format a web browser opens, and "standalone" means everything the tool needs - code, styling, the trained model - is packed inside that one file, so opening it is enough. Weeks seven and eight.)

The threat to the date wasn't code. It was packaging. The tool normally lives as many separate source files, and turning them into that one file was manual: I concatenated the files by hand (pasted them end to end), inlined the CSS and JavaScript (pasted the styling rules and the program logic directly into the file instead of linking to them from elsewhere), base64-encoded the libraries (converted the non-text parts into plain text so they fit inside a text file), checked the result. Each run of this was a "build" - one pass that produces the finished file. About 30 minutes a build, and it broke roughly one time in five - I'd inline a file in the wrong order or miss one, and the failure only showed up when a manufacturing engineer opened the file. And I rebuilt again and again as I fixed things across the suite. So 30 minutes at a one-in-five failure rate was eating the calendar and shipping defects into the deliverable itself. (What those numbers count and how solid they are: 30 minutes is my typical working time per build and one-in-five is the share of hand-builds that broke - both my own recollection from the weeks of doing it, not logged or measured data; the basis is in the follow-ups.)

So I stopped packaging by hand and wrote the compiler - here just a small program that does the packaging automatically: source files in, finished file out, not a language compiler in the C++ sense. About 200 lines of Python (a plain, readable programming language), three stages: collect every HTML, CSS, JS, and library file; process each by type - CSS into style tags, JS into script tags in dependency order (each piece placed before the code that calls it), binaries base64-encoded (text-converted so they fit); assemble the document. Two details mattered. Ordering: the build reads a manifest - a simple checklist file stating exactly what goes in and in what sequence: CSS before the HTML that uses it, utility scripts before the business logic that calls them - instead of trusting the filesystem's order (the arbitrary sequence the computer happens to list files in), which is what had been biting me. And traceability: it stamps the git commit hash - a version fingerprint from the tool that tracks my code history - into the HTML title, so I could tell which build any file in the field came from.

The result: a build in about 8 seconds that stopped failing on ordering. Before, about 30 minutes and one failure in five; after, 8 seconds and zero. (What this counts and how solid it is: the 8 seconds is my stopwatch average over release builds, and "zero" means zero of that one wrong-order-or-missing-file failure class since the checklist took over - small samples, stated as estimates, not logged metrics; method in the follow-ups.) The artifact itself - the shipped file - is unchanged: the same roughly 25MB single file, that is, one file in the tens of megabytes: big for a web page file, nothing a factory PC can't store and open, and it runs the whole suite offline.

The call I'd defend: a 30-minute manual step that repeats under a deadline is a schedule problem, and it was worth an hour of tooling - the compiler paid for itself by the second build. And I kept it simple: string manipulation (the program just pastes text into a template), not a Webpack setup (Webpack being the heavyweight industry-standard packaging tool for large web projects). What I'd add now is a checksum on the output (a content fingerprint, so accidental corruption becomes obvious) and a diff mode between builds (an automatic side-by-side comparison of two finished files), so a corrupted file gets caught by the tool instead of by me.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: the weeks-7-8 standalone milestone was gated by a ~30-min manual packaging step that failed ~1 in 5 builds (my recollection, not logged) - eating calendar and leaking order/missing-file defects (a part inlined in the wrong sequence or skipped entirely) into the artifact (the shipped file)
- Customer: manufacturing engineers opening one file on locked-down factory machines (machines where users cannot install anything) - no server, no network, no installs
- Insight: under a deadline, a repeated error-prone manual step is a schedule problem, not a chore to absorb - an hour of automation is cheaper than one missed date or one bad field build
- Action (mine): wrote `compile_tool.py` (~200-line Python): collect -> process-by-type -> assemble; manifest-driven inline ordering - the manifest being the ordered checklist of what goes into the file (CSS before HTML, utilities before business logic); OpenCV.js WASM loader patched to decode at runtime (WASM = WebAssembly, the fast binary format browsers execute; its loader was changed to decode the copy stored inside the file instead of fetching a separate one); git commit hash - a version fingerprint - stamped into the HTML title for build traceability (knowing which build a field file came from)
- Result: ~30 min and ~1-in-5 failures -> ~8 s and zero of that failure class (stopwatch-timed, small samples, scoped to the ordering class); artifact unchanged (~25 MB single file - tens of megabytes, large for a web file but routine for a PC - full suite offline)
- Learning: automation pays back immediately when the manual step repeats; get correctness controls (ordering, stamp) first, name the assurance (checksum, diff mode) as deferred debt

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Was there a real deadline, or did you decide it was urgent? - The eight-week delivery window is documented and the standalone compilation (building the one-file, no-server version) was the weeks-seven-and-eight milestone. The compiler wasn't an external demand - I decided the turnaround was a risk worth removing to protect the date. I say that plainly rather than dress it as an imposed deadline. [SAFE]
2. Why not Webpack or a real build tool? - The logic is string manipulation - no module bundling (automatically weaving many code modules together), minification (squeezing code smaller), or source maps (lookup tables that map squeezed code back to the original for debugging). The script is about 200 lines and does exactly what the artifact requires; Webpack adds config, plugins, and a learning curve for a step that runs once before each release. [SAFE]
3. Where do 30 minutes and one-in-five come from? - Honest labels: both are my personal recollection from the weeks of hand-builds, roughly 15-20 of them before I wrote the compiler, with three or four order/missing-file breaks - a file pasted into the wrong sequence or skipped - that surfaced when a file was opened in the field (on an engineer's machine). One-in-five is that remembered fraction - no logs, no instrumented rate (nothing automatically counted it; I'm estimating from what I lived through). The 30 minutes is the typical wall time I worked to. [PARTIAL - recalled, small sample]
4. And the 8 seconds and zero? - Timed by hand with a stopwatch across release builds: ~8 s average, ~12 s worst case on a slow disk; the bottleneck is reading and base64-encoding (text-converting) OpenCV.js - the biggest embedded library, the image-processing "eyes" of the comparison - at about 8 MB. Zero means zero order/missing-file failures since the manifest drove the build - small n (only a handful of builds watched), and it's a failure class removed by construction - the fix's design makes that mistake impossible, not merely unlikely - not a universal defect guarantee. [PARTIAL - stopwatch-timed, scoped claim]

It reads the order from a manifest (an ordered checklist of what goes in), not the filesystem - that's what removed the ordering failures - and stamps the git commit hash (a version fingerprint from my code-history tool) into the title. [SAFE]

The rest of the file is the model weights (the trained classifier's learned data) plus the app itself - embedding the browser libraries together with the weights and the app is what pushes the single file into the tens of megabytes; the ~25 MB is one soft overall figure, not a sum to be multiplied. It loads in roughly five seconds on a factory machine against about two on the server version, and runs the full suite - BOM reconciliation (matching the board's actual parts against its bill of materials, the official parts list), layout comparison, alignment, ML inference (the trained model judging a photo), auto-save - with no network. [SAFE - canonical STORY 4 artifact account]
8. Hardest part? - Not the compiler. The diagnosis. Under deadline pressure every instinct says write more code, not spend an hour of calendar on tooling. I had to treat the packaging step itself as the deliverable's risk (the thing most likely to make me miss the date was the packaging, not the product). [SAFE]
9. Any disagreement with stakeholders? - Solo project; I won't invent a scene. The argument I actually had was with my own default - absorbing a 30-minute manual step because "we're almost done." [GAP - no documented conflict, stated plainly]
10. Main trade-offs? - An hour of automation against immediate progress (paid back by the second build); a 200-line script against a bundler toolchain (a heavyweight packaging system); correctness controls done now (ordering, version stamp) against assurance deferred (checksums - content fingerprints that catch corruption - and diff mode - automatic file-vs-file comparison) and named as debt. [SAFE]
11. Would this scale to a team or a pipeline? - The compiler is plain Python with a manifest - it drops straight into CI (continuous integration: a team's system that automatically rebuilds and checks the software on every code change), and the ordering and commit-stamp are exactly what a release process would enforce. My read, not something I built or load-tested. [PARTIAL - qualitative]
12. Do differently? - Ship the checksum and the two-build diff mode with the compiler, so a corrupted or silently changed build is caught by the tool instead of by me - and build the parity harness (an automated checker that runs both versions side by side and proves the outputs match) before the deadline, not after. [SAFE]

# Q32 - tell me about a time you had to earn the trust of a skeptical colleague

**LP:** Earn Trust.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the manufacturing engineers who didn't trust the BOM tool's verdicts, and the debug-view transparency layer that changed that (PREP STORY 11, with the reliability half from STORY 1).

## Core Answer

The people I had to win over were the manufacturing engineers who used my BOM reconciliation tool. (A BOM - "bill of materials" - is the parts list for a circuit board; "reconciliation" means cross-checking that list against the board's design.) I built the inspection suite solo, so their skepticism came from the floor, and they had good reason. The tool compared a bill of materials against the layout - the design drawing that shows where each part goes - and printed a verdict, a pass-or-fail call, but it showed the conclusion and hid the reasoning. When it flagged a part as a mismatch, the engineer couldn't see why. So for anything that mattered they re-checked by hand - exactly the work the tool was supposed to replace. A verdict you can't check is a verdict nobody trusts.

The naive parser - the first, plain version of the program that reads the parts list - handled maybe 70% of real BOMs: roughly seven of ten actual files it read correctly, and that's my rough sense from early use, not a counted study. It then broke in production one edge case at a time - an oddball input the code hadn't met: process-code prefixes glued onto references (manufacturing codes stuck in front of a part's label, like a code bolted before "R1"), cells exported as hyperlinks (list items that arrived as clickable links instead of readable text), variants like `R1||R2` (one spot on the board that can hold either of two interchangeable parts - the double-pipe is the list's way of writing "this or that"), DNP positions left empty on purpose (DNP = "Do Not Place": a part listed but deliberately not fitted on some board versions). I fixed each at the root, backed every change with a fifteen-BOM regression suite - a fixed set of fifteen real parts-list files that every future change has to pass, so nothing that worked before can silently break - and got to zero false positives and false negatives on those files: on that set, no good part wrongly flagged and no bad part missed. Necessary - but it didn't touch the real complaint. They still couldn't see why a flag was a flag.

So I built them the view. In debug mode - a hidden diagnostic screen that shows the tool's working, not just its answer - it showed, per component, the raw BOM text (the parts-list line before any processing), what the parser extracted after each cleanup step, which layout entry it matched, and the exact rules that fired - which specific checks caused the flag - plus a decision tree: reference valid? matching layout entry? pin count acceptable (does the part have the right number of electrical connection legs)? type correct? My rule was simple: if an engineer asks why the tool flagged something, the view has to answer completely. If a step were missing, they'd just have to ask me instead - and a tool you fact-check with me isn't trusted.

That changed behavior, not words. In the first week they used the debug view to find two real edge cases - unusual component naming the parser handled wrongly - and I fixed both. Then the hand-verifying stopped being universal: they relied on the tool for production verification - the checks on boards actually being manufactured, not trials. They used my tool to find where my tool was wrong, and trusted me to fix it.

What I'd do differently: their skepticism was predictable, and I treated transparency as an afterthought. Trust came from making decisions auditable, then making good on the fixes they surfaced. The next automation I build makes its reasoning checkable from the first commit - the very first saved version of the code.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: The BOM tool printed verdicts (pass/fail calls) but hid its reasoning; engineers re-checked everything by hand and wouldn't rely on it for critical decisions.
- Customer: The manufacturing engineers on the floor who used the tool - I built the suite solo, so this was my daily trust relationship.
- Insight: Accuracy alone doesn't buy trust - verifiability does; a verdict you can't check is a verdict nobody relies on.
- Action (mine): Root-cause parser fixes behind a 15-BOM regression suite (fifteen fixed test files every change must pass) - zero FP/FN (no false alarms, no missed defects) on that suite; per-component debug view (hidden diagnostic screen) exposing raw text -> each parse step -> matched layout entry -> rules fired -> decision tree (a chain of yes/no checks); rule: the view must fully answer "why" without me.
- Result: Two naming edge cases (unusual part-name formats) surfaced by them via the debug view in week one, both fixed; they shifted from hand-verifying everything to relying on the tool for production verification (checks on real manufactured boards).
- Learning: Build the transparency layer day one, not after the skepticism; trust = auditable decisions plus making good on the fixes they find.

## Follow-Up Bank

Even correct verdicts got re-checked by hand, because they had no way to know when the tool was wrong. The view answered the real objection: not "trust the black box" (a system whose inner workings you can't see), but "here's how you check it." [SAFE]

Showing an engineer which rule fired beats asserting the result is correct. [SAFE]

# Q33 - tell me about a situation where you had to dig deep, what was the outcome, how did you know you were focusing on the right thing, would you do anything different?

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary; touches Learn and Be Curious, Deliver Results)   **Story:** AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 9 - the data-analysis half: learning-curve read + label self-agreement audit (defect classifier, solo build)

## Core Answer

I'd point to the stretch where I stopped trying to make my PCB defect classifier better and spent the time figuring out what was capping it. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside almost every electronic device. The "classifier" is the part of my tool that looks at a photo of a board and sorts any fault it finds into a kind - missing part, wrong part, damaged part.)

The classifier sat at 94% on a holdout of roughly 300 images, split from about 2,000 labeled component images. In plain terms: it got 94 right for every 100 photos it had never seen before. (A "holdout" is a batch of examples deliberately set aside and never used for training - the final exam, so the score can't come from memorizing the answer key. "Labeled" means each photo had its correct answer written on it, by me, by hand. The 94% is measured on that exam - a real number, and every other figure in this story starts from it.) The obvious next move was more model work - a different architecture, learning-rate schedules, more epochs - which in everyday words means: swap in a fancier model design, adjust the training dials, run more passes over the same data. I held off, because I didn't know what the limit was. The question I dug into was narrow: is 94% a model-capacity ceiling or a data ceiling? Capacity ceiling = the model itself is too simple and needs a bigger "brain"; data ceiling = the photos are too few or too messy, and no smarter model would help. Those call for completely different work.

So I measured two things.

First, learning curves during training - validation performance against how much training data went in. A learning curve is a simple chart: feed the model more and more training photos, and plot its score on the set-aside practice photos after each step. The curve is the diagnostic: where it flattens, adding capacity buys less than adding data - a bigger model is wasted effort, more or cleaner photos are what pay off. Ours had flattened, and reading it gave me an estimate - doubling from 2,000 to about 4,000 images would land near 96%, and past that the gain looked marginal. About that 96%: it's a projection read off the shape of the chart - what the curve suggests would happen - not a model I actually trained at 4,000. Solid as a planning number; not a measured result. A number for the next labeling push, not a feeling.

Second - the part I'd almost skipped - I audited the labels. I'd made every one of them myself, so trusting the set was tempting. Instead I re-labeled the whole dataset a week later, without looking at my first answers, and compared. That check is called label self-agreement: how often I still agree with myself. I agreed with myself 92% of the time. What that counts: the share of the ~2,000 photos where my second answer matched my first; where it came from: my own blind re-label, a week apart; how solid: an actually-counted figure, but it measures whether my labels are consistent, not whether they're right. One label in twelve wasn't reproducible. And if I can't label the same image twice, the model can't be expected to learn that distinction - so part of that flattening was noise in the data - unclarity in the "correct" answers themselves - not capacity in the model. I went back through the 8% one by one and assigned the primary defect - when a photo could count as two kinds of fault, I picked the dominant one - so the set that trained the model was one I'd re-audited.

That combination is how I knew I was on the right thing. The curve gave the direction and size of the payoff; the audit showed part of the ceiling was label quality - a different fix from more labels or a bigger model. So I stopped treating model tuning as the bottleneck and pointed effort at the data.

What I'd do differently: batch labeling for near-identical images. Many crops were the same component at a slightly different angle, and near-duplicates add images, not information - exactly the padding that makes a learning curve look rosier than the data behind it: more photos to count, but nothing new to learn from.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: classifier plateaued at 94% (300-image holdout from ~2,000); next step unclear
- Customer: the inspection suite's verdicts - engineers trusting a model whose real limit was unknown
- Insight: "is 94% a capacity ceiling (model too simple) or a data ceiling (not enough or too-messy photos)?" - the two call for different work, so measure before tuning
- Action (mine): plotted learning curves; re-labeled the full set a week later, blind to pass one (without seeing my own first answers); re-adjudicated every disagreement to the primary defect (the dominant fault when a photo could count as two)
- Result: curve read - 2,000->94%, ~4,000->~96% (estimate), flat beyond; 92% self-agreement (re-label matched my first answers 92% of the time - consistency, not correctness), 8% resolved; effort moved from tuning to data quality
- Learning: audit your own labels before blaming the model; near-duplicates pad a curve without adding information (more photos counted, nothing new learned)

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What did the learning curves actually show? - We were in the flattening part: marginal value per extra image was shrinking - each new photo moved the score less than the last. (Learning curve = accuracy on the set-aside practice photos, plotted as you add more training photos.) Reading the curve gave the estimate - 2,000 -> 94%, doubling to ~4,000 -> about 96%, marginal beyond. That turned "collect more data?" into a number.  [PARTIAL - curve-based estimate, not a trained 4,000-image model]
2. Did you ever verify the ~96% by actually training on 4,000? - No. It's a read off the curve - extrapolated from the chart's shape, not a measured result - and I'd present it that way. The decision it supported - stop collecting at that regime - held either way, because the cost side was clear on its own.  [PARTIAL - honest estimate]
3. 92% agreement with yourself sounds low. How did you use it? - As a ceiling, not trivia. If one label in twelve changes a week later, that fraction is genuinely ambiguous and no model can learn a distinction I can't make consistently. (Self-agreement = how often a second, blind re-label by the same person matches the first - like taking the same test twice and seeing if your answers stick.) Part of the plateau was label noise, so the next move was data quality, not architecture. All 8% were re-examined and assigned the primary defect.  [SAFE]
4. Does 92% prove the labels are correct? - No - it measures stability, not correctness. Being sure twice isn't being right; a consistent habit of mislabeling the same way would pass this test untouched. Same labeler (me), a week apart, blind to the first pass. A second labeler - another person labeling the same photos so we could compare - would be the stronger check; there wasn't one on a solo project.  [PARTIAL - honest limit]
5. How do you know the model wasn't just under-trained? - I measured both sides instead of assuming. (Under-trained = the model simply hadn't learned enough yet - a training problem rather than a data problem.) Curve flattening is the signature of data-limited, not capacity-limited - a chart that goes flat says the photos, not the model's size, are the lever; the label audit independently showed the data itself carried noise. Two measurements pointing at the data is why I redirected effort there rather than running another tuning sweep.  [SAFE]
6. Why stop near 4,000 instead of collecting more? - Return versus cost. Past the flat part of the curve the gain is marginal, and labeling (~3 seconds an image - my own stopwatch timing for writing one answer onto one photo) is the cheap half - finding and cropping new board images takes far longer. Stop when the curve flattens, not when the count looks impressive.  [PARTIAL - 3s is my own timing]
7. Where did the 94% come from? - A holdout of roughly 300 images, a 70/15/15 split of the ~2,000-image set - meaning I divided the ~2,000 photos into 70% to teach the model, 15% to fine-tune it along the way, and the last 15% (~300) kept back untouched as the final exam. That's the number the curve read starts from.  [SAFE]
8. Weren't the labels just your own opinion? - They were, which is exactly why I tested their reproducibility instead of trusting them. Genuinely ambiguous images went to a skip file (a parked folder for "I can't honestly answer this," instead of a guessed label); the 8% disagreements were resolved one by one to the primary defect.  [SAFE]
9. How is this different from the training work where you improved accuracy? - That was model-side - what the network adapts and how. This was data-side - whether the data could support a better model at all. The decision here came from the curve and the audit, not a hyperparameter change (not fiddling with the model's training dials).  [SAFE]
10. Who pushed back on your conclusion? - Solo builder, so there's no documented stakeholder pushback to claim. The real disagreement was with my own first-pass labels on the borderline set.  [GAP - do not invent conflict]
11. Hardest part? - Not the analysis. The grind: the whole set labeled twice, then re-adjudicating roughly 160 borderline images (~8% of 2,000 - arithmetic, not telemetry: figured by percentage, not counted by any system) without just confirming my first guess.  [PARTIAL - 160 derived]
12. What breaks this approach at larger scale? - Self-agreement is the wrong audit with multiple annotators - my agreeing with myself says nothing about whether two different people see the same fault. I'd want inter-annotator agreement on a shared sample (how often two people label the same set of photos alike) plus an adjudication rule (who settles the disagreements and how) before a second person touches the set.  [SAFE - framed as what I'd do]

## Risk Check
1. "The ~96% at 4,000 - measured or guessed?" - Defensible only as labeled: an estimate read off the curve (a projection from the chart's shape), never a trained result. Must correct any reframing as "measured impact" on the spot.
2. "92% - so your labels were 92% right?" - No: stability, not correctness - it only shows my answers didn't move in a week, not that they were true; same labeler; no second annotator on a solo project. This is the weakest joint - answer it honestly, don't inflate it.
3. "Isn't this the same STORY 9 you told for Ownership?" - Defensible: different LP and different evidence role. Here the analysis is the subject; no tool-UI, no assigned/unassigned framing (that was the Ownership story's angle on the same project).
