# Q34 - tell me about a time where you introduced a new process and why was it not already in place at your company ?

**LP:** Invent and Simplify (primary - made testing structurally possible before mandating it; complexity deliberately avoided); Ownership (strong - solo project, the gap was mine to notice and close).   **Story:** the audit finding that my codebase was untestable by construction - zero tests, 67 blocking browser popups, files that touch the live page at load - and the headless-core + known-input regression + escape-everything process I introduced as the response (BAR_RAISER_TECHNICAL_PREP.md Finding 6, :231-241); distinct from Q85 (the same audit's scoring-metric finding) and Q46 (the verification-checklist rule).

## Core Answer

The process I introduced was a regression harness - a fixed set of inputs with known-correct answers, re-run on every change - plus the step that made it possible at all. Why it wasn't in place: the codebase could not have had tests. Not skipped. Could not.

I built the PCB inspection suite alone - the tools that compare a photo of a circuit board against its design. After a while I audited the repo and counted what was there: no package file, no test file, zero tests. My first read was that I'd been undisciplined. The second read was harsher and more useful: testing had been architecturally impossible. There were 67 alert() calls - blocking popups that freeze the page until a human clicks OK, so no automation gets past the first. The analysis functions read the page directly - grabbing live elements, writing results into a shared global. And the module holding shared state queries the page at load, registers listeners, even implements a magnifier - import it outside a browser and it dies on line one.

The real cost of no tests showed up when I traced a scoring bug: the similarity scorer was padding images to equal size, and the padding quietly poisoned its numbers on letterboxed boards. The bug had survived because nobody - me included - could write a test for a scoring function without a browser. The scorers themselves were already pure functions: images in, number out. They were just trapped in files that touched the page at import time.

So the process had two parts, in that order. Make testing possible first: pull the pure scoring functions into a headless core - code that runs with no browser open - a mechanical change, not a rewrite. Then lock behavior down: the known-input regression set, run on every change, so fixing one format can't silently break another. One more rule came out of the same audit: one line puts a part label parsed from a customer design file straight into live page markup - untrusted text executed as page content, an injection risk - so the process requires every string from a parsed file to be escaped before it touches the page.

What I stopped doing: treating "add tests" as a willpower goal. It's an architecture question. When nobody can test something, find the thing that makes testing impossible, fix that, then write the test.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: solo-built browser tool with zero tests, 67 blocking popups, DOM (live page) touched at import - regression testing impossible by construction; a padding bug in a scoring function survived because it could not be unit-tested
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers on whose machines a silently-wrong build lands with no network, no tools, no IT to ask
- Insight: "add tests" fails when the architecture forbids tests; the process starts with making testing mechanically possible (pure functions pulled into a headless core), then keeps them pure via a known-input harness
- Action (mine): the audit (counts, import-time DOM, innerHTML interpolation of parsed CAD labels - all recorded); defined the headless-core extraction rule; introduced the known-input regression harness run on every change; added the escape-all-parsed-text-before-DOM rule
- Result: a repeatable pre-release check where none could exist before; the injection path and the un-importable module documented and gated by rule [PARTIAL - landing details below]
- Learning: when a practice is missing, ask whether the structure forbids it before blaming discipline; processes for correctness beat heroics at review time

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Where do "zero tests" and "67 alert()" come from? - My own audit of the repo: no test file anywhere, 67 alert() calls counted across the deployed tool folders, analysis functions reading page elements and writing a global results variable - all line-referenced in the audit notes. Counts at audit time, not a CI statistic. [SAFE]
2. Why wasn't this already in place at the company? - The suite was a solo build; company practice never entered the picture. The deeper answer: the tools were browser-first by requirement (they run offline inside one page), and browser-first done naively means page access at import time, which makes any test framework choke before a line of logic runs. The absence was an architectural symptom, not a culture one. [SAFE]
3. What exactly is the process, not the script? - Three rules a person follows: pure logic lives in files that never touch the page at load; a fixed known-input set re-runs on every change and must stay green; no text that came from a parsed customer file enters the page unescaped. The harness is enforcement, the rules are the process. [SAFE]
4. Which functions moved to the headless core? - The four similarity scorers (structure, edge, histogram, shape-description comparisons) were already pure (image pair in, number out) - the extraction was mechanical. That's why I frame the fix as architecture, not rewrite. [SAFE]
5. Does the harness exist in the repo today? - The checked-in snapshot at audit time still had no test files - the harness is the corrective I introduced as the go-forward rule; I tell it that way and never offer to show committed test files from the audited snapshot. [PARTIAL - corrective introduced, snapshot doesn't show it landed]
6. What's the injection line exactly? - Analysis code interpolated a component label parsed from a customer CAD (design) file straight into innerHTML - the browser's "insert page markup" call. If a label contains markup, the browser executes it. Fix: treat every parsed string as untrusted and escape it before display. [SAFE]
7. Alternatives rejected? - Bolting a browser-automation framework on top (runs the whole page headlessly - works, but pays browser setup per test and still can't import the module); and "just add a test file someday" (fails on the import-time DOM). Extraction beat both. Reasoning, not a measured bake-off. [PARTIAL]
8. Who adopted it? - One engineer: me. The value at handoff is that release claims stop depending on my memory. I don't dress a solo habit up as an org rollout; on a team I'd add a reviewable diff for the input set and CI (an automated pipeline that re-runs checks on every saved change). [PARTIAL - honest solo framing]
9. What would you do differently? - Keep the core headless from day one and put the page behind a thin shell, instead of discovering that every correctness function is welded to the browser. The alert() popups were meant as user feedback; they should have been one notification component from the start. [SAFE - reasoning]

## Risk Check
1. "Did you actually build the harness, or is this your own audit's prescription?" - Biggest challenge. Honest status: audit facts (zero tests, 67 popups, import-time DOM, injection line) are verifiable in the snapshot; the extraction rule and escape rule are mine and landed as process; the committed test files post-fix - GAP, present as corrective introduced, never as shipped artifacts. [PARTIAL]
2. "67 - instrumented?" - Recountable from the repo text itself; it counts alert() call sites in the deployed folders. Defensible.
3. "Is a solo habit a 'process'?" - Defensible as framed: the answer states it was a solo project up front, defines the process as three rules plus enforcement, and claims no rollout. Never invent a campaign. [PARTIAL by design]

# Q35 - a time when you worked on something outside your comfort zone

**LP:** Learn and Be Curious   **Story:** Tab Scroller (personal Chrome extension, Manifest V3 + LLM command layer) - distinct axis from Q21's vision-math learning

## Core Answer

The hardest part about building Tab Scroller wasn't any one feature. It was that I left the kind of program I actually knew. Everything I'd built before was a single self-contained page - one document, one context, deterministic in, deterministic out. This was a Chrome extension, Manifest V3, and it broke both assumptions at once: my program doesn't stay alive, and a language model sometimes decides what happens next.

I found the first problem the hard way. The feature was tab snoozing - close a tab now, it reopens at a time you pick. My first version set a timer inside the background script, which looked right in testing. Then I closed the browser and the snoozed tabs never came back. In MV3 the background script isn't a process you own; the browser tears it down whenever it likes, and my timer died with it. So the climb was learning to trust state I don't hold. I rebuilt it on chrome.alarms - a one-minute tick the browser owns - and moved the snoozed tabs into extension storage as url, title, and wake time, re-opening them as background tabs when the time comes. It survives restarts because nothing depends on my code being alive at the wrong moment.

Then came the AI command layer, which was its own discomfort. You type "close all my YouTube tabs" and the model maps words to a browser action. The output isn't a number on a screen - it's something that can erase your work, and a confident wrong answer is destructive. The local model I tested was flakier than I expected too; it sometimes wrapped its JSON in polite prose and my parser choked. Temperature zero and a fallback that digs the JSON out of the text fixed that, but it taught me not to give the model the whole blast radius. Simple commands are answered by local rules and never reach a model; what does reach it sees only a pre-filtered slice of relevant tabs.

What I can do now that I couldn't before: design for a program that might not be running when it's needed, and treat a model as one unreliable part inside a deterministic envelope instead of the brain of the thing. I also know where my line is now - destructive actions should have shipped with confirmation and undo. I designed that, didn't build it, and I say so plainly.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: left my familiar world - single-page, deterministic tools - for a stateless MV3 extension with an LLM choosing browser actions
- Customer: me as the user; the real risk was the user's open work (tabs) destroyed by one confident wrong model call - no adoption claims, personal build
- Insight: two discomforts on different axes - (a) code that isn't continuously running, (b) a probabilistic model in a destructive control path; the fix for both is "don't hold it yourself, bound it"
- Action (mine): failed first with an in-worker timer for snoozing, rebuilt on chrome.alarms + storage ({url, title, wakeTime}, 1-min tick, restart-safe); routed simple commands to local rules; pre-filtered tab context; temp 0 + regex-JSON fallback for Ollama; cloud Gemini and local Ollama both supported
- Result: snooze survives browser restart; model sees only a reduced, relevant slice and is the last resort, not the first hop; guardrail design (confidence bands, undo, telemetry) exists on paper, not in the build
- Learning: when a model is in the control path, the work isn't prompt tuning - it's the deterministic envelope around it; and confirmation/undo are part of a destructive feature, not polish

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What exactly was unfamiliar? - Two things: the MV3 execution model (service worker torn down between events, message passing, no long-lived state) and putting a probabilistic model where a crash isn't the failure mode - closing the wrong tabs is. [SAFE]
2. Walk me through that first failure again. - I wrote snoozing the obvious way: schedule a wake-up from inside the background script. It worked while the browser stayed open and silently did nothing after a restart, because the worker and its timers were gone. That's my own build-process recollection, not a logged incident - but the shipped design is the evidence: alarms plus storage exist precisely because process-held state doesn't. [PARTIAL - personal observation, not instrumented]
3. Why alarms specifically? - It's the platform's own scheduler: the browser owns the wake-up, and storage is the only state that outlives the worker. The design question changed from "what's my state?" to "who wakes me up, and what's on disk before I stop running." Built in three iterations - alarm/storage engine, message handler, context-menu UI. [SAFE]
4. Why use an LLM at all instead of rules? - Useful requests are open-ended ("group my travel research"); hardcoding phrasings is linear effort against unbounded input. So rules are the default and the model handles only the residual. [SAFE]
5. What stops the model from doing something destructive? - In the build: routing (simple commands never call a model) and a pre-filter narrowing the tab set by domain category and keyword, plus parallel metadata extraction. Designed but NOT shipped: confidence gate (>=0.75 auto-execute, 0.4-0.74 confirm, <0.4 clarify), transactional undo for closes, telemetry. I state that gap rather than imply protection that isn't there. [PARTIAL - honest split between shipped and designed]
6. I see big perf numbers in your docs - measured? - No. The 50k->3k token reduction, 8s->3s and 5s->0.5s timings, and ~70% offline coverage are design targets from my implementation guide, not measurements. The measured behavior I can speak to is qualitative: rule path handles common commands with zero API calls. [SAFE - labeled as projected]
7. Who used this? How many users? - It's a personal build. I'm not claiming adoption numbers, internal or public. [SAFE]
8. Why carry both Gemini and Ollama? - To find the fallback boundary by testing, not assuming - provider availability and the user's tab data leaving the machine. Which one runs is a settings choice, not a rewrite. [SAFE]
9. What actually broke with the local model? - It sometimes emitted prose around its JSON, which failed strict parsing. Fix was temperature 0.0, a JSON response format, and a regex extraction fallback. Small thing, but it's where I learned to treat model output as untrusted input. [SAFE - fallback exists in the code]
10. Hardest part? - Unlearning the assumption that my code is always running. Every design decision after that followed from it. [SAFE]
11. Do differently? - Ship the guardrails with the action layer, not after it. The moment a model picks destructive actions, confirmation and undo are the feature. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "The timer failure - is that in your repo history or just a story?" - Needs honesty: my own build recollection (personal observation), supported by the shipped alarms+storage design; never present as a logged, dated incident.
2. "So the safety layer doesn't exist?" - Defensible only because I volunteer it: routing and filtering are shipped; confidence gate/undo/telemetry are design-only. Any inflation here collapses under probing.
3. "Are those perf numbers real?" - Defensible: always labeled design targets, per the docs; the only "measured" claims are qualitative (rules make zero API calls).

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5 / Ownership: 5 / Judgment: 4 / Impact: 3 / Credibility: 4 / Naturalness: 4

# Q36 - a time when you had to compromise quality over a prescribed timeline

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary); Deliver Results; Insist on the Highest Standards.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the copied-fork shortcut: tool two cloned from tool one to hit a this-week date, six months of divergence, and the designed-but-not-done collapse plan (`BAR_RAISER_TECHNICAL_PREP.md` :227, :346; migration design :307-311). Reframed from Q13: the core there is the bounded five-day prototype that was repaid; the core here is the compromise that is *still being repaid* - the honest one.

## Core Answer

Yes. And the example that really tests this question isn't the prototype where I paid the debt back fast - it's the copy that cost me six months. (The prototype was the first tool's quick five-day build, finished properly within two weeks - the shortcut that got repaid. This one hasn't been yet.)

I had one PCB inspection tool built. A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device. The manufacturing side needed a second one, with different inputs but the same comparison core - the check that compares a photo of a finished board against the board's design file and flags what looks off - and the timeline was fixed: working that week. The clean path was to factor the shared logic out - rewrite the code so both tools ran on one shared copy instead of two - and build tool two on top of it, and that plainly took longer than my week. So I did the smaller thing: I copied the first tool's code, changed the parts the new tool needed, and it worked on schedule.

The quality I gave up, stated exactly: a copy is never free. I now had two codebases answering the same question, and they drifted - each copy picked up small edits over time, so slowly the two became different. The worst concrete drift was that they grew two different anomaly formulas - different scoring logic, meaning two different versions of the rule that decides whether a flagged spot on a board is a real defect or just noise - so the two tools could look at the same board and disagree about whether a part was wrong. Same board, two answers. That's not a bug. That's two standards.

And I own the second half: I let it run for six months before I treated the divergence as debt with a due date. (That "six months" = the span from making the copy to finally calling it debt - it comes from my own prep notes, a documented recollection, not an instrumented measurement, so I say "about.") The rule I keep from it now is that a copy is only acceptable if you give it a merge-back deadline the day you make it - merge-back meaning a date by which the copy gets folded back into one shared codebase. I didn't give this one a date.

There's a collapse plan now, and I won't say it's finished. First a golden-output harness - record what each tool says today on a fixed input set: a standard batch of test cases whose current answers get saved as the reference, so any later change that moves an answer shows up. Then extract the shared scoring core - one copy of the deciding logic both tools use - without changing behavior, prove the outputs come out byte-identical, meaning every saved answer matches exactly as before, and only then fix the formula disagreement, with the harness watching so the change is visible. Designed and tracked; not done.

The trade in one line: I bought a week and paid about six months of drift, and the fix is now harder than the refactor I skipped - the refactor being that restructure where both tools would have shared one copy of the logic. What didn't move is the standard - the bar is one source of truth, and I'm tracking the gap to it.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: second PCB inspection tool demanded, working that week; shared-logic refactor wouldn't fit the week.
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers needing consistent verdicts across both tools.
- Insight: a copy is debt, not a resting state - it's only safe with a merge-back deadline set the day you make it.
- Action (mine): shipped tool two by copying tool one; let the copies drift ~six months (two different anomaly formulas); later defined the collapse: golden-output harness -> behavior-preserving extraction of a shared scoring core -> byte-identical proof -> then the formula fix under test.
- Result: deadline met that week; cost was ~six months of divergence and same-board disagreement risk; repayment designed and tracked, not done - stated that way.
- Learning: name the price of a shortcut before you take it, and put a date on it; a dated shortcut collapses, an undated one compounds.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What were the two tools? - Both PCB inspection tools sharing a comparison core (the same photo-versus-design-file check); tool two took different inputs. I built both solo, so the copy was cheap to make and expensive to keep honest. [SAFE]
2. Why copy instead of a shared module? - The week. The factor-out - restructuring the code into one shared module both tools use - was the right long-term move and plainly took longer than the date I had; I chose to meet the date and - this is the part I'd do differently - didn't book the refactor as debt the day I copied. [SAFE]
3. Who prescribed the timeline? - My notes record it as "needed working that week" - a commitment to the team that needed the tool. The notes don't record whose date it was, so I won't invent a name. [GAP - keep general]
4. Have you made this trade when you did repay it? - Yes: the first tool was a five-day monolithic prototype - monolithic meaning built as one tangled block for speed rather than tidy separate parts - with the limits named before the demo; three gaps the team found in an hour (three problems the engineers caught in roughly one hour of testing - from my notes, a recollection of the demo, not a tracked count); fixed alignment -> illumination -> export (in plain terms: getting the photo lined up with the design drawing -> handling lighting and reflections -> producing the saved report); production-ready in two weeks (5 + 9), with comparison verdicts lifting from roughly 85% to over 98% on a ~20-photo controlled set I built myself - the percentage is how often the tool's defect-or-not call matched the hand-checked answer on that ~20-photo set I collected and verified by hand; small and self-built, so the size of the gain is believable, the exact figure is soft. Same numbers I give everywhere for that story. [PARTIAL - self-built set, state method first]
5. How did you find the divergence? - The cost showed up as disagreement: the tools scored the same board differently because the anomaly formulas - the defect-versus-noise deciding rules - had drifted. Once I could point at that, the copies stopped being "done." [SAFE]
6. How solid is "six months"? - It's from my own technical prep record - the span the fork drifted before it got flagged as debt (a "fork" is the copied tool: code branched off to go its own way) - a documented recollection, not instrumented. I say "about six months." [PARTIAL]
7. What exactly is the collapse plan? - Step 0: golden-output harness capturing current outputs on fixed inputs (save each test case's present answer as the reference to check later changes against). Steps 1-3: extract the pure scoring functions - the deciding math with no screens or file handling around it - into a shared headless core (one hidden, screenless copy both tools call) and prove byte-identical outputs - every saved answer matches exactly as before - no behavior change yet. Step 4: fix the formula disagreement with the harness watching. Deliberate order: you can't safely change behavior until you can prove what behavior is. [SAFE - and explicitly designed, not done]
8. What went wrong / hardest part? - Sitting on an undated shortcut for six months. Hardest was admitting the shipped copy wasn't finished work; the code I'd written had quietly become two standards. [SAFE]
9. Any disagreement in this one? - No person-vs-person dispute is documented; the real disagreement was with my own earlier call that "shipped copy = done." I won't inflate it into a conflict with someone. [PARTIAL - don't embellish]
10. At larger scale? - The suite grew to three tools off shared code - my notes call it a three-way fork (three copies that grew apart from the one original) - which is exactly why the modularization after the prototype and the planned shared core matter: undated copies multiply. [PARTIAL]
11. Do differently? - Two things: price the shortcut before taking it - one sentence to the team: "this buys the week, it costs a merge-back" - and set that merge-back date the day the copy is made. [SAFE]
12. Doesn't this trigger your own "highest standards" bar? - I hope the answer shows the bar working: I name the drift, quantify the cost, and I'm not allowed to say the fix is done because it isn't. The prototype story shows the repayment habit; this one shows me catching myself when the habit lapsed. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "Six months" challenged as unmeasured - defensible only as a documented-recollection span from my prep record; always say "about," never present as audited. [PARTIAL - state source]
2. Collapse plan not finished - a Bar Raiser can press "so the standard still isn't met." Status line is the defense: designed, tracked, deliberately sequenced; claiming completion is a fabrication GAP I won't touch. [defensible as stated - rehearse the "not done" sentence]
3. Who set the deadline - not in the record; keep it as "the team needed it working that week"; no invented manager. [GAP -> stay general]
4. Two anomaly formulas vs "three-way fork" - one telling: the copies of tool one diverged, with two anomaly formulas in circulation across the growing suite; don't mix counts mid-answer. [SAFE if kept precise - rehearse]
5. Overlap with Q13 (same suite) - this answer never re-tells the five-day demo as the core; the prototype appears only in follow-up #4 with identical numbers. [SAFE if rehearsed]

# Q38 - tell me about a project where you chose the UI/middle layer/database/etc

**LP:** Are Right, A Lot (primary - the data-structure call under a hard environment constraint, and naming where it breaks); Invent and Simplify (chose the boring structure that solves the measured bottleneck; complexity deliberately avoided)   **Story:** the per-component scan over the whole CAD drawing - O(NxM), ~25M distance checks per board - and the uniform spatial hash I chose as the middle layer to replace it (BAR_RAISER_TECHNICAL_PREP.md Finding 2, :134-152); distinct from Q81 (the sibling hot-loop decode finding in the same audit) and Q21 (learning the browser stack)

## Core Answer

The layer I chose was a data structure - the part of the tool that answers "what's near this point" - and in a browser tool that effectively is the middle layer: the structure of the data between the screen and the computation. In my PCB inspection suite, every component detected on a board photo had to find its matching shape in the CAD drawing - the engineer's design file - to get the right crop size. The first version answered with a scan: for each component, loop over every layer and every shape in the drawing and measure the distance. That's a choice nobody makes on purpose; it writes itself.

A board carries a few hundred components. The drawing carries roughly 50,000 shapes. Multiply: about 25 million distance checks per board - and it was nested inside another loop that was already doing too much work, so the costs compounded. It worked; it just slowed with board complexity, and the factory boards are the complex kind.

The options were: keep scanning, buy a faster machine, or change the data structure. A faster machine isn't an option when the tool has to run as one offline file on locked-down factory computers. So the choice was the structure. I picked a uniform spatial hash: bucket every shape once into grid cells sized to the typical shape, then ask only about the 9 cells around a component instead of the whole drawing. Build once per load, proportional to shape count; each query touches only local density. The multiplication becomes an addition.

The call I'd defend isn't "I knew about spatial hashes" - it's naming where my choice breaks before someone else finds it for me. A uniform grid degrades when shape sizes vary wildly, because a board's outline polygon spans every cell. The known mitigations are size-bucketed grids, or an R-tree - a balanced tree over 2D space - if the size distribution is genuinely heavy-tailed. I took the simple structure that fixed the real bottleneck and documented its failure mode, rather than picking the sophisticated one to look careful.

One honest flag: I found this by reading the code and multiplying recorded counts, not by a profiler's trace. Before I'd quote a speedup in seconds, I'd want the profile - the 25-million figure is arithmetic about the shipped loop, which is itself the point: the loop was visible, and it was wrong.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: every component's crop-size lookup scanned every layer x every shape of the CAD drawing - O(NxM), ~25M distance checks per board, nested inside an already-expensive loop
- Customer: manufacturing engineers on slow, offline, locked-down factory machines - "buy a faster computer" was not a deliverable option
- Insight: the middle layer choice is the data-structure choice; the bottleneck was a range query over 2D points that had been answered with a linear scan
- Action (mine): chose a uniform spatial hash - one-time bucketing of ~50k shapes into grid cells sized to the median shape, queries narrowed to the 9 surrounding cells; kept the simpler structure over an R-tree and documented its size-variance failure mode + mitigations
- Result: per-component full-drawing scan replaced by local-cell queries; preprocessing once per load [PARTIAL - no committed benchmark numbers; found by reading, not profiling]
- Learning: name where your chosen structure fails before the interviewer does; the boring structure that fits the access pattern beats the clever one that fits your resume

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Where do 50,000 shapes and 25M checks come from? - The shipped loop iterates layers x shapes per component; the audit records ~500 components x ~50,000 CAD shapes = ~25M distance checks per board. Arithmetic on recorded typical counts, not a measured distribution. [PARTIAL - computed, labeled]
2. Did you profile it? - No. I found it by reading the code; the audit's own standard is to get the profile before claiming a speedup number, and I hold that line. If pressed: the trace plan is Chrome DevTools' performance panel, looking for the distance-check loop dominating. [SAFE - honest label]
3. Why not a real database - SQLite or the like? - The whole tool ships as one offline HTML file inside a browser (no server, no installs); the "database layer" had to be plain in-memory JavaScript structures. The spatial hash is the database choice under that constraint. [SAFE]
4. Why a hash grid and not an R-tree or kd-tree? - Access pattern is static (bucket once after load, query many), queries are small-radius, and a grid is dozens of lines that I can debug on a factory machine. An R-tree buys balance the static workload doesn't need at the cost of code complexity; kd-tree degrades with the heavy-tailed size mix. Reasoning about structure fit, not a benchmark bake-off. [PARTIAL - reasoning]
5. How did you size the cells? - Side ~ median shape size: too small and a query spans many cells; too large and the cells degenerate back toward scanning everything. The grid constant is a tuning knob, and the size-variance failure is the knob's known limit. [SAFE]
6. What was it nested inside? - A second, separate inefficiency in the same loop (a full-image decode per component) - that one is its own story (Q81); here it's one line: fixing the lookup without fixing the decode would still have crawled, because the costs compounded. [SAFE - cross-reference, not a retell]
7. Who felt the slowness? - The suite went to about 15 engineers across 2 sites; they told me it saved roughly 20 hours a week - engineer-reported recollection, not instrumented, and the same account I give everywhere. No per-feature timing claims. [SAFE - canonical, labeled]
8. What would you do differently? - Instrument before rewriting (the profile I skipped), and make the index a shared module across the two comparison tools - they had diverged from a copy, so a fix in one didn't reach the other. [PARTIAL - reasoning + documented fork divergence]

## Risk Check

# Q39 - tell me about a time when you had a conflict with a team member, tell me about a time when you stepped out of your comfort zone, tell me about a project you recently worked on and what the...

**LP:** (a) Have Backbone; Earn Trust - GAP-bridge; (b) Learn and Be Curious; (c) Deliver Results; Invent and Simplify   **Story:** (a) no peer conflict documented - labeled bridge per Q10/Q22; (b) the five-day prototype demo (STORY 8 axis, not Q21/Q71's); (c) PCB suite at work + Tab Scroller at home, inverted from Q94's framing

## Core Answer

**(a) The conflict.** Straight answer first: I don't have a documented conflict with a teammate I can stand behind. I built the inspection suite solo - no teammate across the table in the record - and I won't invent one. The closest true things: a manufacturing engineer corrected my parser (the code that reads a board's parts list and breaks it into pieces) - I'd dropped `R1||R2` variant references as invalid (a part written `R1||R2` means one spot that can hold either of two interchangeable components; that's a valid way to write a parts list); he was right about the floor, so I rewrote the splitter (the piece that splits a combined label like that into its parts) to match either reference. And I pushed back on a measurement rule, not a person: literal pin-count matching (comparing the number of electrical connection points a part lists against the design) flagged normal package variants (the same component sold in different physical housings), so I sorted twenty production BOMs (bill-of-materials files - a board's parts list) into three buckets and replaced the rule with that. My framework for a real peer conflict is the same reflex: raise it once, directly, with data; argue the finding, not the person; ask what evidence would change the outcome; then commit fully and not relitigate sideways. The lived event itself is a gap, and I treat it as homework.

**(b) The comfort zone.** The uncomfortable part wasn't technical - it was being seen doing it. I'm fine alone with a hard problem; putting unfinished work in front of people is not my default. My first browser inspection tool sat in a backlog six months as "too complex to scope" (too big to even define the work). Instead of arguing scope, I spent five days on a working prototype and demoed it half-finished. The team found three real problems in the first hour - more than weeks of polishing alone would have caught. Two weeks later it was production-ready. The scariest single technical moment was coding a warping algorithm (a formula that bends one image so it lines up with a photo taken at an angle) straight out of a 1989 paper because no library (ready-made code someone else had already written) existed - but the habit that actually changed was demoing unfinished work, early and on purpose.

**(c) The recent project.** Most recent at work: the PCB inspection suite (a PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device) - three browser-based tools I built solo in eight weeks: BOM reconciliation (checking the parts list against what's actually placed on the board), board-photo-versus-design comparison, and a vision model (an AI program that looks at images) reading mismatch reports. Locked-down factory machines, no installs, no network - so it shipped as one offline HTML file (a single web page you just open in a browser), no server, no IT approval. About 15 engineers across 2 sites used it; they told me it saved roughly 20 hours a week - reported, not measured. Most recent overall is personal: Tab Scroller, a Chrome extension (an add-on for the Chrome browser) where you control tabs in plain English on a cloud or local model (an AI that runs on someone else's servers over the internet, or on your own computer). Happy to go deep on either.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: three-in-one - (a) no peer-conflict event exists in the record; (b) comfort zone is working alone, not exposing unfinished work; (c) "recent" spans the day job and the personal build
- Customer: (a) the engineers whose floor semantics beat my model (what the factory floor really means beat what my code assumed); (b) the lead + team judging a "too complex" backlog position; (c) ~15 engineers on restricted machines; me, for Tab Scroller
- Insight: (a) data moves decisions, corrections are free learning; (b) working code ends scope arguments that talking can't; (c) the hardest constraint picks the architecture - one offline file
- Action (mine): (a) rewrote the `||`/`/` splitter after the correction; built the 20-BOM three-bucket pin rule; (b) five-day prototype, demoed unfinished; (c) solo 3-tool build shipped as a single HTML file; Tab Scroller personal
- Result: (a) mixed-board false positives (crying-wolf flags) ~12% -> under 2% (pin rule); (b) three issues found in hour one, production-ready in two weeks; (c) 15/2-site usage, ~20 hrs/wk engineer-reported; Tab Scroller in my daily use
- Learning: (a) keep a real record of peer disagreements - this gap partly exists because I never logged one; (b) demo early on purpose; (c) say "reported" when it's reported

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Was there really no peer conflict? - No. Solo build (I built the suite alone, so there was no peer to clash with); Have Backbone is the thinnest part of my record, and the two real events are a correction I accepted and a pushback against a rule. I keep them separate; blurring them into a "conflict" is fabrication. [GAP - stated plainly]
2. How would you handle a peer who won't accept your data? - Framework, labeled: put the finding in writing, ask what evidence would change their mind, bring in whoever holds context I'm missing, and once decided, commit and stop relitigating in side conversations. [PARTIAL - framework]
3. What exactly was the pin-count pushback? - Literal pin-count-vs-pad-count matching (comparing how many electrical pins a part has against how many solder pads - the connection points on the board) called normal package variants (the same component in different physical housings) mismatches. I categorized 20 BOMs with pin differences into three cases: footprint larger = review, smaller = genuine mismatch, exact = match (footprint = the area the part covers on the board). False positives (wrong alarms) on mixed boards dropped from about 12% to under 2%. [PARTIAL - documented rule fix, don't widen beyond mixed boards]
4. Was the variant correction a conflict? - No - it was me being wrong. The engineer's floor knowledge beat my model of the floor; I adopted his semantics completely (his naming rules, entirely). That's the commit half of disagree-and-commit, exercised. [SAFE - cross-ref Q6/Q71]
5. Why prototype instead of arguing the scope? - "Too complex" had survived six months of debate; a five-day build was cheaper than another meeting. The demo surfaced three concrete issues within the hour and the tool was production-ready in two weeks. [SAFE]
6. Was the demo genuinely uncomfortable, or just nerves? - Honest: alone-with-the-problem is my default; presenting half-working code to a group was new. The technical version of that discomfort - implementing thin-plate-spline warping (a formula that bends a flat image to match a warped photo, like flattening a crumpled sheet) from the Bookstein 1989 paper with no library (nobody had published ready-made code for it) - is a fuller story I tell separately. [PARTIAL - framing; TPS = one-sentence nod, don't re-tell Q21 here]
7. Your role on the PCB suite? - Solo. Only engineer: requirements, build, verification, packaging (what it should do, coding it, testing it, and shipping it as a single file). [SAFE - canonical ownership]
8. How solid is the 15-engineers claim? - Roughly 15 engineers across 2 sites, from their own reports - including the ~20 hours a week. Not instrumented (no tracking code counted anything); I say "they told me." [PARTIAL - engineer-reported]
9. Tab Scroller - who uses it, and is it fast? - Only daily user is me. Speed figures (simple commands back locally in under 10 ms - thousandths of a second, "locally" meaning on my own machine; deep extraction - asking the AI to pull meaning out of a whole page - ~8 s down to a 3 s target) are design targets (goals I set, not measurements), never measured. Biggest miss: the action layer (the part that actually acts on your tabs) shipped without its guardrails - confidence gate (a check that only acts when it's sure), undo, telemetry (background usage-tracking) are designed, not built. [PARTIAL - targets disclosed as targets]
10. Do differently? - Log real disagreements as they happen (this gap is partly an empty notebook); demo even earlier - hour one beats week one; and build guardrails before the action layer, not after (the safety checks before the part that takes action). [SAFE]

## Risk Check

1. Part (a) demands a lived conflict; this is a bridge - GAP, survivable as honesty, not as a full answer. Never let the correction + rule-pushback blur into an invented dispute; only a real event from outside the record closes it.
2. Part (b)'s "comfort zone" framing is self-reported emotion over documented facts (six-month backlog, five days, three issues, two weeks) - defensible as long as I don't inflate the anxiety or the authorship; the axis (exposure, not tooling/domain) is distinct from Q21/Q71.
3. Part (c): 15/2 and ~20 hrs/wk must come out as engineer-reported, never "measured"; standalone must stay "one offline file" per the unified stance; Tab Scroller numbers are design targets.
4. TPS nod (the image-warping algorithm) vs Q21 overlap - one sentence in-core; if probed, say the full version lives in that answer and re-derive nothing new here.

# Q40 - Tell me about a time you made an unorthodox decision.

**LP:** Are Right, A Lot (primary); Invent and Simplify; Bias for Action.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - GPT-4o VLM as the inspection engine instead of the purpose-built classifier (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 8; decision-framed telling of the same event Q1/Q3 used).

## Core Answer

The unorthodox call: I used a general-purpose cloud vision model as the inspection engine - that means an AI that can look at a photo and answer questions about it, running on someone else's computers over the internet and paid for per use - instead of the trained classifier machine-vision inspection says to build: a custom image model you train yourself on labelled photos of your own defects.

I was the only engineer on a PCB inspection suite for manufacturing engineers. A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device. The comparison could tell you *where* a board didn't match its design - it drew a red region - but not what the region *meant*. Wrong part? Rotated? Just a reflection? An engineer read every flag by eye, about thirty seconds a pop - their own estimate of one zoom-and-decide, not a timed study. Interpretation was the bottleneck.

The orthodox fix was a bespoke classifier - a custom image-recognition model you train yourself: label photos of each defect type, train a model on them - it runs offline, cheap, and it's yours. I did the opposite: cropped each flagged region from both the layout and the photo, sent both to GPT-4o with a structured prompt - an instruction that demands the answer in a fixed fill-in-the-blank form the software can read mechanically - and got back a verdict: component type, mismatch type, and a confidence (the AI's own score for how sure it is).

That was odd here, and each oddity was a real risk. One: a cloud dependency - the tool leaning on someone else's paid internet service - in a tool built for factory machines with restricted networks. Two: the "intelligence" was a black box (a system you can't open up and inspect inside) I didn't train or own, and wrong verdicts on a production tool are expensive. Three: I inverted the job - building the pipeline (the automated steps around the AI: cut the images, send them, read the answer back) and the prompt around someone else's model, not my own model. That looks like less engineering until you've done it.

I treated it as a bet, measured first. I hand-compared candidate models on the real task: speed, small-part accuracy, hardware fit - my own side-by-side trials, not a formal benchmark. Then I bounded each risk. Only flagged regions went to the model, so cost scaled with mismatches, not components - the price follows how many red marks a board has, not how many parts sit on it. The cloud path lived only in the server build - the suite existed in two versions: the server build, which ran through our own server and could reach the internet, and a self-contained offline file running straight on the factory machines; "server-build only" means the AI lived in the first version alone, and the offline factory-floor tool never touched it. The output was labeled "AI Analysis" - a suggestion with a confidence the engineer confirmed or overrode, plus a correct/incorrect feedback loop (a right/wrong button on every answer). If the API - the point where software plugs into a paid online service - died, the tool kept working.

It worked out. The thirty-second eye-read became a five-second answer - API time, the computer's reply, not a stopwatch saving for the human; the engineer went from interpreting to confirming and, by their own word, saved most of their ~30 seconds per flag. It read component and mismatch type right about eighty-five percent of the time - my rough check against the engineers' right/wrong clicks, not a measured rate from a formal test. The misses were images too poor or parts too small.

What I got wrong: I thought it could read values off small surface-mount parts - the tiny components soldered directly onto the board. It can't - context, not OCR (reading printed letters off a photo, the way a scanner does). And I'd start with the simple prompt, not the clever one. The call was right because I bounded the risk before I took it, not because I trusted the model.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: comparison flagged *where*, not *what*; every red region cost the engineer a ~30-second eye-read (engineer-estimated, not timed). Interpretation was the bottleneck.
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers using the suite on the factory floor.
- Insight: a general vision model (cloud AI that reads photos and answers in words) already had the "expert eye" I'd otherwise spend months training - my work was crop, prompt, parse.
- Action (mine): solo; hand-compared model candidates on the real task; built the dual-crop structured-JSON pipeline (cut-out images + fixed fill-in-the-blank reply form + parsing); server-build-only (AI on the server build; the offline floor file runs none) and optional; confidence display + correct/incorrect feedback + graceful degradation (tool still works with the AI absent); rewrote the failing first prompt to a fixed schema.
- Result: ~30 s eye-read (engineer-reported) -> ~5 s answer (AI reply time - computer time, not measured human time); ~85% on component/mismatch type by rough self-assessment (no formal test behind it); engineers triaged dense boards with the labels; offline build untouched by the VLM (vision-language model - the image-reading cloud AI).
- Learning: reach for the general model where a bespoke one would be maintained forever; bound risk before betting; don't trust a VLM for OCR on tiny text; start with the simple prompt.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Why wasn't a red box enough? - Every flag was a manual judgment call: wrong value, wrong orientation, or a lighting artifact (a reflection or shadow that only looks like a defect). About thirty seconds a region by the engineers' own estimate - not a stopwatch study; a dense board typically threw five to twenty of them - a reported typical, not an instrumented count. Detection was solved; interpretation wasn't. [SAFE]
2. A trained classifier is offline, cheap, and yours. Why not that? - Because it's a labeling-and-retraining project that restarts for every new defect type, and I was a solo engineer already carrying three tools. Reusing an existing "expert eye" pointed my effort at preprocessing and the prompt. It also wasn't either/or: the deterministic comparison stayed the core (the fixed-rule red-marking math - same input, same answer, no AI judgment); the VLM was an escalation for flagged regions only. I'd build the custom model if cost or privacy ever became the binding constraint. [SAFE]
3. Why GPT-4o specifically? - Hand-tested side by side on the real task (my own observations on real flagged regions, not a formal benchmark): GPT-4V ran about eight seconds per request versus about three for 4o - that's the wait for the answer; Claude 3 saw well but its API was less mature then; Gemini Pro Vision was weaker on small-object detection, which is exactly what SMD parts need (SMD = surface-mount devices, the tiny components soldered straight onto the board). A local LLaVA-style model (a free model you run on your own hardware instead of paying a service) was the self-host option but wanted at least 8 GB of VRAM the factory machines didn't have - VRAM is the memory on a graphics card - so it was rejected on hardware, not preference. [SAFE]
4. How reliable is that 85%? - As a rate, not very. It was my rough check against the correct/incorrect marks on flagged-region reads - no held-out set, no n, no confusion matrix. In plain words: a "held-out set" is a batch of fresh, hand-checked examples deliberately kept from the model so it's tested on things it has never seen; "n" is how many examples a rate actually rests on; a "confusion matrix" is a table showing which mistake got called which. It was acceptable because the model's output was a first-pass suggestion, never the decision. If you want a validated number, I'd build the labeled eval set first - that's a real gap. And note: 85% in my alignment story measures something else entirely - different tool, different loop; I never mix them. [GAP - no measured accuracy exists; lead with the label]
5. Was 30 s -> 5 s an instrumented saving? - No. The 30 s is engineer-reported - their own guess at one eye-read's duration; the 5 s is the API's response time - the computer's wait for the AI's answer - and the confirm step was never costed. The honest claim: the engineer saved most of their thirty seconds per region. Not a timed study. [PARTIAL]
6. Was putting board photos into a cloud API even allowed? - I put it through the security team before shipping the cloud path; they approved because the images contain no trade secrets. And the offline build runs no VLM at all, so the network constraint on the floor never became a failure mode. [SAFE]
7. What when the API is down or slow? - The VLM is an enhancement, not a dependency. Comparison and red highlights still render, the UI says AI analysis is unavailable, and the engineer inspects as before. Typical 4o response was about three seconds, inside the under-five-second design budget. (The "design budget" is the reply-time ceiling the tool was specified to stay under; the ~3 s is my hand-observed average in use, not a measured distribution.) [SAFE]
8. What does it cost, and where would you NOT use the model? - Roughly a cent an analysis, so a ten-mismatch board is about a dime. (The cent = the provider's published price per request times a typical call - an estimate from the price list, not a billed-and-audited figure.) Never on every component - hundreds of components across thousands of boards a day wrecks cost, latency (how long each call takes to answer), and auditability, since you can't reproduce a hosted model's verdict months later. Never offline. A cost-aware cascade - a two-stage funnel where cheap fixed-rule image code screens every flagged region and only the unsure ones escalate to the paid AI - is a design target - designed, not built. [SAFE; cascade PARTIAL - target only]
9. What went wrong while building it? - Two things. The first prompt was verbose natural language and returned junk I couldn't parse reliably; I rewrote it to a fixed JSON schema with examples (JSON = the rigid fill-in-the-blank answer form software reads mechanically). And I overestimated the model: it couldn't read value text on small surface-mount parts - context, not OCR. [SAFE]
10. Did anyone push back on the idea? - I was the only engineer, so the argument was with my own default - the domain reflex says build the bespoke model. I settled it with a bounded-risk checklist rather than a debate. I won't claim external opposition I didn't have. [PARTIAL - no recorded external disagreement]
11. Hardest part? - Not the code. Committing to an engine I couldn't audit line-by-line, and designing the human loop so that *not* being able to audit it was okay. [SAFE]
12. Bigger scale / do differently? - Build the labeled eval set before shipping - a kept-back batch of hand-checked examples to score on, so accuracy is measured, not judged. Start with the simple structured prompt instead of the clever one. And keep the rule: general model for judgment, deterministic core for detection. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. The ~85% has no held-out set behind it - defensible only in the labeled form used ("my own rough check, not a measured rate"); pressed for audited accuracy, it's a GAP, and follow-up 4 owns that.
2. "30 s -> 5 s" could be heard as a measured human-time saving - it's engineer-reported baseline + API turnaround; defensible with the labels in follow-up 5.
3. "A cloud model on a factory-floor tool is disqualifying" - defensible: server build only, optional, deterministic core always works, security-team-reviewed, offline build runs no VLM.
4. "Calling an API isn't unorthodox" - defensible as judgment: the domain default was a bespoke classifier; the unorthodox parts were inverting build ownership and accepting a cloud dependency in a restricted environment - each bounded, not ignored.

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5 / Ownership: 5 / Judgment: 5 / Impact: 4 / Credibility: 4 / Naturalness: 4

# Q41 - tell me about a time you took on a task outside your job description

**LP:** Ownership (primary)   **Story:** **[GAP]** - no documented out-of-role event. Closest true ownership act shown as bridge: the unassigned one-day browser-CV spike (STORY 5, `AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md`); the labeling tool (STORY 9) and debug view (STORY 11) appear only as bounded evidence of the pattern, never as crossed lines. Distinct from Q23 (STORY 9 as the story), Q24 (STORY 11), Q30 (STORY 4)

## Core Answer

I'll be blunt: I don't have a story where I took a task past my job description, and the reason is structural. On my main project I was the sole builder and architect - the only person who both designed the software and wrote it. The role was defined by an outcome, not a narrow task list, so almost everything I did sat inside the charter (the job's official scope). I won't relabel assigned work as a bold step over a line that never existed.

The closest true thing I can show you is this. Nobody assigned me the browser-computer-vision question - "computer vision" is software that looks at photos and checks them, and "browser" means it runs inside an ordinary web browser, like the one you read email in, instead of a program someone installs. But it sat between me and the outcome. The inspection suite - the photo-comparison tools the factory used - had to run on factory machines with no server and no installs, meaning the locked-down shop-floor computers couldn't connect to a central machine and wouldn't accept new software, and I didn't know if that was even possible in a browser. So I ran a one-day spike - a spike is a short, deliberately throwaway experiment built to answer one question - the smallest prototype that could work: load two images, run one operation. That made an unknown that could have cost me weeks cost a day, and the architecture call got made on evidence instead of guessing - the decision about how to build the whole tool, settled by what the experiment showed rather than a hunch. Plainly, about those two numbers: the day is real time the experiment took; the weeks are my own estimate of finding the same answer the hard way - a judgment, not a measured figure.

Two adjacent things show the same instinct, and I'll keep their bounds honest. The defect model - the part of the tool that names what kind of flaw a board has - needed labeled images, which are example photos a person has marked up to show what each one contains and what's wrong with it, and they didn't exist, so I built the labeling tool rather than report a blocker - but my own notes record that as my responsibility. Engineers didn't trust the reconciliation verdicts - the yes/no answers the tool produced when it cross-checked a board's parts list against its design file - so I built a debug view exposing the reasoning, a screen that shows how the tool reached each answer so a person can check it, but it shipped inside the tool I was assigned. Both are owning an unowned dependency - something the work needed that was nobody's job - not taking a task outside the job.

The pattern I can defend: when something blocks the outcome, nobody owns it, the cost of trying is bounded (small and capped, so a wrong attempt is cheap to undo), and I'm closest to it - I pick it up, and I say out loud what I'm taking and why.

The gap, openly: **[GAP]** - I have no documented moment where a clear line existed and I stepped over it. A real example belongs to team experience, with somebody else's duty or an orphaned one in it, and I'd bring that prepared instead of stretching this record.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: the question demands a crossed role line; on the record (sole builder/architect - one person who designed and built the software) there was barely a line to cross, so no lived instance exists
- Customer: the factory engineers - the spike existed because the suite had to actually reach their machines
- Insight: "unassigned" != "outside my job"; unowned blocker + bounded cost + closest person = mine to raise, and I raise it visibly
- Action (mine): ran the one-day browser-CV spike (a throwaway photo-checking experiment in a web browser) on my own judgment; labeling tool and debug view cited only as pattern evidence, each explicitly bounded as assigned work
- Result: a weeks-long unknown resolved in a day, so the browser architecture decision rested on evidence, not guesswork
- Learning: don't mine assigned work for hero framing; source the real boundary-crossing example from team experience before interview day

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Why doesn't the labeling tool qualify? - STORY 9's own Task line names it as my responsibility. Claiming it as out-of-role contradicts my record, and Q23 already tells it honestly as the assigned unblock. (The labeling tool is where a human marks up example photos so the defect-classifying software can learn from them.) **[GAP - event disqualified by its own source]**
2. What about the debug view or the standalone build (the single-file version of the tool that ran with no server and no installs)? - Both live inside assigned deliverables; Q24 and Q30 already bound them the same way. Re-cutting them here as scope-jacking - making work that was already mine sound like I went beyond my role - would duplicate their evidence and weaken all three answers. **[GAP - no distinct instance]**
3. Then what do you actually own here? - The one-day spike: nobody tasked it, it was the risk-reduction move I chose - shrinking a big unknown cheaply before betting weeks on it - to make the stack decision (the choice of which technology the whole tool would be built on) defensible. It's unassigned work inside a broad charter - the closest true thing, still not a crossed line. [PARTIAL - pattern, not the event asked for]
4. How do you decide what unowned work to take? - Three tests: am I closest, is a wrong attempt cheap to undo, can I keep the scope visible (say out loud that I'm taking it and why). If any fails, I flag it to whoever owns it and hand over what I learned instead of quietly absorbing it - silently making the work mine without telling anyone. [SAFE - decision procedure, no invented facts]
5. What would a real example look like? - Criteria, not content: a duty belonging to someone specific (or provably to nobody), evidence I took it (a ticket, a message, a teammate's account), and a cost I paid. Gather it from non-project work before the interview. [SAFE - checklist]
6. If a Bar Raiser (the interviewer Amazon trains to probe hardest) pushes for "one concrete task"? - Repeat the concession; never upgrade the spike or the tooling into a boundary crossing. That inflation is the move that turns a weak-but-honest answer into a failed one. [SAFE]

## Risk Check

1. "Recite your job description, then name the line you crossed." - No answer exists in the record. This is the GAP itself; survivable only because I state it first and bridge to the spike as clearly-bounded evidence. Lead with the admission - if the interviewer finds the gap before I say it, credibility dies.
2. Same trap Q24/Q30 refused.

# Q42 - tell me about a time where you received critical feedback, how did you implement it?

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary - took "your feature silently dies" seriously and chased it); Learn and Be Curious (the model/provider differences behind one bug report); Deliver Results (the command layer works across both backends)   **Story:** Tab Scroller - the "AI commands silently do nothing" feedback, traced to markdown-fenced and prose-wrapped JSON from the model, and the contract + tolerant-parser + explicit-failure fix I implemented (AI_WORKSPACE_FIX.js:72-128; background.js:1520); distinct from Q35 (same extension, comfort-zone spine) and Q91 (critical feedback on the BOM parser)

## Core Answer

The feedback on my Chrome extension was one line: "your AI commands silently do nothing sometimes." Tab Scroller is my personal extension - a searchable strip of all your open tabs - and typed commands like "group my research tabs" have an AI model pick which tabs the action applies to. [PARTIAL - the fix file records the failure and the repair; the session where the complaint came in isn't in the record, and I won't quote a person]

Silent was the worst kind of report: nothing to point at, nothing to reproduce. So I chased it through the plumbing. The AI's answer to my program has to be machine-readable: a small JSON object - a strict text format my code parses into tab numbers. The calls failed when the model answered correctly but not cleanly: it wrapped its JSON in markdown code fences - the backtick marks chat interfaces use for code - or prefixed a "Sure, here you go" sentence. The parser threw on the extra characters, and the old error handling swallowed it. The command just stopped. The feature wasn't broken; my plumbing called a good answer garbage because of its wrapping paper.

I implemented the feedback in three layers. First, tighten the contract: the instruction now states the exact shape, with examples and an empty-list rule, and the call requests a JSON response type from providers that support it - format as a property of the request, not a hope. Second, make the reader forgiving: trim the answer, strip a leading or trailing code fence, and if JSON is still buried in text, extract the outermost curly-brace object and parse that - with the model's temperature, its creativity dial, turned down. Third, make silence speak: a missing answer now says "the AI did not respond" instead of vanishing, and the same JSON-only reminder went into the local, on-my-machine model's prompt path, which had the same disease.

The judgment I'd defend: no single layer is trusted alone. The contract reduces messiness, the tolerant parser absorbs what survives it, and the explicit failure keeps the user informed when both give out. Any one of the three alone would have halved the bug and kept the mystery.

What stuck: whenever a probabilistic system - one that answers differently each time - feeds my code: contract shape, forgiving reader, loud failure. Never again a swallowed error in a user-triggered action.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: "AI commands silently do nothing" - model returned correct JSON wrapped in markdown fences or prose; JSON.parse threw; error handling swallowed it; dead buttons, no signal
- Customer: extension users (me first); silence was worse than an error because nothing was actionable
- Insight: the answer was right and the reading was rigid - the bug sat at the boundary between a probabilistic writer and a strict parser
- Action (mine): rewrote the instruction to an exact JSON contract with examples + empty-list rule + requested JSON response type; fence-strip + embedded-object extraction before parse; low temperature; explicit "AI did not respond" path; same JSON-only reminder for the local model path
- Result: commands parse across wrapped and bare answers on both hosted and local backends; failures surface visibly - behavioral verification on known-answer commands; no error-rate metric exists [PARTIAL]
- Learning: contract + tolerant reader + loud failure is the full fix for AI-output plumbing; silent catch blocks are half of every "does nothing" bug report

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Show me the code trail. - The fix file documents each layer: system instruction demanding only-valid JSON with example shapes and an empty-array rule; the call setting responseMimeType application/json with temperature 0.1; parsing that trims, strips leading/trailing triple-backtick fences, extracts the outermost {...} match, then JSON.parses; a guard that messages the user "AI did not respond" when the reply is empty (AI_WORKSPACE_FIX.js:72-128). The local-model path appends "Respond ONLY with valid JSON. No additional text before or after" (background.js:1520). [SAFE]
2. Who gave the feedback? - Not recorded - personal build, users were me and whoever tried it. My account: the complaint's content is proven by the fix file; the conversation around it isn't documented, so I don't stage one. [GAP - reporter unknown]
3. Why did the parser choke instead of handling it? - Original code did a naive JSON.parse on the raw text and caught the exception without surfacing anything. One bug (rigid parse) plus one habit (swallowed catch) = silent death. [SAFE]
4. Why not just always request JSON from the API? - The strict response-type flag exists on the hosted provider but not everywhere - the local model path needed the prompt-level reminder and the tolerant reader regardless. One mechanism can't cover both backends; three layers can. [PARTIAL - consistent with the two-path code]
5. Could the fence-stripping ever corrupt a good answer? - The extraction takes the outermost curly-brace span and only after fence removal; a malformed answer still ends at the explicit failure path - visible, not silent. No stress-test exists; this is read-the-code reasoning. [PARTIAL]
6. How did you verify the fix? - Ran commands whose correct tab sets I already knew on both backends, including fenced and prose-wrapped replies; the raw response also gets logged now so a future mystery is inspectable. No before/after error count. [PARTIAL - personal checks, uninstrumented]
7. Alternatives rejected? - Retrying the same call hoping for a clean answer (same wrapping, same failure); regex-only parsing without fixing the contract (brittle and still silent on failure); switching providers (migrates the disease). [PARTIAL - reasoning, no debate recorded]
8. How does this differ from your other feedback story? - Q91 is a stakeholder correcting domain semantics in a parts-list parser, implemented as splitter + test matrix. This is a plumbing bug in my own AI interface - no expert taught me the format; I reverse-engineered the failure. Different project, different lesson. [SAFE]
9. What would you do differently? - Design the parse boundary this way from day one, and never let a catch block be the final word in a user-triggered path. The three-layer fix should have been the first layer. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "Feedback from whom?" - Unrecorded; told as user-facing complaint proven by the fix file, no invented quote or scene. Defensible with the GAP stated before it's pressed.
2. "Did the silent failures stop?" - No metric exists; the claim is behavior-level across both backends on known-answer commands. Never upgrade to an error rate. PARTIAL.
3. Sibling consistency - same extension as Q35 (MV3/alarms spine) and Q80 (rate-limit spine): no shared claims, and this extension's published performance figures are design targets and stay out of every telling. [defensible - locked]

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5 / Ownership: 5 / Judgment: 4 / Impact: 4 / Credibility: 4 / Naturalness: 4
