# Q44 - tell me about a project where you had to learn a new skill and eventually excelled at it

**LP:** Learn and Be Curious (primary); Deliver Results (the excelling evidence).   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the defect classifier I taught myself to train (PREP STORY 3, training arc from STORY 14; canonical ~300-holdout telling).

## Core Answer

Before this project I had ML theory (machine learning - software that learns a task from examples instead of hand-written rules) and zero shipped models. The PCB inspection suite needed a defect classifier - a cropped component photo sorted as good, wrong value, wrong orientation, or missing (in plain terms: software that looks at a photo of one circuit-board part and files it into a category). The bar was explicit, set by what the floor needed: high accuracy on held-out data - photos the model never studied during training, so the score is honest - fast enough to keep up with the line (the factory's production pace), and retrainable when new defect types appeared (able to learn a new fault later without rebuilding the system). I had to learn the whole discipline - data, architecture, training, deployment - to clear it (from preparing the photos, to picking the model design, to teaching it, to shipping it).

I learned in the order the problem demanded. I read across model families - ResNet, EfficientNet, vision transformers (named designs for image-recognition networks, like choosing between engine models) - and chose against my actual situation: a few thousand small images, no big compute (no bank of graphics cards). Transformers want far more data than I had. The smaller EfficientNet variant gave nearly the accuracy of the big one at a fraction of the training cost. Then the data: I built a small labeling tool with keyboard shortcuts, and normalized the wild factory lighting with contrast enhancement (evened out glare and shadows across the photos), so the model learned components instead of lamps.

Then the failure that taught me the most. My first fine-tune: 99% on training data, 72% on validation (fine-tune = re-training a ready-made model on my photos; validation = a check-only slice of my own photos, set aside for grading and never studied; the pair counts correct answers on the photos it had studied versus the ones it hadn't - one logged run, measured, just ugly). It was memorizing, not learning. My instinct said grab a bigger model - that would have just memorized faster. Instead I learned *why* it happened: the randomly initialized classifier head (the layer that makes the final call - good, wrong value, wrong orientation, missing - and the only part starting from scratch) fires huge noisy gradients early on (the error signals used to adjust every setting in the model) and overwrites the useful features - learned edges, textures, shapes - borrowed from ImageNet (the huge public photo library the base model was pre-trained on). The fix was a training strategy I'd never used - freeze the base (lock most of the network so it can't change), train the head alone, then gently unfreeze the top layers (release the outermost layers, gradually) at a much lower rate (tiny adjustments instead of big ones). And I logged every run, so how many layers to unfreeze was a measured choice, not a guess.

The result is where "excelled" stops being a claim. 94% on a roughly 300-image holdout I never trained on - above the bar - with the train-to-validation gap closed, so it was generalizing (genuinely recognizing new parts, not recalling studied ones). What that 94% counts: correctly sorted photos out of the ~300 unseen ones; it comes from my final logged run - solid as a measured score, but a single run, not several. The model ran inside the same single-file browser tool the engineers already used (browser ML: the trained model itself runs inside an ordinary web page - no server, no installs). I judged on per-class recall (for each defect type, what share of the real ones did it catch - checked type by type, because one overall score can hide a category the model keeps missing) - the honest metric, since good boards far outnumbered defects - and a retrain on new data stayed cheap (a short refresh, not a rebuild).

What stuck wasn't any framework. It was learning how to make a number trustworthy - name the set it's measured on - and how to find the next failure and close it.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: Needed a production defect classifier; had ML theory but never shipped a model. Explicit bar: >90% held-out, <100 ms/image, retrainable for new defect types.
- Customer: Manufacturing engineers; the inspection tools were already live on the floor.
- Insight: The skill wasn't the API - it was the training dynamics. A 99%/72% split means memorizing, and the cause (random head overwriting pretrained features) dictates the fix.
- Action (mine): Chose the ~21M-param EfficientNet variant by matching model to data; built the labeling tool and fixed illumination myself; transfer learning + two-phase progressive unfreezing; logged every run; component-level 70/15/15 split; up-weighted rare defects and judged on per-class recall.
- Result: 94% on the ~300-image holdout vs the >90% bar; ~3-point train/val gap; ~45 ms CPU single-image benchmark vs <100 ms; >90% recall every defect category; ~30-minute retrain on one GPU; ran in-browser in the shipped tool.
- Learning: I learn by building the smallest real version, measuring honestly, and fixing the binding failure - and a number is only as good as the named set behind it.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What exactly was new to you? - Everything past theory: dataset design, transfer learning (reusing a model already trained on generic photos as the starting point), training dynamics (how a network actually behaves while it learns), and exporting a model to run inside the browser tool (packing the trained model into a web page instead of a server). I built the whole suite solo, so there was no one to hand it to. [SAFE]
2. How did you learn it fast enough to ship? - In pipeline order, validating each piece before the next: labeling tool, then lighting normalization, then fine-tune a pretrained network (re-train a ready-made model on my photos), then the training strategy. Not study-until-ready - build the smallest real version and measure it. [SAFE]
3. Why transfer learning instead of training from scratch? - ImageNet already encodes the edges, textures, and shapes a component crop needs. A few thousand images can't train a network from zero (from zero means re-learning even edges and shapes, and a few thousand photos isn't enough) - that was a simple-vs-complex call made deliberately. [SAFE]
4. Why that model size - did you consider bigger? - ResNet, EfficientNet, and vision transformers researched. Transformers want more data and compute than existed. Within EfficientNet, the ~21M-param variant (parameters = the tunable knobs inside the model) trailed the big one under two points on my data (less than two percentage points of accuracy) at roughly a third of the training cost (about a third of the time and compute to teach it) - right point on the curve, not a compromise. [SAFE]
5. Walk me through the failure. - First run: 99% train, 72% validation (the memorized-versus-check pair from my logged first run). I thought "more model" - what actually happened was the random head's early gradients scrambling the borrowed features. Changed to two-phase unfreezing: head alone first, then the top layers at a tenth the rate (the rate = how large each adjustment to the model is). Learned that the gap is the signal and the training number is vanity (the train-versus-check gap tells the truth; the studied-photos score just flatters). [SAFE]
6. How do you know 94% is real, not a lucky split? - Held-out ~300 images, above the explicit >90% bar, split by component so the same part never appears twice. What the 94% counts: correctly sorted photos out of those ~300 never-studied ones; it's from my final logged run - solid as one measured score, but not yet repeated. ~3-point train/val gap; per-class recall instead of one aggregate a majority class could inflate (one blended score can look great just by coasting on the abundant good boards). Honest caveat: single final run, no repeated seeds (re-running the whole training several times to see how much the score wobbles). [PARTIAL]
7. Where did the ~2,000 labeled images come from? - A labeling tool I wrote myself - keyboard shortcuts, CSV out (plain spreadsheet export) - fast enough that the whole set was an afternoon's work, not a week. The labeling speed-up numbers belong to another story; the point here is the data supply was part of the skill I learned. [SAFE]
8. Why per-class recall above accuracy? - Good parts outnumbered defects about 5:1, so an always-good model would score around 83% (with 5 good parts for every 1 defect, a lazy program stamping "good" on everything would look 83% accurate while catching nothing). Weighted defects 5x (told the training to count each missed defect five times as costly) and tuned on precision-recall (precision = how many of its "defect" alarms were real; recall = how many real defects it caught); every defect class came back above 90% recall (caught more than 90% of each defect type). [SAFE]
9. The 45 ms - measured how? - Single-image benchmark on CPU against the <100 ms bar (the time for one photo through the model on an ordinary computer processor, versus the under-100-milliseconds-per-photo requirement); hardware not recorded, and the deployed path ran in-browser, so I call it a benchmark, not a production floor. The ~30-minute retrain is what made it maintainable (the cost of teaching the model a new fault type later). [PARTIAL]
10. Hardest single thing to learn? - That unfreezing *more* of a pretrained network can make things worse on a small dataset - too few layers underfit, too many overfit (underfit = too little learned to do the job; overfit = memorizing the study photos); the middle was found from logged runs, not intuition. [SAFE]
11. Biggest trade-off? - Speed versus trust: I could have shipped the flattering 99% headline into a tool people already used (the studied-photos score, which looks great only because the model had already memorized them). Chose to block my own ship on the ugly validation number and root-cause it. [SAFE]
12. Any disagreement? - No person-vs-person dispute - solo build. The disagreement was with my own first instincts: bigger model, raw accuracy, unfreeze everything. All three were wrong and the measurements said so. [PARTIAL]
13. What would you do differently? - Collect far more than ~2,000 images; use a learning-rate schedule instead of a fixed rate in phase two (easing the size of the adjustments over time instead of holding them constant); assert input shape at inference so a train/serve preprocessing mismatch fails loudly (inference = the model running for real, not in training; the check is that incoming photos are preprocessed exactly as during training, so a mismatch crashes visibly instead of silently mis-sorting). [SAFE]
14. Can you show me the code? - Partly. The repo's checked-in training script is a later hardened variant for a different binary task (a two-outcome yes/no job); the 4-class pipeline behind the 94% isn't in the repo - it's the documented run from my records. And a separate note says "500-image test set," which doesn't reconcile with ~300 of ~2,000 at a 15% split (15% of ~2,000 photos is about 300, not 500 - the records conflict) - so I keep the canonical ~300 number and don't blend the two. [GAP - own it first]

## Risk Check
1. "Excelled" without an artifact for the exact 94% run - real GAP; defensible only if I lead with the documented, canonical ~300-holdout account and name the repo mismatch before it's found. [GAP -> disclose]
2. The 94% set attribution (~300 holdout vs the "500" note) - must stay on the canonical ~300; quoting 500 here contradicts Q11 and the bank-wide anchor. [defensible if locked]
3. 45 ms CPU vs in-browser shipped path - say "single-image benchmark," never "production latency." [PARTIAL]
4. Overlap with Q11 (same project, same failure) - distinction must hold: Q11 is the Dive Deep root-cause; this one is the learning arc + clearing the explicit bar; unfreezing mechanics stay brief. [defensible]

- LP fit: 5
- Ownership: 5
- Judgment: 4
- Impact: 4

# Q45 - a time when you did something which was very difficult and how you dealt with negative feedbacks

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary); Learn and Be Curious; Deliver Results   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - non-rigid alignment stage (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 2), canonical alignment telling; difficulty primary, feedback = documented corrective input on that work

## Core Answer

The hardest thing I built was the alignment stage of the PCB-vs-layout tool. A PCB is the green circuit board inside electronic devices, and the "layout" is its design drawing; "alignment" means lining up the photo of the real board against the drawing so they match point-for-point. The comparison flags a mismatch at 10 pixels - a part whose photo position sits more than 10 picture-dots away from the drawing's position gets marked - so the photo had to line up to about 2 or 3 pixels or everything after it was just noise. A normal shop-floor photo isn't a flat, straight shot, and a plain perspective correction - the standard software fix that straightens a photo taken at an angle, as if it were aimed head-on - left the far edge of the board off by 15 to 20 pixels (those numbers are distances measured in picture-dots, or pixels, on my own test photos, before and after the fix). Closing that gap is the difficulty.

To close it I needed non-rigid warping - not just straightening the image, but bending it to follow the board's actual curves, like flexing a rubber sheet. I chose thin-plate splines over elastic deformation and B-splines - three different mathematical ways of bending an image; the thin-plate spline imitates how a thin metal plate flexes, spreading each anchor's pull smoothly with distance. I picked it because it minimizes bending energy (the bend it produces is as gentle as possible), it's deterministic once you fix the control points (same photo, same anchors, same result every time - "control points" being the anchor spots matched between photo and drawing, which the rest of the image follows), it needs no physical constants like stiffness that don't mean anything for a board, and OpenCV - the standard free image-processing library - supports the math. The catch was that no JavaScript library did it, so I implemented it from the original Bookstein 1989 paper (the academic paper that first defined the method), in a browser.

What made it genuinely hard wasn't the formula, it was the failure mode. The spline bends the whole field through its control points, so one badly matched point pulls the entire warp the wrong way - you get output that looks precise and is silently wrong: everything appears neatly lined up, no error is reported, and the result is still bad. Correctness lived in rejecting weak control-point matches, not in getting the equation right. I also over-built it first: I wrote full SURF feature matching - an advanced technique for automatically locating distinctive reference points across two images - before I found that simple board-outline contour finding (tracing just the board's outer edge) handled most boards.

The feedback was concrete. Engineers told me the comparison was crying wolf - false alarms, meaning it flagged mismatches on warped boards that were actually fine. And when I brought them in to overlay the aligned photo on the layout - placing the two images on top of each other so a person can see whether the parts line up - their eye caught boards where my average looked good but the warp was subtly off at the edges. That eyeball-on-top-of-each-other review is the overlay spot-check, and it is the feedback: a plain-language correction from real users, not a formal review.

I didn't defend the average. I treated their overlay as a real check, not a courtesy, reproduced each flagged board, and kept the human overlay in the loop afterward, because an average can hide one wrong board. Now I ask for the failing board, not a verdict.

With the spline stage in, far-edge misalignment went from 15 to 20 pixels down to 2 or 3, and comparison accuracy on warped boards went from about 85% to over 98% - that's the share of warped-board comparisons the tool got right, measured on my own test boards, before versus after. The false alarms stopped. The lesson I keep: my number is the hypothesis, their observation is the data, and on a task this sharp the only way to settle it is to reproduce the case, not defend the metric.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: 10-pixel mismatch threshold forced alignment to ~2-3 px; perspective-only left the far edge 15-20 px off, so downstream results were noise
- Customer: manufacturing engineers who'd asked for the comparison tool and were getting false alarms on warped boards
- Insight: the error is structural - reflow warps boards non-uniformly, so no global transform can fix a mid-board bow; you need a non-rigid warp, and the metric's average can hide a single wrong board
- Action (mine): picked TPS over elastic/B-splines on stated grounds; implemented it from Bookstein 1989 in-browser; gated control-point matches by template similarity; added the human overlay check after the spot-check disagreed with the metric; owned the SURF over-build
- Result: 15-20 px -> 2-3 px far-edge misalignment; comparison accuracy ~85% -> >98% on moderate warping; false alarms stopped
- Learning: the number is my hypothesis, the user's failing case is the data - reproduce the case, don't defend the average; start with the simple method and add complexity only when data demands it

## Follow-Up Bank

1. What was actually hard, apart from the feedback? - Implementing thin-plate splines from the primary literature with no JS library, in a browser. The math is a radial-basis sum plus a linear term solving an (n+3)x(n+3) system - in plain words: every anchor point contributes a smooth ripple that fades with distance, and all those ripples are solved together as one block of simultaneous equations - but the operational danger is that one bad control point bends the whole field the wrong way, so a wrong result looks right. [SAFE]
2. Why TPS and not elastic deformation or B-splines? - It minimizes bending energy (gives the gentlest possible bend), is deterministic given the control points (same inputs, identical bend every time), needs no physical constants that have no meaning for a rigid-ish PCB, and is mature in OpenCV. I chose it on those grounds, not by default. [SAFE]
3. Was that really "negative feedback," or a QA finding? - Two documented pieces, and I'll be precise. Engineers reported the tool crying wolf on warped boards - a user complaint ("crying wolf" = reporting mismatch alarms when nothing is actually wrong). And their overlay spot-check corrected my result: it caught cases my metric passed but the warp was subtly wrong. The one formal team-review event in my record is the five-day-prototype review, which I use for other questions and am not re-telling here. I won't inflate this into a manager one-on-one that didn't happen. [PARTIAL - premise labeled, never inflated]
4. How did you keep from getting defensive? - I treated the claim and my metric as different kinds of evidence. My average - a single summary number across my test photos - said the alignment was fine; their eyes said a specific board was off. I asked which board and reproduced it, instead of arguing the average. [SAFE]
5. How did you verify the fix landed? - Quantitatively, a 20-image controlled test: average far-edge offset 2.1 px, standard deviation 0.8 px. In plain terms: across 20 board photos I tested under the same conditions, the far edge sat an average of 2.1 pixels from where the drawing said it should be, and the standard deviation of 0.8 measures how much individual photos varied around that average - typically within about a pixel of it. It's my own measurement on my own small test set, not a lab study, but it is the solid, repeatable one. Qualitatively, the engineers overlaid the aligned image on the layout and checked pads lined up - "pads" are the small metal contact areas where components solder on - that's what caught what the average hid. I kept both checks. [SAFE - these are the canonical alignment numbers]
6. What did you change because of the feedback? - Two things. The human overlay check became a standing part of how I validated alignment, not a one-off courtesy - it stayed in my routine rather than being done once to be agreeable. And I started asking for the specific failing case, because a case is reproducible and a verdict isn't. [PARTIAL - "standing" is my practice claim; the overlay-as-validation is documented]
7. How big is the warp it handles, and where does it still fail? - It handles photos up to about 30 degrees off-perpendicular (the camera tilted up to roughly 30 deg away from pointing straight down at the board) and roughly 3 mm of warp (a board buckled or lifted by up to about 3 millimetres). Above about 5 mm of deformation the control points can't capture it and a physically based model - one that simulates how the board actually flexes - would be needed - rare on the floor. I named the boundary instead of implying the warp was universal. [SAFE]
8. What's the real lesson, not the polish? - I over-built. I implemented full SURF matching (the advanced automatic reference-point technique) before finding board-outline contour detection (simply tracing the board's edge) was enough for most boards - more general, but slower and harder to debug. I should have started simple and added the non-rigid stage only where the data demanded it. [SAFE]
9. What's the judgment call in here? - Build vs reuse: I could have reached for an elastic or B-spline method, or a server-side library, and instead implemented the one method whose properties matched a deterministic in-browser check. Simplicity vs generality: I later rejected my own over-general SURF choice for the simpler contour method. Both were mine to decide. [SAFE]
10. Who did the work? - Me. The PCB suite was built solo; I was the only engineer on it. The alignment stage, the Bookstein implementation, and the response to the overlay check were all mine. No "we" in this story. [SAFE]

# Q46 - a time when your project deadline was very near, but you still took time to verify or test the data/code before submission

**LP:** Insist on the Highest Standards (primary); Deliver Results; Earn Trust (the reports came from users).   **Story:** the two bugs that reached users in the board-overlay tool - layer crop only working after a manual slide, saved layer position squished to the image boundary - recorded in the repo's Issues.txt, and the verify-reported-failures checklist they made me adopt before every submission (PCBvsLayoutnew/Issues.txt:1-2); distinct from Q81 (the pre-submission performance audit) and Q88 (owning fault for false alarms)

## Core Answer

Two bugs reached users in my board-overlay tool - it lays a circuit board's design layer over a photo of the real board - and they became my standing pre-submission plan.

The window was short. The tool drags the design layer onto the board photo so the automated crop inspection works on the matched area. On my machine it passed - I tested the way I designed: align, save, reopen, all inside the image. I shipped inside the date, which felt like speed and was actually luck. [PARTIAL - no dates in the file; the near-deadline is my account]

Then the reports arrived as plain notes in the project's Issues.txt file. First: the AI detection only worked if the layer was slid slightly into place, because the crop wasn't fitting correctly - the report asked for a robust way to move the layer over the board image. Second: a saved layer position always came back squished to the boundary of the image, even when the layer had legitimately been sitting partly outside the photo. Neither note records who wrote it - they read like the users of the tool, and I won't quote a person. [GAP - reporter unnamed in the record]

Both had one shape: user-visible interactions - sliding, saving, restoring - I'd treated as polish and never checked. Deadline math said skip. Users' math said the tool didn't work. So the fix round came with a rule I've kept since: before submission, run the reported failure as a named test case. I rebuilt the layer-move so the crop follows the layer, not a lucky nudge. Save now round-trips out-of-frame positions instead of clamping them to the image boundary. And the pre-submission list for anything touching overlays: slide the layer a little, slide it a lot, save with the layer partly outside the photo, close and reopen. Five minutes, stopwatch estimate, and both bug classes now have named checks. [PARTIAL - the two fixes are my account of the follow-up work; the issue file records the problems verbatim, the diffs aren't quotable]

Near deadlines stopped being a reason to skip verification and became the reason to do it: builds ship by email and USB to offline machines, a bad one spreads before I can react, and one report-diagnose-fix-redistribute cycle costs far more than five minutes up front. [PARTIAL - cost is qualitative; hours were never tracked]

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: two bugs reached users under a short window - crop only fitting after a manual layer-slide, and saved positions clamped to the image boundary - both invisible in my happy-path testing
- Customer: the engineers using the overlay tool day to day; their reports arrived as raw notes in Issues.txt, author unrecorded
- Insight: near a deadline, user-visible state transitions (drag, save, restore) are exactly what gets skipped - and exactly what ships broken
- Action (mine): rebuilt the layer-move to be robust without the nudge; fixed save/restore to keep out-of-frame positions; instituted the pre-submission checklist that runs each reported failure as a named case (~5 min, my stopwatch estimate)
- Result: the two reported classes have named checks; no instrumented before/after - the record is the issues file plus the follow-up rule [PARTIAL]
- Learning: verification time is not the budget line to cut when the date is near; a shipped bug costs a full report-diagnose-fix-redistribute cycle on offline machines

## Follow-Up Bank

We need to find a robust way to move the layer on the pcb image." Issue 2: "Saved layer position is always squished to the boundary of the image even if the last time the layers were exceeding the image coordinates." Verbatim in PCBvsLayoutnew/Issues.txt:1-2. [SAFE]

4. How do you know the fixes landed? - The issues are verbatim in the repo; the fixes are my account of the follow-up work and I can't produce the diff from the audited snapshot. I say "fixed and given a named check," not "here is the commit." [PARTIAL]

# Q47 - tell me about a time you had to make a design trade-off that prioritized the customer experience over technical convenience

**LP:** Customer Obsession (primary - the tool meets the user's camera, not the other way around); Invent & Simplify (touch - one import-step conversion, no user-facing pipeline change); Deliver Results (touch - the file kept shipping whole)   **Story:** the iPhone .heic photo problem in the PCB Analyst tool - users' photos were unopenable by any browser, and I paid the cost inside the tool with a runtime conversion at pick time instead of handing users a homework assignment (file_io.js:87, index.html:14); distinct from Q8/Q74/Q79 (same project, other spines)

## Core Answer

The trade-off was about a file format. Users of my PCB analyst tool photograph circuit boards with whatever is in their pocket, and a chunk of those pockets are iPhones - which save .heic, Apple's compressed photo format ordinary browsers can't open. My tool was refusing exactly the files my customers brought it.

The technically convenient answer was one line in a guide: "convert your iPhone photo to JPEG first." It costs me nothing - no new code, no new weight on an offline tool that carries every library inside itself as one double-clickable HTML file. And I knew what that line would do: some users wouldn't find a converter, couldn't install one on a locked-down factory machine anyway, and the tool would quietly stop existing for them. My documented friction was their wall.

The customer-first answer was to convert on their behalf, inside the tool, at the moment they pick the file. That's what I shipped: the import step looks at the chosen file, and if it's a .heic, a small converter library rewrites it to an ordinary JPEG right there in the browser, at a quality I set deliberately - 0.7 on the converter's scale: small enough for slow machines, good enough for comparison input, not for prints. The rest of the pipeline never learns the difference; the person at the bench picks their photo and it works like any other file.

I paid for that convenience twice. The bundle grew by a third-party library - code I didn't write - inside a single file already carrying everything it needs to run offline. And conversion runs on the user's machine at pick time, so choosing an iPhone photo is a beat slower than choosing a JPEG. [PARTIAL - neither the library's weight nor the conversion time is measured in the record; I keep both qualitative]

The judgment I'd defend: "supported formats" is a customer-experience decision, not a file-extension one. The format in the room was iPhone, so iPhone became a supported format - and the cost of that sat on my side of the wall, where I could absorb it once, instead of on theirs, where everyone would pay it every day.

One limit I own: the check looks at the file's extension, not its actual contents - a .heic renamed to .jpg slips past and fails downstream. I documented it rather than pretending the path was closed.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: factory users bring iPhone photos (.heic - Apple's compressed photo format browsers can't open); the tool refused the exact input its customers produced
- Customer: the engineers/inspectors photographing boards; locked-down machines can't install converters
- Insight: a documented workaround is a wall for the user; the pipeline should absorb format reality at the boundary
- Action (mine): import-step runtime conversion - detect .heic, convert to JPEG via heic2any at quality 0.7, swap the converted image into the pipeline (file_io.js:87-92); shipped the converter inside the tool (index.html:14)
- Result: users pick iPhone photos like any file; costs accepted knowingly - one extra bundled library, a slower pick for .heic (both unmeasured [GAP]); known limit: extension-based detection, renamed files slip through
- Learning: choose where pain lands - absorb it once in the build, or distribute it daily to users; pick the first, and measure the second only honestly

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Where's the code? - The file-input handler checks the chosen name for .heic, calls heic2any with the raw file as a blob, converts to image/jpeg at quality 0.7, and replaces the image URL with the converted one (file_io.js:87-92). The converter library loads with the page (index.html:14). [SAFE]
2. What is heic2any? - An open-source browser library that decodes HEIC - High Efficiency Image Container, Apple's photo format - into common formats like JPEG, so no server or install step is needed. [SAFE]
3. Why quality 0.7 and not lossless? - The converted photo feeds image comparison, not archival; a mild lossy setting trades invisible-for-the-job fidelity for a smaller working image on slow machines. The value is recorded in the code; the reasoning is mine, and it's a tunable constant. [PARTIAL - rationale not recorded]
4. What if the library isn't loaded or conversion fails? - The guard only converts when the library is present; otherwise the raw .heic URL flows on and the browser fails to display it - a visible dead end, not silent corruption. Honest weak point; no user-facing error message was built. [SAFE - from code]
5. What did it cost in size/speed? - Bundling one more library into an offline single-file tool, plus one conversion per iPhone photo at pick time. No measurement in the record - I won't put numbers on it. [GAP]
6. Why not convert server-side or pre-process? - There is no server: the whole point of the build is one offline file on machines with no network and no installs - the conversion had to live inside the browser or not at all. [SAFE - consistent with the canonical standalone account]
7. Did users ask for this? - No request is recorded and I won't invent a quote. My account is that iPhone-shot boards were the live failure the import guard answers; volume untracked. [GAP - reporter/volume unknown]
8. Alternatives rejected? - User-side conversion instructions (the trap this story is about), a desktop helper app (installs - ruled out by the environment), and extension-only support lists (same wall, differently worded). [SAFE - reasoning]
9. What would you do differently? - Detect by file contents, not name, and time the conversion on factory-class hardware so the "beat slower" gets an honest number instead of a hedge. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "Do you know how many users hit .heic, or what it cost?" - No, and the story claims neither; it's held as a qualitative input-reality fix with a recorded code path. Defensible as scoped; GAP if I ever upgrade it to measured impact.
2. "Renamed .heic files still break - so your trade-off leaks." - True and stated: extension-based detection is the shipped limit; the answer is the documented follow-up (content sniffing), not a claim the path is closed. Defensible.
3. Sibling consistency - this file no longer retells the deployment-format trade-off (it now lives with the surviving standalone files); the single-file/offline facts quoted here match the canonical account (one file, embedded libs, tens of megabytes, seconds to open). [defensible - locked]

# Q48 - tell me about a time when you had a blocker in your work and how did you resolve that blocker?

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary); Deliver Results   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the first EfficientNetV2S training run produced an unusable model (PREP STORY 14, backed by STORY 3). Training/dataset blocker - deliberately distinct from Q29's OpenCV.js deployment blocker; same event as Q11/Q44 retold here as blocker -> resolution.

## Core Answer

The blocker wasn't infrastructure - it was the deliverable itself. I was building the defect classifier for the PCB inspection suite - the PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device, and a "defect classifier" is a program that sorts a photo of one board part into one of a few labelled buckets: a cropped component photo in, a label out - good, wrong value, wrong orientation, or missing. The classifier was the heart of the tool, and everything downstream - the verification work, the ship date - sat behind it. My first training run gave me a model I couldn't use: 99% accuracy on training data, 72% on validation. In plain terms: "accuracy" is just the share of photos the model labels correctly; "training data" are the images it already studied during training, and "validation" is a practice set it checks itself against while training is still running - so it got 99 out of 100 right on work it had already seen, but only 72 out of 100 on fresh examples. The model was memorizing, not learning - textbook overfitting: it had memorized the answers instead of learning the rules. So the deliverable was blocked and the clock was running.

What I didn't do was retrain blindly at different settings, or grab a bigger model - a bigger model would have just memorized faster. I treated the gap itself as the diagnosis: 99 against 72 is what memorization looks like. That led me to the cause, which has a name - catastrophic forgetting. In plain words, I'd been fine-tuning - starting from an image model already trained on huge generic photo collections and continuing the training on my pictures - with the whole pre-trained network "open," meaning every borrowed layer was still allowed to change. The "classification head" is the new final layer that outputs my four labels, and a fresh head starts random, so early in training it fires big noisy gradients - the "you were wrong by this much" signals used to adjust a model - back into the pre-trained layers and overwrites the general features - edges, textures - that transfer learning (borrowing a trained model's eyes instead of teaching one from scratch) was supposed to give me for free. I was destroying the thing I was trying to reuse.

The fix was two-phase training: freeze the pre-trained base completely - lock the borrowed layers so they can't change - and train just the head until its gradients settled; then thaw the top layers of the base (unlock them again) at a much lower learning rate - the learning rate is the size of each adjustment step, so lower means gentler nudges - so they adapted to PCB images without being rewritten. I logged every run in Weights & Biases - an experiment notebook that records each training attempt so settings can be compared side by side - and measured instead of assuming - thaw too few layers and it underfits (doesn't learn enough), thaw too many and it overfits (memorizes again), and the middle was where it worked.

The unblock: 94% on a holdout of roughly 300 component images it had never seen - a holdout is the final exam: examples kept away from both the studying and the tuning, unlike the validation practice set the tuning process does peek at - so 94 out of 100 fresh photos judged correctly, with the gap between its training and validation numbers closed - that's what real generalization looks like: still right on material it has never met. The learning was that when the blocker *is* the result, bias for action doesn't mean guessing fast - it means moving fast on the cause, not the symptom.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: First classifier training run produced an unusable model - 99% training / 72% validation vs a >90% validation ship bar (the accuracy needed on the never-studied practice set before the tool was allowed to ship); the inspection deliverable stalled behind it.
- Customer: Manufacturing engineers; the inspection suite was live on the floor and the classifier was the heart of it.
- Insight: The 99/72 gap is the diagnosis - catastrophic forgetting: random head's early noisy gradients overwrite the borrowed pre-trained features (the new output layer starts knowing nothing; its early error signals damage the layers I was trying to borrow).
- Action (mine): Root-caused instead of retraining blind or scaling up the model; two-phase progressive unfreezing (frozen base + head, then thaw top layers at ~10x lower rate - adjustment steps shrunk tenfold); logged every run in W&B (the experiment notebook); found the thaw depth empirically (too few underfit, too many overfit).
- Result: 94% on the ~300-image holdout (final-exam images kept away from training and tuning alike); train-validation gap ~3 points; deliverable unblocked at the cost of roughly a week of schedule (estimate).
- Learning: When the blocker is the result itself, move fast on the cause - a flattering training number is not progress.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What exactly was blocked? - The classifier was the core of the inspection deliverable; a model that memorizes can't be trusted on boards it hasn't seen - and a false negative means a defective board ships (the model calls a bad board good). The bar to ship was above 90% on validation, so nothing that consumed the classifier could move until it generalized - performed well on fresh examples, not just studied ones. [SAFE]
2. What was the exact recipe? - Phase one: whole EfficientNetV2S base frozen (the off-the-shelf image model I borrowed, locked so it can't change), train only the head, 10 epochs at 0.001 (an epoch is one full pass through all the training photos; 0.001 is the size of each adjustment step). Phase two: unfreeze the last 30 layers, 20 epochs at 0.0001 (10x lower), with early stopping at patience 5 (training stops by itself once the validation score stops improving for 5 rounds in a row). [SAFE]
3. Why two phases - couldn't you just lower the learning rate? - Lower rate (smaller adjustment steps) alone doesn't fix the ordering: the random head's gradients corrupt the base either way. Freezing while the head settles is what stops the forgetting; the 10x drop is what lets the thawed layers adapt without being rewritten. [SAFE]
4. How did you pick "30 layers" - was that luck? - I tested thawing fewer and more in logged W&B runs: too few underfit (didn't learn enough), too many overfit (memorized again) on my ~2,000 images, the middle validated best. Honest caveat: directional evidence across runs - I never measured run-to-run variance (how much the score moves when you repeat the exact same training twice - same recipe, different roll of the dice), so I defend it by mechanism plus the closed train/validation gap, not confidence intervals (a stated range showing how precise a number is). [PARTIAL]
5. Which set is the 94% on? Isn't there a "500-image test set" in your notes? - Yes, and I'd flag it. The 94% I lead with is the documented ~300-image holdout - the final-exam set, kept away from both training and tuning, unlike the validation practice set - 15% of ~2,000, split by component so the same part never appears on both sides (the split was done by physical component, not by photo, so two pictures of the same part can't sit on both sides of the exam). An older note says "500-image held-out test," which doesn't reconcile with that split; I keep them apart rather than blending. [GAP - disclose, don't merge]
6. Per-class numbers? - What I stand behind is recall above 90% for every defect category - recall means, out of every 100 real instances of a defect, how many the model catches, and "per-class" means the bar holds for each defect type separately, not just on average. My notes carry exact decimals per class, but at this set size each defect class is only a couple dozen images - one sample moves a point (one photo flipping from right to wrong swings that class's percentage by roughly a point) - so I won't quote them as defensible. [PARTIAL]
7. Did it hit the speed bar too? - The bar was above 90% on validation and under 100 ms per image. Inference benchmarked ~45 ms on CPU (inference = the model judging one photo; ~45 ms is the machine's thinking time on a regular processor) - but that's a single-image benchmark, hardware unrecorded, and the shipped path ran in-browser under TensorFlow.js (a version of the model that runs inside an ordinary web browser, no installs), so I call it a benchmark, not a production floor. [PARTIAL]
8. Was this yours to solve or to escalate? - Solo build (I was the only engineer), so it was inside my own pipeline with a concrete path - escalating only adds delay. The version where I'd raise it: a blocker on input I don't control, say labeled boards I couldn't get. [SAFE]
9. What did the week actually cost, and where did it go? - Roughly a week against the schedule - estimate, read off the dates on the logged runs. Each training run was only ~30 minutes on one GPU (a graphics card - the chip models like this train on), so the cost was diagnosis and the layer/rate comparisons, not compute. The payback: the same recipe retrained on new defect types in that half hour, so the pipeline could absorb them without stalling again. [PARTIAL - estimate]
10. How do you know 94% wasn't luck? - Component-level split blocks memorization from leaking into validation (because the same physical part never appears on two sides, the model can't pass the exam by having already studied the answer); the ~3-point train-to-validation gap is the generalization evidence (it performs nearly as well on fresh photos as on studied ones); per-class recall checks no majority class is inflating one aggregate (if most photos were one easy defect type, a single average could look great while a rare defect got missed - checking each type separately rules that out). Single final run, no repeated seeds (I did not rerun the identical training several times to see how much luck moves the score) - that's the limit of what I claim. [PARTIAL]
11. What would you do differently? - Use a learning-rate schedule like cosine annealing in phase two instead of a fixed rate (a standard recipe that eases the step size down smoothly over time instead of holding it constant); collect far more than ~2,000 labels, which would make the thaw-depth choice less delicate. And I'd assumed more unfrozen layers always help - the overfitting config falsified that. [SAFE]
12. Can you show me the code? - Partly. The repo's checked-in training script is a later hardened variant for a different binary task (a yes/no job with two labels, not my four); the 4-class pipeline behind this run is the documented run from my records, not a hand-over-able artifact - which is why I name the set and the logs instead. [GAP - own it first]

## Risk Check
1. Attribution of the 94% (~300 holdout vs the "500-image" note) - defensible only if I lead with the documented ~300 and disclose the 500 as unreconciled; blending them is the exact error I claim to have caught. [GAP -> disclose]
2. No 4-class training script in the repo / checked-in script is a different task - real GAP; own it up front, never present the 94% as an artifact. [GAP]
3. "About a week" cost - estimate from logged run dates, not instrumented; say "roughly," and the per-run ~30-minute retrain keeps it plausible. [defensible as estimate]
4. 45 ms CPU vs the in-browser shipped path - label it a single-image benchmark, not a floor. [PARTIAL]
5. Same event as Q11 (dive deep) and Q44 (new skill) - if the interviewer hears both, own it: one project, different lens; this telling is the blocker-and-unblock, and Q29's deployment blocker is a genuinely different moment. [defensible - frame deliberately]

# Q49 - Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer.
**LP:** Customer Obsession (primary); Deliver Results.   **Story:** PCB inspector suite - 5-day prototype + install-free standalone build for the manufacturing engineers (STORY 1/8/12 + PREP STORY 4).

## Core Answer

The customer was the manufacturing engineers on the factory floor, and the ask was a tool to compare circuit boards automatically - a tool that looks at two pictures of a board and points out where they differ. Going past the ask, for me, was not stopping where the comparison logic worked - it was staying until they could actually double-click it on their machines and share it with each other.

First I went to them. Before I wrote any code I sat in on a few of their screen-sharing sessions. They flipped between two photos and circled the problem areas with Zoom's annotation tool. They didn't need a similarity score - a single number grading how much alike two boards are; they needed to see where the difference was. So the tool was built around color-coded highlighting that matched the workflow they already had.

Then I built a working prototype fast and put it in front of the team instead of polishing in private. The request had sat in a backlog for months as "too complex to scope," and the prototype surfaced the real problems inside an hour: it broke under lighting changes, it couldn't handle boards photographed at an angle, it couldn't export results. I fixed them in the order that mattered to them - alignment first, illumination second, export third. In plain words: line the two pictures up correctly even when the board was shot at an angle; keep working as the factory lights change; and let them get the results out as a file.

Then the environment. Their machines sat on the factory floor: no internet, no permission to install anything, IT stretched thin. The easy delivery was a Flask server (the tool running on one central computer everyone connects to), but it needed Python and configuration the team couldn't manage - deliver that and it ran nowhere. So I took on work nobody had asked for: I compiled the whole suite into one self-contained HTML file - a single web-page-style file that opens in the browser with a double-click and carries everything it needs inside itself. That meant rewriting the OpenCV.js loader (the ready-made image-analysis code that does the comparing) to decode its WebAssembly binary (its fast math engine) from an embedded data URL (packed inside the file itself instead of downloaded over the internet) at runtime, and moving auto-save into localStorage (the browser's own saving space on that one computer) with quota handling (respecting its fixed size limit). It opens in seconds on their machines. All of it so the engineer's job became a double click: no install, no network, no IT ticket.

I handed the file out by email and USB (a small drive you carry between machines), and it spread to fifteen engineers across two sites, who reported saving roughly twenty hours a week together. That last part is in their own words - what they told me, not something the tool ever counted.

What I'd do differently: treat the locked-down environment as the design driver from day one instead of after I'd built the server version. And I'd compress the embedded libraries (the code packed inside the file) harder - the twenty-five-megabyte file ran into a twenty-megabyte email cap: the file held about 25 MB of data, and the company's email refuses attachments over 20 MB.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: board-comparison request sat unscoped in a backlog (a queue of pending work) for months; "too complex."
- Customer: manufacturing engineers - factory-floor machines, no internet, no install rights, thin IT.
- Insight: they need to see *where* the difference is (their Zoom-circling workflow), and a tool they can't run isn't delivered.
- Action (mine): observed their sessions before coding; 5-day prototype (working version in five days); fixed their issues in their order; embedded the browser libs into one HTML file; rewrote OpenCV.js WASM loader off a data URL (the image code's math engine boots from inside the file instead of the internet); localStorage autosave with quota handling (the browser's on-computer saving space, within its fixed size limit); distributed by email/USB (carry-between drive).
- Result: before -> manual toggle + circling; after -> color-coded diff from a double-clicked file; ~15 engineers, 2 sites, ~20 hrs/wk engineer-reported (their words, not tool-counted).
- Learning: deployment environment is a day-one design driver; "above and beyond" must name a customer cost or it's gold-plating (polish the customer never asked to pay for).

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What did they ask for vs what you delivered? - The ask was automated comparison. I delivered one they could run on locked-down machines and share - a comparison tool that needs Python on the factory floor (needs that programming system installed on their machines) is a tool nobody uses. [SAFE]
2. How did you know highlighting, not a score? - Watched their screen-shares first: toggling between images, circling concerns in Zoom. The output had to show *where*, in a form they could point at. [SAFE]
3. Why ship a rough prototype? - It replaced my guessing with their words. The prototype took me five days, and lighting, angle, export came from them in the first hour; six months of scoping had produced nothing. I fixed in their priority order: alignment, illumination, export - lining tilted pictures up correctly, handling lighting changes, getting results out as a file. [SAFE]
4. Was export an unrequested delight? - No, be honest: the team explicitly flagged missing export at the demo. It was their ask, answered fast - above-and-beyond was the packaging (how it was delivered, not what it does), not the features. [SAFE]
5. Why not just the Flask server? - Server (the central-computer version) was less work for me but zero workability for them. Trade-off: I absorbed the build pain (embedding, loader rewrite, quota handling - stuffing the code into the file, reworking how it starts up, and respecting the browser's size limit) so their side became one double click. [SAFE]
6. What's actually in the single file / how big / how fast? - One self-contained HTML: embedding the browser libraries (ready-made image-analysis and document-reading code that runs inside the browser) plus the model weights (the trained numbers a defect-detection model carries with it) and the app itself pushed the file into the tens of megabytes - around 25 MB. Base64 WASM decode at startup adds ~2 s (unpacking the image code's fast math engine from the text form it's stored in inside the file); ~5 s to open on a factory machine vs ~2 s on the server build - that's the time from double-click to a usable screen. Verification: same known boards through both builds, outputs matched (I ran identical test boards through both versions and compared - same results). The load times are my own stopwatch over a handful of boards - rough, not instrumented (the software never measured it itself). [PARTIAL]
7. Why touch localStorage? - Server filesystem auto-save doesn't exist in a single HTML file; moved it to localStorage (the browser's own saving space on that one computer) with the 5 MB quota handled (the fixed 5 MB size limit - warn the user, then clear old entries). [SAFE]
8. Where do 15 engineers / 2 sites / 20 hrs/wk come from? - Engineer-reported recollection: they told me their comparison time dropped, based on how often they'd run boards. In plain terms: 15 = how many people used it, 2 = how many factories, ~20 hrs/wk = time they believed the group saved together. Not instrumented - "instrumented" means the software counted it, and it never did - I'd present it as "their reported savings," nothing stronger. [PARTIAL]
9. How do you avoid gold-plating? - Anchor extra work to a named customer cost. Offline packaging had one: machines with no installs, no network, no tickets. I left formal versioning/CI out on purpose (numbered releases with automated release checks) - no engineer's experience changed if it was in. [SAFE]
10. Hardest part? - Getting OpenCV.js to boot with no network: it wants to fetch its WASM from a URL (the image-analysis code tries to download its fast math engine from the internet when it starts). Had to embed the binary as a data URL (pack it inside the file itself) and patch the loader to decode it at runtime, debugging on a locked-down machine with no dev tooling (no debugger or developer tools installed). [SAFE]
11. Disagreement? - No conflict - the server default was the easy path and *I* rejected it against my own convenience. If pressed, that's the pushback: I pushed back on myself, not a stakeholder. [SAFE]
12. Larger scale / do differently? - Distributing a 25 MB file by email bumped a 20 MB cap (the company's email server refuses attachments over 20 MB, and this file was bigger than that); gzip (standard file compression that shrinks a file before sending) would have brought it near 15 MB. And I'd have treated the locked-down environment as the design driver before building the server version at all. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "Wasn't the standalone build just assigned work?" (the install-free single-file version) - Defensible: the assigned ask was comparison logic; nobody specified surviving a no-internet, no-install machine. The loader rewrite and packaging (reworking how the file starts itself up, and putting everything into one file) were self-initiated, aimed at a named customer cost.
2. "~20 hrs/wk, 15 engineers" - needs the honest label: engineer-reported recollection, not instrumented. In plain words: people told me their time went down; nothing was counted by software. Say so before they ask; don't defend it as a measurement.
3. "5 s / 25 MB load claims" - candidate's consistent account (matches STORY 4 anchor: ~25 MB, ~5 s factory vs ~2 s server - the seconds are time from double-click to usable screen on slow factory machines vs the server version); verify by "same boards through both builds"; never surface the repo-snapshot caveat in interview.

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5 / Ownership: 5 / Judgment: 4 / Impact: 4 / Credibility: 4 / Naturalness: 4

# Q50 - tell me about a time when you didn't know what to do next or how to solve a challenging problem
**LP:** Learn and Be Curious (primary); Dive Deep; Bias for Action.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - implementing Thin Plate Spline non-rigid warping with no JavaScript library (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md STORY 5; alignment telling = AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 2).

## Core Answer

The hardest "I didn't know what to do next" moment was implementing Thin Plate Spline (TPS) warping - a mathematical way of smoothly bending one image onto another, like flexing a clear sheet until marked points line up - when there was no JavaScript version anywhere. JavaScript is the language that runs inside a web browser; "no version" meant there was no existing browser-ready code of this method I could borrow. I knew what I needed - a non-rigid correction on top of the global alignment. Non-rigid means the bend can vary from one area of the board to another, not one fixed tilt for the whole picture; the global alignment is the single tilt-and-shift correction that lines the photo and the design up roughly.

The setup. I was matching photos of PCBs - the green circuit boards inside electronic devices - to their CAD layouts, the board's digital design drawing. A homography (one flat tilt-and-turn correction applied to the whole image) fixed the global tilt, but boards come out of a reflow oven - the oven that melts the solder and can warp the board - bent, and the bend isn't even - the middle bows more than the edges. A single global transform can't undo a local bend, so the comparison only meant something with a non-rigid stage. I searched for a JS TPS library - ready-made browser code for that bending method - and found none. The problem flipped from "call the right function" (use someone's finished piece of code) to "derive the algorithm" (work the math out myself), and that's a different kind of stuck.

Before I wrote code I picked the method. Elastic deformation - a warping method that simulates a stretchy material - needs material constants, stiffness numbers, that don't mean anything for a PCB. B-splines, another warping technique, add a control-grid resolution - how fine a grid of bending anchors to use - I'd have to guess. TPS minimizes bending energy, meaning the math keeps the bend as gentle as possible, and is deterministic once the control points - the anchor locations where photo and layout are known to match - are fixed. Deterministic means same inputs, same output every time, which mattered, because with no reference build - no existing implementation to compare my results against - I needed something to check against, not to tune.

The way out was the source. I read the original paper, Bookstein 1989 - the academic paper that first defined this method - because the easy explanations skipped the math. I implemented it piece by piece and checked each intermediate result against the worked examples in the paper. With no library to test against, those examples became my test - my controlled check: a repeatable, purpose-built test rather than just looking at day-to-day results. I wired it in after the homography and chose control points by template-matching known features - the software finds each landmark automatically by searching the photo for a small picture of it - corners, fiducials (small reference marks printed on boards for positioning), pads (the metal dots parts solder onto), dropping any weak match, because one bad point drags the whole warp.

The payoff was real. Far-edge misalignment - how far photo and layout still miss each other at the board's far edge, counted in pixels, the tiny dots a picture is made of - dropped from about 15 to 20 pixels down to 2 or 3, and the engineers stopped getting false alarms (boards flagged as defective that were actually fine) on warped boards that used to flag. In plain terms: the pixel drop is from a controlled test I set up on purpose (20 images - solid); the false-alarm relief is the engineers' own reports, not something I measured. I kept the boundary honest: it holds to roughly 30 degrees off - the board tilted that far from facing the camera straight-on - and 3 mm of warp; beyond that it breaks.

What I took from it: learn just enough for the next feature, then build it. I learned Canny (a standard algorithm that traces the edges and outlines in an image) for edges, CLAHE (an automatic contrast fix for uneven lighting) for lighting, TPS for the warp, only when each blocked me. A smaller version bit me too - I built full SURF matching (a heavyweight method for finding the same physical points in two images) before finding contour detection - just tracing the board's outline - was enough for most boards, and I lost about three hours to a TensorFlow.js tensor-shape bug. TensorFlow.js is Google's machine-learning library that runs in the browser; a tensor is a multi-dimensional grid of numbers and its "shape" is the order of that grid's layers, and mine were stacked in the wrong order. Now I check shapes before I run anything.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: No JavaScript implementation of Thin Plate Spline non-rigid warping existed, and global homography structurally cannot fix reflow-oven board warp.
- Customer: The manufacturing engineers running the inspection line (I built the suite solo; the engineers were the users and validators).
- Insight: With no reference build, pick the method whose ground truth you can verify - TPS minimizes bending energy, is deterministic given control points, so the original paper's worked examples could serve as the test.
- Action (mine): Searched and found no JS TPS; chose TPS over elastic deformation and B-splines on verifiability; implemented from Bookstein 1989, validating each intermediate stage against the paper's examples; wired it after the homography; selected control points by template matching with low-similarity rejection.
- Result: Far-edge misalignment ~15-20 px -> 2-3 px; engineers' false alarms on warped boards resolved; the comparison's 10-px threshold became reliable; holds to ~30 deg off-perpendicular / 3 mm warp.
- Learning: Learn just enough for the next feature, then build it; start simpler (I over-built full SURF before contour detection sufficed); check tensor shapes up front (lost ~3 h to a TF.js shape bug).

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Why not an existing library or a simpler method? - I searched; there was no browser JS TPS. And "simpler" wasn't: elastic deformation (the stretchy-material simulation) needs material constants with no clear meaning for a PCB, B-splines add a control-grid resolution I'd have to guess. TPS is deterministic (same inputs, same output every time) and verifiable, which is what I needed with no reference to test against. [SAFE]
2. How did you validate an implementation with nothing to compare it to? - Against Bookstein 1989 itself. The paper has worked examples, so I checked intermediate results stage by stage rather than only eyeballing the final image. Template-matched control points plus low-similarity rejection (any auto-found landmark that only vaguely matched its picture was dropped) kept a wrong point from silently pulling the warp. [SAFE]
3. Explain TPS simply. - It fits a smooth deformation through a set of control points while minimizing a bending-energy measure - like flexing a clear sheet so it passes exactly through marked dots while staying as unstrained as possible - so the warp is exact at the points and smooth between them. I supply correspondences (this photo point -> this layout point); it returns the local warp a global transform (one uniform tilt/shift for the whole image) can't represent. [SAFE]
4. How was 15-20 px -> 2-3 px measured, and how reliable? - It's far-edge misalignment: how far the photo and layout still miss each other at the board's far edge, in pixels. A 20-image controlled test - a repeatable test I built for the purpose on 20 board images, not day-to-day use - averaged 2.1 px, sd 0.8 (standard deviation: the typical spread around that average, so most results land near 2 px). Comparison accuracy - the share of board comparisons judged correctly - went ~85% -> >98%. The false-alarm fix on warped boards is engineer-reported recollection, not an instrumented count. [PARTIAL - the outcome half is engineer-reported, not logged]
5. What does it NOT solve? - It handles up to ~30 deg off-perpendicular (tilted that far from facing the camera straight-on) and ~3 mm of visible warp. Severe warp beyond about 5 mm still defeats it (would need a more physically based model - one that simulates how a real board bends), and steep angles past roughly 45 deg break feature matching (the automatic landmark-finding) outright. I'd say the boundary rather than imply it's universal. [SAFE]
6. How did you avoid being stuck for days? - I changed the question. "Find the function" (look for a ready-made piece of code) had no answer once no library existed, so the tractable version was "pick a method with a verifiable ground truth" (a known-correct answer you can check against), then build against it. The paper's examples gave checkpoints, so even with no next answer I always had a next test. [SAFE]
7. A real mistake in here? - Yes. I implemented full SURF feature matching (a heavyweight method for finding the same physical points across two images - works on almost anything, but slower and harder to debug) before discovering board-outline contour detection (tracing just the outer edge of the board) was sufficient for most boards. SURF is more general but costlier and harder to debug; building it first was the wrong order. Now I start with the simplest thing that could meet the threshold and escalate only if it fails. [SAFE]
8. The three-hour debug you mention. - A TensorFlow.js shape bug: TensorFlow.js is Google's machine-learning library for the browser; a tensor is a multi-dimensional grid of numbers and its shape is the order of that grid's layers. I fed the model a [1, 3, 224, 224] tensor when it wanted [1, 224, 224, 3] - same total of numbers, layers stacked in the wrong order. It "ran" but produced garbage, which is why it took ~3 hours to isolate. I now assert (automatically test) the input shape before inference (running the model on real data) as a reflex, so that failure is one line instead of three hours. [SAFE]
9. Was this depth worth it vs a workaround? - The comparison runs on a fixed 10-px threshold (a cut-off: any photo-vs-layout difference bigger than 10 pixels counts as a mismatch), so if alignment is off, everything downstream is noise. The warp was visible in the images and the requirement concrete, so the depth was tied to whether the tool worked at all - not polish. Had a simpler fix met the threshold, I'd have taken it; that's why I compared the three methods before committing. [SAFE]
10. Could you point to the exact paper examples and residuals you matched? - Honestly, I validated qualitatively (comparing by eye against the paper's figures) against the paper's worked examples as I went; I did not log per-example numeric residuals (the exact error distance for each test point). The durable evidence was the 20-image test and the engineers' spot-checks. [GAP - no per-example residuals recorded]
11. Hardest part and any disagreement? - The hardest part wasn't the coding, it was the self-doubt of no reference: a warp can look right while being quietly wrong, so discipline (checkpoints against the paper, not eyeballing) was the actual work. No teammate disagreement to report - I built the suite solo, so the engineers served as external validators, not collaborators. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. Headline 15-20 px -> 2-3 px (far-edge misalignment in pixels) / ~85% -> >98% (share of board comparisons judged correctly) - defensible; these are the bank's canonical STORY 2 alignment values, consistent with Q14/Q20, with a stated method (20-image test, 2.1 px / sd 0.8 - sd = standard deviation, the typical spread around the average).
2. "No JS library existed" - defensible but the sharpest probe; if pressed, my honest line is "none I could drop into a browser build at the time," not "none on Earth." Needs no number.
3. Engineer-reported false-alarm fix (the engineers' own telling, not measured) - needs a real number if pushed hard; currently a recollection, not instrumented (PARTIAL in the bank).
4. Solo authorship of advanced CV (computer-vision) math could read as over-claim - defensible: implemented from a primary paper and validated against its examples; the SURF over-build and the TF.js shape bug show real, imperfect authorship.

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5
- Ownership: 5
- Judgment: 4
- Impact: 4
- Credibility: 4
- Naturalness: 5

## Source
- No JS TPS / implemented from scratch / read Bookstein 1989 / validated against paper examples / "learn just enough" rule / Canny+CLAHE; TF.js [1,3,224,224]->[1,224,224,3] ~3 h debug -> `AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREP.md` STORY 5 (Action ~203-205; follow-ups ~216, 219).
- Reflow-oven non-uniform warp that homography can't fix; TPS chosen over elastic/B-spline (bending-energy, deterministic); wired after homography; control points via template matching with low-similarity rejection; 10-px threshold; 30 deg/3 mm capability; >5 mm and >45 deg failure modes; SURF over-build reflection -> `AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md` STORY 2 (Task 188; Action 196, 200, 202; Result 208, 210; Reflection 214, 216; follow-ups 240, 256).
- Canonical alignment numbers 15-20 px -> 2-3 px, ~85% -> >98%, 20-image 2.1 px / sd 0.8 (per STORY_FORMAT CANONICAL ANCHORS). STORY 12/13 excluded bank-wide. Distinct from Q29 (OpenCV.js/WASM blocker), Q48 (overfitting blocker), Q14/Q20 (alignment risk / deep-dive tellings), Q21 (out-of-comfort-zone arc). # Q51 - Have you ever sacrificed a short-term goal to achieve a better long-term outcome?
**LP:** Ownership (primary); Think Big.  **Story:** STORY 7 - From Monolith to Modular Architecture (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md).

## Core Answer

Yes - I gave up about 40 hours of visible feature work to restructure a tool that was already live and already working. "Restructure" here means a refactor: reorganizing the code without changing what the tool does. The 40 hours is my own estimate of the time it took me - not a timesheet record.

The tool was the PCB-vs-layout comparison - it checked a photo of a finished circuit board (PCB) against the board's design file - and by then it had grown into a single HTML file over 4,000 lines: markup, CSS, logic, configuration, even the SVG icons. In plain words: one web-page file with everything mixed together - the page's structure, its styling (CSS), the actual rules of the job, the settings, and even its little built-in drawings (SVG icons). The 4,000 figure is simply a count of the file's lines of code. When it was just me and the tool was young, that was fine. Then it became a tax. Debugging meant scrolling through thousands of lines. Reusing anything in another tool meant copy-pasting, and the copies drifted. A change in one section broke an unrelated one. And I was heading toward three tools on that base - the cost was about to multiply.

The short-term goal I sacrificed was feature velocity - how fast new capabilities actually reached the engineers: the start of my second tool slipped about a week - my estimate, not tracked - and every hour extracting modules was an hour delivering nothing they could see. ("Modules" = self-contained pieces of code, each doing one job; "extracting" one meant lifting it out of the giant file into a file of its own.) The refactor shipped zero user-visible features. The move the moment rewarded was to keep patching the monolith - the nickname for one giant file with everything tangled into everything else - and keep shipping. I chose the other path because a tool that's expensive to change eventually stops improving.

The tool was in production - engineers used it daily - so I couldn't take it offline. I mapped the natural boundaries first - UI components, business logic, utilities, configuration - the clickable pieces, the comparison's actual rules, the small helper functions, and the settings - then extracted one module at a time in dependency order: the pieces nothing else relies on before the pieces everything relies on. Independent utilities first, because they couldn't break anything; then UI components; the heavily coupled business logic - the parts most tangled with everything else - last. Each extraction followed the same loop: move the code, update imports (fix the references so every piece points to where its moved parts now live), run the regression suite plus manual checks, then move on. (A "regression suite" is a standing set of known test cases re-run after every change to catch anything newly broken.) If something failed, I reverted just that extraction - undid only that one move, not the whole day's work. The hardest was the alignment pipeline - the step that lines the board photo up with the design drawing so the two can be compared - which leaned on implicit global state: image dimensions, parameters, intermediate results sitting in shared variables that any code could quietly read or change, instead of being passed in on purpose. I turned those into explicit parameters and return values - inputs handed to each step, outputs handed back - which made it testable but forced careful interface design.

The payoff: 21 modules, each testable on its own. (The 21 counts those self-contained pieces; it's the number the natural boundaries produced, not a target picked in advance.) Debugging went from searching a monolith to opening the right file. Shared parts got reused instead of copied, and when the suite grew to three tools, one fix to a shared piece - like auto-save - improved all three at once. The engineers noticed no change in functionality. Exactly the goal.

What I'd do differently: start modular. The monolith was a shortcut that became debt - technical debt: the later cost of an earlier structural shortcut, paid in slower, riskier changes - and some debt remained, because a few modules still shared implicit state.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: 4,000+ line monolith HTML tool (one giant web-page file with everything tangled together), live in production, becoming expensive to change; three tools about to share the base.
- Customer: manufacturing engineers using the suite daily on the factory floor.
- Insight: a tool that's expensive to change stops improving; the maintenance cost was about to compound across tools.
- Action (mine): mapped boundaries; extracted 21 modules one at a time in dependency order, on the live codebase; regression suite (known test cases re-run after every change - 15 BOMs, the boards' parts lists, + 10 board images) after every extraction; converted alignment pipeline's implicit globals into explicit parameters/returns.
- Result: 21 modules ~150 lines each (a count of lines of code per module), independently testable, reused across the 3-tool suite, zero user-visible disruption; cost: ~40 hours of feature velocity (my own effort estimate, not a timesheet).
- Learning: start modular - the shortcut became debt; and some implicit-state debt still remained after.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What exactly was the short-term goal you sacrificed? - Feature velocity - the rate at which new features reached the engineers. The engineers had a request queue, and the refactor produced no user-visible output at all. The payoff was entirely in how fast and safely I could change the tool afterward. [SAFE]
2. Nobody assigned this - how did you justify 40 hours of invisible work? - I was the only engineer, so the trade-off was mine to make. The alternative had a cost I could already feel: scrolling 4,000 lines of code to debug, copy-pasted components drifting, changes breaking unrelated sections. And I was about to build two more tools on the same base - paying it three times later vs. once now. [SAFE]
3. How do you refactor a live tool without breaking it? - Small incremental extractions, verification after each: imports updated, 15-BOM + 10-board-image regression suite plus manual tests, revert on failure (undo just that one move). The regression suite is a standing set of known test cases - 15 boards' parts lists (BOMs) and 10 board photos - re-run after every change to catch accidental breakage. Refactor commits kept separate from feature commits, so any failure had exactly one possible cause. [SAFE]
4. How did you pick the extraction order? - Dependency and risk. Utilities (small helper functions - image preprocessing, file handling) had no dependents -> first. UI components (the clickable pieces) -> next. Coupled business logic, especially the alignment pipeline (the step that lines the photo up with the design drawing) -> last, with the most careful interface design. [SAFE]
5. Wasn't "just work around the monolith" cheaper? - Working around it was the problem. Ad-hoc patches add coupling - more tangling, so touching one piece moves others - they don't reduce it. The cheap option was cheap only for the week you did it. Caveat I'd own: a refactor can gold-plate - keep polishing past the point of benefit - I stopped at boundaries causing real pain (debuggability, reuse, testability), not a perfect architecture. [SAFE]
6. Give me an example of the global-state problem. - alignImage() read currentImage from global state: a function quietly fetching its input from a shared, file-wide variable; became alignImage(image, params) returning alignedImage: the image and settings are handed to it, and the result is handed back. More verbose calls, but clear data flow and a function I could test in isolation - checked on its own, without the rest of the file around it. [SAFE]
7. How do you know the refactor actually paid off? - Honest status: qualitative plus structural. Evidence: shared components genuinely reused across the three tools; a single auto-save fix improved all three; per-module testing of the 21 modules, averaging about 150 lines of code each, existed where none did before; debugging was subjectively faster. The numbers here are structural counts - how many pieces the code came out as, how long each is - while the speed claim itself is my experience, not a measurement. I never instrumented bug-fix time before vs. after. [PARTIAL]

9. What stayed broken or unfinished? - Some modules still shared implicit state after the refactor - a few hidden shared variables were left in place; a stricter pass would make every dependency explicit - every input visibly handed in and out. I left that debt named, not hidden. [SAFE]
