# Q85 - describe a time when you needed to deep dive to solve a problem

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary); Are Right, A Lot (touch - changed my belief about the score on evidence).   **Story:** BGSW PCB suite - the code audit that found the letterbox-padding bias in the SSIM component score (BAR_RAISER_TECHNICAL_PREP.md Finding 3). Distinct from Q11/Q16/Q20/Q33/Q52: this is the scoring-metric audit, and it is diagnosis-only - the fix is scoped, not landed, and I claim exactly that.

## Core Answer

The deep dive I'd point to is one where the numbers looked fine and the metric - the formula that turns a comparison into a score - was quietly wrong. I was building the component comparison in the PCB inspection tool - crop a part from the board photo and from the layout, score how different they are, flag the ones that differ. ("Crop" = cut out the small picture of one part; "layout" = the board's design file; "score" = one number saying how much the two cut-out pictures match.) The pipeline produced plausible scores. I didn't trust the pass rates - how often parts sail through as OK - so I went into the scoring code to see exactly how the number was made.

The first thing I found was a normalization step - a make-the-pictures-the-same-shape step taken before comparing - doing more than it admitted. To compare crops of different shapes, I letterboxed each one to a 128x128 tile (a square picture 128 dots across by 128 down), padding with a constant gray to keep the aspect ratio - the width-to-height proportions - the way a widescreen movie gets bars on the sides instead of being stretched. Then SSIM - structural similarity - was computed over the entire tile, padding included, and reduced to a single number by taking the mean of the similarity map: instead of reporting how alike each spot is one by one, all those spot-scores get averaged into one figure. SSIM is a standard, published formula for how much two pictures resemble each other - not something I invented - and on its scale 1 means a perfect match.

That's where the dive paid off. The padding is identical in both images by construction - by the very way the framing step works, same gray, same rectangle - so local SSIM there is essentially a perfect match. The mean drags the score toward "pass," in proportion to how much of the crop is padding. A part with a 2:1 aspect ratio - twice as wide as tall, or the reverse - is about half padding, so half its score is guaranteed "identical." That "half" is plain geometry, not a measurement: a 2:1 picture forced into a square frame is half border by area. The detector was systematically most blind on exactly the parts I cared about - tall connectors and wide ICs (integrated circuits - the chips on a board).

I read the scoring path - the whole chain of code that produces the score - end to end, checked the full-tile mean was live in every copy of the file, and traced the aspect-ratio dependence to the one step that correlated with shape. That part of the work is done and solid.

The fix I want to be precise about: it's diagnosed and scoped, not landed - I worked out what's wrong and exactly what the change would be, but I have not made the code change and nothing has been re-measured. The change is small - restrict the mean to the valid region using the crop bounds the letterbox step already computes, meaning the code already knows where the real picture sits inside its frame, or pass a validity mask - a per-pixel flag marking which dots are real image and which are just padding. It's on my to-build list. I didn't make the change, I didn't re-measure it, and without a labeled set - pictures with the right answer recorded by a human - I couldn't quote a recall delta, i.e. how much better at catching real problems the fix would make the tool - so I won't.

What I keep from it: a metric is only as good as the region it's averaged over, and a normalization step can inject a bias that never crashes anything - it just makes the numbers plausible and wrong. And a diagnosis is something I did; a fix and its delta are things I'd have to show.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: component-similarity scores looked plausible but pass rates didn't hold my trust; metric suspected quietly wrong
- Customer: factory engineers relying on the flags - the detector was least sensitive on connectors/wide ICs, the parts whose absence matters most
- Insight: letterbox padding is identical in both images -> local SSIM  1 there -> full-tile mean dilutes real content in proportion to padded fraction; bias scales with aspect ratio
- Action (mine): read the scoring path end to end; isolated padding as the only shape-correlated step; confirmed the full-tile mean live in the shipped code; scoped the fix to the already-computed crop bounds (ROI-restricted mean or validity mask)
- Result: a documented, mechanistically-explained bias + a precise fix plan - diagnosis landed; fix NOT applied, NO measured delta claimed
- Learning: metrics are only as good as the region they average over; normalization can inject silent bias; claim the diagnosis, not an unshown fix

## Follow-Up Bank
1. How did you find it - did something crash? - No. Nothing crashed; that's what made it worth the dive. There was no score anomaly to chase - I just read the scoring path, the entire chain of code from the cut-out pictures to the final number, end to end, and padding was the only step correlated with shape. [SAFE]
2. Walk me through the mechanism. - Crop padded to a 128x128 square - 128 dots by 128 dots; that size is a configuration value set in my own code and read straight from the shipped file, so it's exact, not a measurement - with constant gray. SSIM computed over the whole tile, reduced by a mean. In the padding the two images are identical by construction, so local SSIM is essentially 1 - the top of its scale, a perfect match; the mean is pulled toward "pass" in proportion to the padded fraction, which rises with aspect ratio. Real-content similarity gets diluted by guaranteed-perfect padding. [SAFE]
3. Have you fixed it? - No, and I want to be exact. I identified the fix - reduce the SSIM map over the offset/width/height rectangle the letterbox step already computes, in plain terms: average only the pixels inside the real picture, whose position and size the code already stores - or pass a validity mask, a per-pixel marker of real-vs-padding - but the code still averages the full padded tile, and my prep notes list "fix and measure" as a to-build item. I won't present designed work as built. [SAFE]
4. What would measuring it take? - A labeled set: pictures of parts with the right answer recorded by a human - roughly two hundred components, deliberately heavy on non-square connectors and ICs, run before and after the ROI restriction (ROI = region of interest, the real-picture rectangle), with a precision-recall curve so the fix has a real before/after - a chart of how many of the flags are genuine defects versus how many genuine defects get caught. The ~200 is my planned sample size, an intent, not a dataset that exists yet. My own training-data collector already does crop labeling - that's the tool I'd reuse. [SAFE - framed as plan, not result]
5. How long to land the change? - The code change itself is a couple of hours - my own estimate as the person who wrote and audited that code, not a tracked figure. The honest part - labels plus the before/after measurement - is the longer loop, and that's the part I hadn't closed. [SAFE - estimate, labeled as such]
6. What else did you find in that function? - Two smaller warts: an intermediate value computed and then recomputed - the code did the same arithmetic twice, with a comment admitting the first pass was a hack - and an allocation that was never used and deleted at the end - memory the program reserved for a value it never read. No effect on results, but they told me the path had never been scrutinized. [SAFE]
7. Why did a bug like that survive? - The scoring functions were pure - they just take inputs and return outputs without touching anything outside themselves - but lived in files that touched the DOM at load time, the live structure of a web page, so nothing could import them and no headless test - an automated test run without opening a browser window - could run. If SSIM had been testable in isolation, one aspect-ratio case would have exposed the bias immediately. Making the core importable is the fix behind the fix. [SAFE]
8. Why not quote how much SSIM counts for in the overall score? - Because my stories give different weight formulations for the comparison engine, and blending them would invent a number. The bias mechanism doesn't need the weight - a biased signal is biased whatever its weight. [SAFE - single-telling discipline]
9. So what did you actually change? - The dive was the change to my understanding, and it's verified work: full read of the scoring path, the aspect-ratio dependence traced to padding, the bug confirmed live in the shipped code. The code change is scoped and scheduled, not shipped. [SAFE - the critic's grounding: "gets work done" = the completed audit]
10. Hardest part? - Saying "I found the bug and I'm not going to pretend I fixed it." The temptation was one confident sentence closing the story; honesty left it open-ended, which is truer. [SAFE]
11. What would you do differently? - Test pure scoring functions headlessly from the start, and treat any averaged metric's denominator - every pixel the average sweeps up, gray borders included - as a first-class thing to audit. And if I'm going to flag a bias, budget the labeled set in the same pass so diagnosis and proof ship together. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "A deep dive with no delivered fix - so what?" - Prepared and honest: the delivered work is the audit itself (follow-up 9); the fix is explicitly scoped-not-landed. Defensible as stated; never let the tense drift toward "fixed."
2. Any measured improvement implied? - None. No recall delta, no before/after accuracy; the 0.71->0.88 figure in the prep doc is a hypothetical payoff and stays unquoted. Defensible.
3. SSIM weight in the composite score - different tellings assign largest weight to different signals; this story quotes no weights. Must keep it that way if pressed. Defensible via follow-up 8.
4. Near-dup risk with Q11/Q16/Q20/Q33/Q52 - distinct artifact (scoring-metric audit), distinct numbers (none shared), and the diagnosis-only close appears nowhere else. Defensible.

## Readiness (1-5)
- LP fit: 5 - Dive Deep across all strength indicators; "gets work done" grounded in the completed audit, not the unlanded fix
- Ownership: 5 - solo-built tool; the audit, the mechanism, and the scoping are all mine
- Judgment: 4 - trust-no-plausible-number call, claim-boundary discipline; the open-ended close costs a point vs a shipped result
- Impact: 3 - real insight, no measured outcome; honest diagnosis-only ceiling
- Credibility: 5 - tense is exact throughout; hypothetical figures refused; weight-blend avoided
- Naturalness: 4 - spoken flow good; the "what I actually changed" paragraph is the beat to rehearse so it sounds grounded, not defensive

# Q86 - a time where you interacted with a customer with negative feedback directly

**LP:** Customer Obsession (primary); Earn Trust; Learn and Be Curious   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - STORY 2 warped-board false alarms and the in-person overlay correction; spine = the direct interaction and how I handled the feedback in the room (distinct from Q45's difficulty spine and Q78's feedback-loops spine)

## Core Answer

The clearest piece of negative feedback I got came straight from the manufacturing engineers who used my PCB-vs-layout comparison tool - told to my face, and they were right. (A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device; the "layout" is its design drawing.) The tool was flagging mismatches on warped boards that were actually fine. Warped means the board bent or curled out of flat. A false alarm is when the tool cries wolf - it says there's a problem where there isn't one - and that's the worst feedback a QA tool can get, because every false alarm sends someone over to hand-check a part that was never wrong.

The context: the tool compares a photo of a real board against its layout and calls out missing or shifted components. It flags a mismatch at about 10 pixels - a pixel is one of the tiny dots a digital photo is made of, so the tool calls a defect when the photo and the drawing sit 10 dots apart over a part. That setting is a fixed choice I made, not a measurement, and it means the alignment - how exactly the photo lands on top of the drawing, part over part - has to hold to a couple of pixels or everything after it is noise. My alignment was one global perspective correction (a single uniform tilt-and-stretch applied to the whole picture equally - one adjustment for everything), and by my own metric it looked good.

I could have pulled up the numbers at them. Instead I asked them to show me. They put the aligned photo over the layout like a tracing - an overlay check - and checked the pads (the small metal spots where components solder on), and right there some pads plainly didn't line up - on boards where my average metric said fine. My number and their eyes disagreed, and their eyes were right. The average was hiding a local problem: boards warped in the reflow oven - the oven that melts the solder joints, whose heat bows the board - and the warping wasn't uniform, so the middle bowed differently than the edges. One global transform can't straighten a bow in the middle of a board.

How I handled the moment mattered more than the fix. I didn't defend the metric and I didn't leave the desk. I had them mark the failing boards, I reproduced each one myself on the same inputs, and I treated their overlay as data I didn't have rather than an opinion to argue with. Then I went back to the physics and added a second, non-rigid stage - a thin-plate spline, a rubber-sheet-style correction that bends the picture by different amounts in different places, anchored at control points I placed at the corners, the fiducials (small engraved reference dots boards carry for machine positioning), and the pads - to correct the local deformation.

Far-edge misalignment - how far the photo sat off from the drawing at the corner farthest from the middle, counted in photo dots - dropped from 15 to 20 pixels to 2 or 3, comparison accuracy on warped boards went from about 85% to over 98% (the share of boards the tool judged correctly - real defects caught and good boards left alone, out of every hundred checks), and the false alarms stopped. Both numbers are measured before/after comparisons from my alignment testing, not guesses. And I kept their overlay check in how I validated, because it caught what the average couldn't.

What I took from it: when a customer says my result is wrong, my number is the hypothesis and their observation is the data. You handle negative feedback by finding the failing case with them, not by winning the argument.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: warped boards triggered false alarms; my global-homography alignment passed my own metric but failed on the pads, and the 10-pixel mismatch threshold made alignment accuracy everything downstream
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers who used the comparison tool - negative feedback delivered directly, in person, and correct
- Insight: averages hide local failures - reflow warps boards non-uniformly, so a global transform structurally can't fix a mid-board bow; the customer's eyes were a measurement I didn't have
- Action (mine): asked them to show the failure instead of defending the number; had them mark failing boards and reproduced each one; added the non-rigid TPS stage (control points at corners/fiducials/pads); kept their overlay check in my validation
- Result: 15-20 px -> 2-3 px far-edge misalignment; comparison accuracy ~85% -> >98% on moderate warping; false alarms stopped; engineers trusted the tool again
- Learning: my number is the hypothesis, their observation is the data; handle negative feedback by finding the failing case together, not by winning the argument

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Was that really direct negative feedback from a customer, or a QA finding? - Two documented pieces, and I'll be precise. The engineers reported false alarms on warped boards - user feedback. Then the overlay check was direct and corrective, in the room, with them driving it. In plain words, the overlay check is laying the aligned photo over the drawing like a tracing sheet and looking to see whether the parts actually sit on their spots. I don't have a verbatim quote, so I won't invent one. [SAFE - premise labeled, never inflated]
2. How did you keep from getting defensive? - I separated the kinds of evidence. My aggregate said fine; their overlay showed specific pads off. I asked them to show me the failing boards and reproduced them, instead of arguing the average. The case decides. [SAFE]
3. What if they'd been wrong - a bad photo, not a bad tool? - Reproducing it would have shown that, and I'd have said so. That's why I reproduced rather than either conceding or arguing blindly. Here the reproduction matched what they saw, so the tool was wrong. [SAFE]
4. What specifically did you change? - A non-rigid thin-plate-spline stage after the homography (the first-stage global correction - one uniform tilt-and-stretch for the whole picture), control points at corners, fiducials, and pads, with template-similarity gating on control-point matches - meaning each anchor is checked against what it's supposed to be sitting on before it's trusted, because one bad point bends the whole warp. [SAFE]
5. Why TPS over elastic deformation or B-splines? - It minimizes bending energy - it picks the smoothest possible bend through the anchors - is deterministic given the control points (same inputs, same output, every time), needs no physical constants that don't mean anything for a board (real material properties like stiffness, which a photo doesn't have), and the math is mature in OpenCV (the standard free image-processing library). Chosen on those grounds, not by default. [SAFE]
6. How measured - how did you know it actually fixed it? - Quantitative: a 20-image controlled test with ground-truth markers - twenty board photos I set up on purpose against known correct positions, so the right answers were fixed in advance - average offset 2.1 pixels (how far the photo landed from where it should have been, on average) with a standard deviation of 0.8 (typical spread around that average - most boards within about a pixel of it). Qualitative: I kept the engineers' overlay spot-check alongside it. Both checks, because the first one alone missed what the second caught. [SAFE - canonical alignment numbers]
7. How reliable are the headline numbers? - In plain terms: the photo's far edge used to sit 15-20 dots off the drawing, now 2-3; and on bent boards the tool judged roughly 85 of every hundred correctly before, better than 98 after. 15-20 px -> 2-3 px and ~85% -> >98% are the bank's one canonical alignment telling (STORY 2); I don't blend the alternate 5-10 px or timing figures from other tellings of the same pipeline. [SAFE]
8. Where does it still fail? - It handles photos up to about 30 degrees off-perpendicular (camera angled up to about 30 degrees away from straight overhead) and roughly 3 mm of warp (how far the board's surface bows away from perfectly flat); above about 5 mm of deformation the control points can't capture it. Rare on the floor - I name the boundary instead of implying the fix is universal. [SAFE]
9. What was the hardest part of the interaction itself? - Letting go of a metric that looked good in front of the people using the tool. The physics fix was work; admitting an average can hide a wrong board changed how I validate. [PARTIAL - my reflection, not a source line]
10. Any disagreement in the room? - Not with the users. The resistance I had to work through was my own prior assumption that a passing aggregate meant the alignment was right. [PARTIAL - no documented user conflict]
11. What's the judgment/trade-off? - Defend the number or find the case; and a simple global transform vs. adding a non-rigid stage that costs compute and complexity. I kept the global stage and added local correction only because their failing boards demanded it, and kept a human check even after the numbers passed. [SAFE]
12. Did the false alarms come before or after the fix? - The source records them in the post-fix result line ("previously triggered false alarms"); I'm telling the pre-fix problem that motivated the work. # Q87 - describe a time when you optimized the performance of an application

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary - located the cost by stage before touching it); Invent & Simplify (deterministic shortcut in front of the model); Deliver Results (common case made cheap inside the extension's constraints).   **Story:** Tab Scroller - the AI command pipeline's latency breakdown and the staged fix (`IMPLEMENTATION_GUIDE.md` "Expected Performance Gains" + `background.js`). Same project as Q66, different spine: Q66 is the routing/simplification arc and owns the token-and-cost headline; this one is *where the seconds actually went*.

## Core Answer

The application was the AI command layer in Tab Scroller - the part that turns a typed instruction into an action - my Chrome extension (a small add-on that adds features to the Chrome browser), and the performance problem was that every typed command cost the same whether it was trivial or hard.

You'd type "group my coding tabs", and it read every open tab, pulled the full text of each page, and sent the whole pile to the model (the online AI service that reads the text and replies with what to do). On a window full of tabs that ran about eight seconds.

My instinct was that the model was slow. I looked instead at what happened before the model call, and the split wasn't close: roughly five of those eight seconds were just reading pages, one at a time - the software copying each page's text off the screen, not the AI taking that long to think. The model was being handed the body text of every page to answer a question that needed titles and URLs.

That reframed the job. The expensive work sat in front of the inference (before the AI was even asked), so I cut it in the order the stage breakdown suggested. Reading first: pull page data in concurrent batches - a handful of pages at the same time - instead of one page after another, which took five seconds down to about half a second. Then read less: a deterministic pre-filter - a fixed word-matching shortcut with no AI in it - scores tabs against a fixed category map and keywords before any extraction happens, so the model sees the relevant handful instead of everything. Then, for commands whose shape is predictable, a local rule layer - simple built-in shortcuts that run directly on the user's own computer - matches and runs them on the machine with no API call at all (no round-trip to an online service).

Those before-and-after figures are the projected gains written in my implementation guide - design targets I set before building, not a benchmark (a formally recorded timing test) I re-ran - and I keep saying it that way. What is real in code is the shape of the fix: extraction does batch, the pre-filter does run before extraction, and the rule path does make zero calls.

The trade-off I took was keeping the pre-filter dull. Keyword and category scoring will miss a fuzzy request; I accepted that instead of pulling in local embeddings - a small word-similarity AI running on the user's own machine - because a miss only means the filter keeps more tabs. It fails toward slower, never toward wrong. Embeddings are the next phase, once telemetry (the app's own timing logs) shows they earn their weight.

And that's what I'd change: I optimized before I could see. There's no per-stage timing or token logging, so every gain is designed rather than measured. Next time I instrument first, then tune.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: one uniform path - a typed command cost the same whether it was "close YouTube tabs" or a fuzzy grouping request; slow, and dead without network.
- Customer: heavy tab user (me); the value was a command that answers fast enough to keep using.
- Insight: the model was not the bottleneck - most of the time was pre-inference work (sequential full-text extraction of tabs that didn't matter), so optimize stages in cost order, not the obvious suspect.
- Action (mine): traced the path stage by stage; concurrent batched extraction; deterministic keyword/category pre-filter ahead of extraction; local rule layer for pattern-shaped commands; compressed prompts behind that.
- Result: extraction projected 5s -> ~0.5s and the command off the model path entirely for predictable requests - the guide's "Expected Performance Gains", labeled projected; the shipped code is the real claim.
- Learning: measure before you optimize - no per-stage telemetry means my wins are designed, not proven; instrument first next time.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What was the application and the exact command path? - Chrome extension, MV3 background worker (the extension's built-in task-runner, which wakes up when something happens). Typed command -> query all open tabs -> extract full page text per tab -> prompt to Gemini (Google's online AI service) or local Ollama (free software that runs an AI model on your own computer instead of online) -> action. The whole path is mine; solo build. [SAFE]
2. How did you find the real bottleneck? - By attributing cost to stages rather than timing the total: the before path queried every tab and extracted text sequentially (one tab after another), so a five-second read step sat in front of an inference (the AI's own answer step) that only needed titles and URLs. That reading of my own pipeline is the dive; the per-stage magnitudes come from the guide, and I don't upgrade that to instrumentation. [PARTIAL - state the method honestly]
3. Are those numbers measured? - No. They live in a table titled "Expected Performance Gains" - the guide's own words for design targets: what the build should aim for, not stopwatch results. The table's headline pairs - a busy-window command about 8 seconds down to about 3, and the page-reading step 5 seconds down to 0.5 - are those targets. The only concrete timing artifact in my notes is a batching check expected to finish ten tabs in around half a second against 5+ seconds sequential - an expectation printed by the test, not a recorded benchmark (a formal, logged timing run). Mechanisms are verified in code; magnitudes are projected. [SAFE - labeled]
4. What's the baseline built on? - Extraction: a per-tab text budget in the code (roughly 1,600 characters per page - a cap on how much text gets copied from each page) times every open tab, done one tab at a time. Token side (tokens = the units an AI service counts and bills text in, roughly word-fragments; kept out of the core so it doesn't collide with Q66): ~1,000 tokens of page text per tab across a fifty-tab window plus the prompt -> ~50,000 tokens before, ~3,000 after, ~$0.50 -> ~$0.03 per query (the price of one command, at the guide's assumed rates). All projected arithmetic on budgeted token counts, never billed traffic. [PARTIAL - estimate, say so]
5. Why batches of ten? - It's the concurrency cap in the code (the maximum number of pages read at once). Low enough not to thrash the browser's tab messaging and get throttled (the browser slowing or dropping the flood of requests), high enough that a filtered set resolves in one or two rounds. I'd tune it against telemetry, which is exactly what I didn't have. [SAFE]
6. How does the pre-filter work with no model? - Deterministic (same input always gives the same result - no AI guessing): a fixed category-to-domain map (coding, video, news, shopping, social, docs, work, learning) plus keyword scoring on titles and URLs; keeps the top ~30% with a floor of five and a ceiling of thirty (never fewer than five tabs, never more than thirty); if nothing scores, it falls back to the full tab set - the safety net is that when the shortcut finds nothing, the AI still sees everything. Runs before extraction, sub-millisecond (far faster than a blink - effectively instant), zero tokens. The guide's own example narrows fifty tabs to eight. [SAFE]
7. What if a rule doesn't match? - The rule set is deliberately narrow (group/close/bookmark/pin/mute by named site, duplicates, cluster by domain, inactive tabs). No match returns null (the code's way of saying "no answer") and the command falls through to the AI path. The failure mode is "slower," never "wrong." [SAFE]
8. Why not just use a faster model? - Because the request distribution isn't the cost driver; the pre-work is. A faster model still pays for fifty sequential page reads and a huge payload (bulk of text shipped over the internet to the AI service), still costs money, still needs the network, and still answers pattern questions with language understanding. [SAFE]
9. Alternatives rejected? - Embeddings in the pre-filter (Phase 2 - converting words into number-lists so the computer can judge how alike two things are in meaning; heavier than the problem, and it would run on the hot path - the step the user actually waits on - I was trying to shorten); batching alone with no routing (still calls the model for "close YouTube tabs"); dropping the AI path for speed (loses the fuzzy commands that genuinely need it). [SAFE]
10. How does it hold up at more tabs? - The expensive steps are bounded by the filtered set (capped five to thirty), not the total; extraction runs concurrently; prompts carry compressed subject-predicate-object triplets rather than page text - tiny "what-acts-on-what" summaries of each page instead of the whole text. That's design intent, exercised at my own window size - not a load test (a formal stress run at bigger scale). [SAFE - say "design intent"]
11. What went wrong, hardest part? - Ordering. I restructured the pipeline before I had any per-stage observability (the app's own logs of where each command's time goes), so I can describe the fix precisely but can't prove the saving. Hardest judgment call was what *not* to automate: keeping rules conservative so ambiguity falls through. [SAFE]
12. Who disagreed? - Nobody. Solo project; inventing a stakeholder fight would be a lie. The disagreement I handled was with my own first conclusion ("the model is slow"). [GAP - stated plainly]
13. Offline? - Routing the predictable commands locally means the common case works with the network off; the ~70% share is an estimate against my own command habits (roughly seven in ten of my typed commands are the predictable kind), no telemetry (timing/usage logs) exists, and Q66 carries that figure so I don't double-count it as a second result. [PARTIAL - estimate]
14. Can you show me the code? - Yes: the pre-filter, batched extraction, rule matcher and triplet compressor are defined and wired into the command handler (connected so the running code actually calls them) in the background worker, with console logging per stage (timing notes the code writes to a developer's debug log) - that logging is the seed of the telemetry I wish I'd built first. [SAFE]
15. What's next / do differently? - Per-stage token and latency telemetry (logging how much text each step sends and how long it takes), then replace keyword scoring with local embeddings only if the numbers justify it, plus progressive context disclosure (sending the AI only the information each decision needs, a little at a time) so even the AI path sends only what the decision needs. Instrument, then tune. [SAFE]

## Risk Check

Never say "benchmark" or "I measured."

# Q88 - a time where you got negative feedback and it was your fault

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary - owned a real fault without excuse, repaired trust with transparency); Learn and Be Curious   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the pin-count false positives in BOM reconciliation (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 10). Same event as Q4, different spine: Q4 = the failure and its root-cause analysis; this one = the users' feedback, the admission, and the trust repair.

## Core Answer

The negative feedback I earned came from the manufacturing engineers who used my first BOM tool - BOM meaning bill of materials, the list of parts that go on a board - and it was my fault: I'd shipped a matching rule (the check that decides whether a parts-list entry and a spot on the board layout are the same part) built on an assumption I never tested, and it flagged correct boards as wrong.

The tool cross-checks a board's parts list against its layout. My rule forced the BOM's pin count - the number of metal legs a part has - to match the layout's pad count - the number of solder spots drawn for it. I'd assumed pin count was a reliable signal that two things were the same part. It isn't - footprints (the solder patterns drawn on the layout for each part) get drawn for several package variants - the same part in different physical housings - and the extra pads are no-connects: placeholders drawn for the bigger variant but wired to nothing, so a legitimate part often lists fewer pins than its footprint has pads. My tool called that a mismatch. On boards mixing component types - boards with many different kinds of parts - it kept flagging good parts. That's a false positive: the tool crying wolf on something that's actually fine.

The engineers told me exactly that: the report was flagging parts that were fine. They were re-checking every flagged pin count by hand - the exact work the tool was supposed to remove - and that's how my false alarms surfaced. Worst feedback possible on a QA - quality-check - tool: every false alarm spends their time and teaches them to distrust the report. And they were right, with no defense from me: not bad data, not an upstream bug. I'd written a rule on a signal I never validated, tested only on the boards I happened to own, and none of those had the case that broke it.

So I told them the rule was mine and wrong, then fixed the semantics - what the rule is actually supposed to mean. More pads than the part needs is a possible match - I flag it for review. Fewer means the part physically can't fit - that stays a real mismatch. I could have dropped pin count entirely; it catches genuine errors, so the call was to keep it and constrain it. The repair I'm proudest of is a debug view: for each part it shows the parts-list count, the layout count, and the decision my code made, so an engineer can check my logic instead of trusting it - and override it when I'm wrong.

False positives on those mixed-type boards - the share of the tool's flags that were actually good parts - dropped from about 12% to under 2%, and the hand re-checking stopped. In plain terms: out of every 100 alarms the tool raised, about 12 were cries of wolf before my fix and fewer than 2 after. Where those numbers came from: a small test set I assembled and sorted by hand myself, re-run after the fix - solid within that sample, not a monitored production number. What I kept: a signal is a hypothesis until it fails on varied samples; now I collect the rule-breaking files from the users before I write the rule. And the deeper one - pin count was never the right signal; the reference designator (a part's own label on the board, like R7 for a resistor) plus the footprint name is. Apologies don't rebuild trust. Showing your work does.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: my first BOM rule compared pin count (the part's legs) to pad count (the board's solder spots) literally; footprints carry package variants and no-connects (pads drawn but wired to nothing), so the tool produced false alarms - flagged correct parts - on mixed-type boards
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers whose report it was - every false alarm spent their time and taught them to distrust the tool
- Insight: the feedback was un-defendable because the fault was an assumption I never validated on samples I never collected; trust repair = admit plainly + fix the semantics (what the rule means) + expose the decision
- Action (mine): told the users the rule was mine and wrong; rewrote it (more pads -> review-flagged possible match, fewer -> real mismatch); kept pin count but constrained it; shipped a per-component debug view - counts and decision laid bare - with a manual override
- Result: ~12% -> under 2% false positives on mixed-type boards (share of all flags that were actually fine; self-categorized 20-BOM sample + 15-BOM regression re-run - a stored set of known test files re-checked after the fix - labeled, not a validated production rate); hand re-checking stopped
- Learning: treat any matching signal as a hypothesis until it fails across varied samples; collect the breaking files from users first; reference designator (the part's board label, e.g. R7) + footprint name is the right signal; show your work to rebuild trust

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Was the feedback really your fault, or bad data? - Mine. The data was fine - real footprints legitimately have more pads (solder spots drawn) than the part fills with pins (legs). I built a rule on an unvalidated assumption and tested on the files I happened to have. That's a decision I made, so it's on me, and I said so to the people whose time it cost. [SAFE]
2. Who told you - a meeting, an email? - No recorded conversation exists and I won't invent one. What's on record: after the fix, engineers no longer needed to hand-verify every pin count - which says they were doing it before, hitting my false alarms (good parts flagged as bad) in their own work, and telling me the report flagged good parts. The feedback anchors to that mechanism, not a staged sit-down. [PARTIAL - anchored to STORY 10's result line]
3. Why not drop pin count entirely? - It catches a genuine error class: a 16-pin part against an 8-pad footprint - a part with 16 legs against a solder pattern with only 8 spots - physically can't fit. Dropping it would let those through. The fix was being smarter about when the signal counts, not silencing it. [SAFE]
4. What exactly was the new rule? - More pads than the BOM count -> potential match, flagged for review; fewer -> definite mismatch; plus a component-type check (does the part kind fit the pattern?) inside a configurable ratio threshold - a limit the users can change - default 2:1, meaning the layout may show up to twice as many pads as the part has pins and still count as a possible match. The 2:1 came from categorizing twenty failing BOMs - the twenty boards whose flags were wrong - legitimate variants ran 2:1 or less. Thin base, so it's a default, not a verdict; at 3:1 the engineer decides. [SAFE]
5. How was 12% -> under 2% measured, and how much should I trust it? - Plain first: the two numbers are the share of the tool's flagged mismatches that were actually fine, before vs after the fix. Honestly: my own categorization of the twenty failing BOMs plus a fifteen-BOM regression re-run after the fix - a regression re-run means re-testing a stored set of known sample files to confirm the fix works and broke nothing else - the five pin-count files came out right, ten unchanged, nothing that matched before flipped. No held-out labeled set (a batch of examples deliberately kept aside, with human-verified answers, used to score the final tool fairly), so it's a sample-scoped rate, not a validated production number. Same label I give this event anywhere. [PARTIAL - self-categorized sample only]
6. What can the heuristic still miss? - Heuristic = a practical rule of thumb, not a guarantee. The remaining risk is false negatives - real errors the tool waves through silently: a wrong component with a larger footprint and the same type letter (two parts whose board labels start with the same letter, like two resistors) can satisfy ratio and type and pass. Unlikely, possible. The debug view mitigates - the engineer sees counts, type match, ratio, and decision, and overrides. A heuristic, not a proof. [SAFE]
7. A failure inside the fix? - My first version of the new rule had its own hole: a wrong component with a larger footprint waved through. I'd repeated the original habit - trusting an untested signal. That's what forced the component-type check. [SAFE]
8. How did you keep from getting defensive? - Nothing to defend. They were naming the exact failure the tool existed to prevent, it reproduced (I could trigger it on demand), and the assumption behind my rule was one I knew I'd never tested. First move was asking for the failing files, not arguing. [SAFE]
9. Why a debug view, not just the fix? - Trust. They'd learned to distrust the report; a lower false-positive rate doesn't prove itself case by case - on any single flag, the engineer has no way to see *why* it fired. Exposing the inputs and the decision, with an override, let them verify me on their terms. Observability (the tool showing what it saw and how it decided) from day one became standard after this. [SAFE]
10. Why not train a model for the classification? - Considered it. Around two hundred known mismatch examples at component level - two hundred individual part positions with hand-verified right/wrong answers - too few for a reliable classifier (a trained statistical model needs far more examples to learn from), and the rules are clear with enumerable edge cases. Revisit if the cases get messier. [SAFE]
11. Did anyone push back on the fix itself? - Nothing on record; I won't manufacture a second conflict. What is on record: the threshold went configurable so the users held the judgment calls themselves. [GAP - stated plainly]
12. If designator + footprint name is the better signal, why keep pin count? - They answer different questions - the key (the part's board label plus its footprint name) decides which part a position should hold; the pin-vs-pad relation still gates physically-impossible fits (legs that can't reach the solder spots). With representative data up front I'd have gone straight to the better signal instead of patching the weaker one. [SAFE]
13. What would you do differently? - Collect diverse files from the floor before writing a rule - the boards that broke this weren't in my test set. And build the debug view from day one - it was an afterthought, and during development it would have shown me the pin-count behavior before the engineers had to. [SAFE]
14. At larger scale? - Volume shifts the risk to false negatives (real errors slipping by) slipping past the ratio-plus-type rule. That's why the threshold is configurable, borderline ratios defer to review, and the measurement plan is real: label ~200 components as ground truth (hand-verified correct answers), plot precision-recall - precision = when the tool flags, how often it's right; recall = of the real errors, how many it catches - pick the operating point (the balance between false alarms and misses) from the false-alarm-vs-miss cost the process engineers give me. [PARTIAL - plan, not executed]

## Risk Check
1. "That's a bug you self-diagnosed, not feedback" - premise risk; handled by anchoring the feedback to the documented hand-verification consequence (the critiques/Q88.md fix) and never inventing a meeting or quote. Defensible as labeled; fails only if inflated.
2. "12% -> under 2% - production rate?" - Needs a real instrumented number to claim that (continuously measured live usage, not a one-off sample count); defensible only as the stated self-categorized sample plus regression re-run. Never let it out validated.
3. Same event as Q4 - structural split holds: Q4's core owns the 20-BOM categorization and the threshold mechanics; this core keeps one before->after and centers reception, ownership, the debug view as trust repair. If both come up, say so; don't re-run the root-cause walk here.
4. Q4's bank concedes the discovery channel is undocumented - no contradiction here if this telling keeps anchoring to the consequence ("they were hand-verifying; that's how it surfaced") and never says "in a meeting they told me."
5. Sibling collision - Q18/Q62 tell the STORY 8 prototype review and Q45 the STORY 2 alignment complaints; different events and tools. The conflicting 15%->under-1% four-edge-case telling of this event stays excluded bank-wide.

# Q89 - tell me about a time where you interacted with a customer with negative feedback directly

**LP:** Customer Obsession (primary); Earn Trust; Invent and Simplify (touch)   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - STORY 8 GPT-4o "AI eye": the engineers' direct in-product feedback - their incorrect-marks showing the AI analysis was confidently wrong - and the reframe from verdict to suggestion. This replaces the earlier STORY 2 re-frame draft in `answers\Q89.md`, which duplicated Q86; distinct from Q45/Q78/Q86 (alignment false alarms + BOM trust loops) and from Q1/Q40 (same feature, Invent & Simplify / Are Right A Lot spines - there the feedback beat is a closing lesson, here it IS the story).

## Core Answer

The negative feedback I remember best was about the AI feature in my inspection tool: the engineers marked it wrong, over and over, and they were right.

Context: my PCB comparison tool - a PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device - takes a photo of a finished board, compares it to its design drawing (the "layout"), and draws a red region where the two don't match, but it doesn't say what the mismatch means. Wrong part, rotated part, just a reflection - the manufacturing engineer had to look and decide, about thirty seconds a region, and that thirty seconds is the engineers' own estimate of how long one check takes, not a stopwatch study. So I added an AI analysis: crop the flagged region from the layout and the photo, send both to GPT-4o (an off-the-shelf AI model that can look at pictures and answer questions about them) with a structured prompt (a strict instruction that demands the answer back in one fixed, machine-readable form), get back component type, mismatch type, and a confidence (the AI's own score for how sure it says it is). A read became a five-second confirm - the "five seconds" is how long the online AI service takes to answer, computer time, not the engineer's time - and it was right about 85% of the time, meaning how often its answer matched what the engineer saw, from my rough tally of their feedback, not a measured rate.

The problem was the other 15% - the share of answers that were wrong in that same rough tally - because a wrong AI can be wrong with a straight face. A confident "false alarm" (the AI saying a red mark means nothing) on a QA tool (a quality-check tool) is the worst failure mode: it ships a bad board - a defective product gets waved through as fine. The pushback came through the channel I built for it: the mark-as-incorrect button (one click by an engineer saying "this answer is wrong," so every disagreement was recorded inside the tool, case by case). I expected occasional use; they used it until it was a signal, on the specific analyses they didn't trust. That was their direct feedback - no quote, nothing to invent.

I could have defended the demo. Instead I treated their incorrect-marks as data. Sorted, they weren't random: one systematic error showed up. I'd assumed the model could read the value printed on small surface-mount parts - the tiny components soldered straight onto the board. The print is too small and too blurry; it could do component type and orientation, not exact values. My assumption was the bug - and "bug" here means my wrong belief about what the AI could do, not broken code.

Then a decision: chase accuracy, or change the feature's job. I chose the second. I relabeled the output a suggestion with a confidence number, never a verdict - the engineer kept the call. I stopped asking it to commit to values. And the feature was optional by design: server build only (the version that ran on the company network; the separate offline build ran no AI at all); no API key (a password that lets software use a paid online AI service), no analysis, the red regions still work.

What they got: a triage aid - something that helps decide which red marks to open first - they trusted because it never pretended to be the answer - they said it changed which mismatches they opened first on dense boards. What I kept: an AI feature will be wrong some fixed share of the time no matter how good the model gets, so customer obsession is deciding who is trusted for what. Tool proposes, engineer confirms. And their incorrect-marks became the best bug reports I ever had - each one a precise, real example of the AI failing, filed by the person closest to the work.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: the AI mismatch analysis could be confidently wrong; on a QA tool, a false "false alarm" (a "nothing here" that isn't nothing) ships bad boards - the engineers' incorrect-marks were the direct signal
- Customer: the manufacturing engineers using the comparison tool; their negative feedback was the incorrect-marks themselves, in-product, on the analyses they didn't trust (no verbal quotes exist - never invent any)
- Insight: the incorrect-marks weren't noise - they clustered on one systematic error: my assumption that a VLM (a vision-language model - an AI that looks at pictures and answers questions about them) can read value print on small SMD (surface-mount device - the tiny parts soldered straight onto the board) parts
- Action (mine): sorted their marks, found the systematic error, relabeled the output as a suggestion with confidence (never a verdict), dropped the value-reading ask, kept the feature an optional enhancement (server build only)
- Result: engineers accepted it as triage - reported it changed which mismatches they opened first on dense boards; ~30 s read -> ~5 s confirm; ~85% right by my rough check (30 s = their own estimate; 5 s = the AI service's answer time; 85% = my rough tally, not a measured test)
- Learning: with AI, design for the wrong share - work backwards from the engineer's trust, not the demo; the feedback path is part of the feature, and tool proposes, engineer confirms

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Dense, per-case evidence - I don't reconstruct a conversation or quote anyone, because the feedback lives in the marks. [PARTIAL - channel honest; feedback is the mechanism + their reported prioritization help, no verbal scene exists]

I changed the promise, not the number. [PARTIAL - defensible inference from the reflection]

Boards ran 5-20 flagged regions - the number of red marks one board could carry, per the engineers' reports. [PARTIAL - reported/typical, not instrumented]

[SAFE]

[PARTIAL - reported]

# Q90 - a time when you optimized the performance of an application

**LP:** Dive Deep (primary - tied parameter count to latency and checked the result against a hard budget); Invent & Simplify (sized the model to the constraint, avoided the biggest model); Deliver Results (shipped inside the budget without losing accuracy).   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite - the defect classifier's **inference-latency engineering** (`AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md` STORY 3/14). Deliberately NOT the Q87/Q66 Tab Scroller telling: same question kind, different application, different mechanism, and none of the tab-scroller projected figures.

## Core Answer

The application was my PCB inspection tool - a PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device. Built solo, browser-based, running on factory-floor machines with no server. One part of it was a classifier - a model whose only job is sorting a photo into a fixed list of buckets - and it judged a photo of a component: good, wrong value, wrong orientation, or missing. That part had a hard budget. "Budget" here means a fixed time limit the tool had to fit inside, not a wish: under 100 milliseconds per image - one-tenth of a second, roughly how fast a computer reply has to be before it stops feeling instant. Not because anyone liked round numbers. If a crop - a small square cut out of the photo around one component - didn't classify inside what a person will wait for, the tool stopped feeling interactive and the workflow on the line broke.

So I optimized against the budget instead of against accuracy for its own sake. I evaluated ResNet, Vision Transformers, and the EfficientNet family - three families of neural-network designs, more like engine models you choose between than one piece of software. The performance decision was sizing. I picked the small EfficientNetV2 variant, about 21 million parameters. A "parameter" is one of the internal settings the model learns from training examples - think millions of tiny dials; more dials usually means a bigger, slower, more capable model, and 21 million of them is what this one carried, where the biggest one I tested was several times that. The reasoning was what the task actually is: a small crop of a single component carries color, shape, printed text - local features, not scene understanding. Across the sizes the accuracy gap on my data was smaller than anything I could justify paying latency and memory for. I took the accuracy I could stand behind and refused to buy the rest.

The cost of inference here is the convolutions - "inference" means the model judging one new image, as opposed to training, which is teaching it in the first place; "convolutions" are the heavy pattern-scanning math this kind of model runs, so they dominate the time. And on a plain factory CPU - the computer's ordinary main chip, no special graphics hardware - that lands at about 45 milliseconds per image: what my own timing test measured, less than half the 100 ms budget. Budget met with room, and I didn't buy the speed with accuracy - the headline number matched the bigger models, and recall on every defect type stayed above the bar I'd set (recall = of the real defects of a given kind, how many the tool caught - the "missed one" error is the expensive one here). The faster hardware paths are documented characteristics, not something I benchmarked, so I don't quote them.

The wrong part was what I thought I was optimizing. The model wasn't the dominant cost of the application - the OpenCV library's cold load, before any compute, was where the time actually went (OpenCV is the image-processing software that reads and crops the photo, and "cold load" is the startup delay the first time it fires up). The classifier's remaining seconds were outside the classifier. Lesson: profile the whole path before picking an enemy. My next optimization plan wasn't a smaller model. It was the load path.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: browser-only, server-less defect classifier on plain factory PCs had to return per-image inference inside a human-patience budget (<100 ms - a tenth of a second per image) or the interactive workflow died.
- Customer: manufacturing engineers using the inspection tool on the floor; latency was their usability constraint, not a benchmark trophy.
- Insight: the budget is the spec - size the architecture to it, don't maximize accuracy; component crops are a local-feature task, so extra capacity buys latency, not correctness.
- Action (mine): evaluated ResNet / ViT / EfficientNet; chose the ~21M small variant (M = millions of learned "parameters," the model's internal dials) over the 54M/119M ones on a measured accuracy gap; kept input small (224x224 pixels - a thumbnail, not full resolution); verified the CPU result against the budget; held per-class recall above the set bar.
- Result: ~45 ms per image on CPU vs the <100 ms budget (target and achieved number, never blended); accuracy matched the larger models within an unpayable margin; then found the real remaining cost was OpenCV.js cold load, not the model.
- Learning: profile the whole path before picking an enemy; the biggest win was outside the component I optimized; label documented hardware figures as documented.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What was the application and who set the bar? - One self-contained HTML inspection suite, solo build; the classifier sorts a crop as good / wrong value / wrong orientation / missing; the <100 ms per image was a documented design criterion in my plan so the tool stayed interactive (a "budget" = the time limit the design had to meet; 100 ms = a tenth of a second, the point below which a reply feels instant). [SAFE]
2. Did you actually optimize, or just pick a smaller model? - The optimization was against a hard budget and the delivered result was the measured 45 ms; the sizing decision is what produced it - ~21M parameters vs ~54M/~119M, with under a 2% accuracy difference on my data, so the larger models spent latency for a gain I couldn't justify. ("Parameters" = the learned internal dials inside the model; the big models carried 2.5-5.5x as many but were wrong on under 2 more answers per 100 test photos - not worth the extra time and memory.) [SAFE]
3. How do you hold the 45 ms number? - Single-image CPU benchmark, hardware not recorded in my notes; the shipped path ran TensorFlow.js in the browser (TensorFlow.js = the AI runtime running inside the web page). It's a benchmark - a timing test I ran myself, on one photo at a time on the ordinary main chip - not a floor. The 100 ms is the target, 45 ms is what was achieved - I never present the target as a measurement. [PARTIAL - labeled]
4. Why not the large EfficientNet for the extra accuracy? - Gap under 2% on my holdout (a "holdout" = examples deliberately kept back from training that the model never saw, so the score is honest); roughly 6x the parameters; ~3x slower to train; and the weights live embedded inside one offline file the factory machines open in seconds - "weights" are the parameter numbers themselves, so every megabyte mattered. [SAFE]
5. What's the compute story? - About 8 GFLOPs per forward pass at 224x224, dominated by convolutions. (A "forward pass" = one run of the model on one image; 224x224 pixels is a small square thumbnail; "GFLOPs" = billions of arithmetic operations - so ~8 billion math steps per image.) GPU is documented at under 5 ms and WebGL sits near it (GPU = the special graphics chip; WebGL = the browser's way of using it) - those are the runtime's documented characteristics, not benchmarks I ran, which is why I only quote the CPU figure. [PARTIAL - only 45 ms is mine]
6. Did the speed cost you accuracy? - 94% on the ~300-image holdout (measured: the model was right on 94 of every 100 photos in a set of about 300 it had never seen), and the small-vs-large difference stayed under the margin I'd pay for; per-class recall held above the >90% bar (recall = of each defect type's real cases, how many got caught; every type cleared 90). I won't quote exact per-class decimals - each defect class is a couple dozen images, one sample moves a point. [PARTIAL]
7. The OpenCV.js bottleneck - measured or noticed? - Stage attribution from my documented pipeline analysis (multi-MB WASM cold load before inference - WASM is a fast binary format that lets heavy code run in the browser; several megabytes of it has to arrive and start up once, the "cold load", before the first answer), not an instrumented profile. That's exactly why the stated next step is per-stage instrumentation. [PARTIAL]
8. What breaks at 10x? - Resolution, not count: fixed 224x224 input means more components is throughput, while higher-res or tiling means more forward passes per item. (Throughput = how many images per second the tool gets through; "tiling" = splitting a bigger image into several 224x224 squares so the model runs once per square.) Both answers point at the same thing - instrument the full browser path. [SAFE]
9. Alternatives rejected? - ViT (needs labeled data and compute I didn't have), from-scratch CNN (data-hungry on ~2,000 images) (CNN = convolutional neural network, the standard image-model design; "from scratch" = with no head start from pretraining on outside photos), keeping the large model and blowing the budget, and any server-side inference (running the model on a distant computer instead of the machine in front of the user - the tool was one embedded file with no server). [SAFE]
10. What went wrong / hardest part? - My assumption that the model was the app's cost center. I optimized what was easy to reason about instead of profiling what the user actually waited through. [SAFE]
11. Who disagreed? - Nobody; solo build, and inventing a stakeholder fight would be a lie. The real argument was with my own "bigger model" instinct and the "the model is the bottleneck" assumption. [GAP - stated plainly]
12. What's next / do differently? - Instrument per-stage latency first, then fix the cold load (defer/parallelize the WASM fetch; a Web-Worker parallelization of the independent comparison signals is projected at ~3.5x - projected, not measured) (a "Web Worker" = a background task inside the browser; ~3.5x = the estimated speedup from running the independent checks side by side). Retraining took about 30 minutes on one GPU, so new defect types never stalled the floor. (Retraining = re-teaching the model when a new defect type is added; ~30 minutes on a single graphics chip, from my notes.) [PARTIAL - labeled projections]

## Risk Check
1. "This is Q83's numbers (21M / 45 ms / 94%) wearing a new coat" - Defensible only with the lens held: Q83 = the model-*selection* decision under uncertainty; Q90 = engineering against a hard *latency budget* plus the whole-path lesson. One shared canonical set; I never re-run the selection narrative here. [defensible - frame deliberately]
2. "45 ms - hardware, method, repeats?" - Single-image CPU benchmark, hardware unrecorded, in-browser TF.js is the shipped path. Keep the PARTIAL label; never say "floor" or "production timing". [PARTIAL]
3. "You never measured a before/after of an optimization" - Correct: this is design-against-budget, not a retrofit speedup, and the core says so; the owned weakness is reasoning about the path instead of profiling it. [defensible - framing]
4. OpenCV.js bottleneck claim - documented analysis and stage attribution, not an instrumented profile; present it as "where my notes say the remaining time lives". [PARTIAL]

"94% on what set?" - Canonical ~300-image holdout (component-level 70/15/15 of ~2,000 - the ~2,000 training photos were split 70% to teach the model, 15% to tune it, 15% held back unseen for this score); an older note's "500-image test set" doesn't reconcile and stays unmerged, same as the dive-deep telling. [GAP -> disclose, don't merge]

# Q91 - a time where you received critical feedback, how did you implement it?

**LP:** Earn Trust (primary), Learn and Be Curious - this telling centers how one user correction got *implemented*: generalize past the reported string, verify, pin it. Distinct from Q42/Q62 (now different events: the extension JSON-contract fix and the prototype team review) and from sibling tellings of the same facts (Q73 the feature, Q28 owns asking the expert, Q6/Q17 own the commit)   **Story:** the manufacturing engineer's `R1||R2` variant-notation correction to the BOM parser - splitter, test matrix, regression pin (AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md STORY 1; debug view from STORY 11)

## Core Answer

The most useful critical feedback I ever got came from a manufacturing engineer using the BOM reconciliation tool I built, and it was specific - down to a single string (one exact piece of text in that file). BOM = "bill of materials," the list of every part that goes into a product; "reconciliation" means cross-checking that list against the board's design.

Context in one line: the tool reads a SAP-exported parts list and matches component references against the board layout. (SAP is the inventory-and-production software most big factories run; a "component reference" is the code naming where one part belongs on the board, like R1; the "board layout" is the drawing showing where every part should sit.) Before it, the engineer cross-checked by hand, and he said that cost twenty to thirty minutes a board. What that number counts: one board's list-versus-drawing check done by eye; where it came from: the engineer's own words; how solid: a self-estimate, never timed. The tool returns a report in seconds - which is why a wrong report costs something. ("Seconds" counts the machine doing that same comparison and producing the report; it's his experience of the wait, not stopwatch data.)

The feedback: some references are variant references - `R1||R2` or `R1/R2` - one physical position that accepts either part, depending on the board variant. In plain terms: every spot on the board carries a label like R1; this notation is two labels written together, marking a single spot that may hold either of two parts because the board is built in slightly different versions ("variants") for different products. My parser (the part of the program that reads the file and works out what each line means) didn't recognize the notation, judged it invalid, and dropped it. Silently - no error, no warning, the reference just never reached the report. He caught it and told me plainly: if the BOM lists `R1||R2` and the layout shows one position, the system should treat that as a valid match for either reference. That was critical, not cosmetic - a dropped reference could mean a real placement went unchecked, and every false mismatch (the tool wrongly claiming a difference where there is none) sent him back to the manual check the tool existed to kill.

How I implemented it mattered more than the acknowledgment. First, I didn't patch the one string I was shown. I built a variant splitter (a small piece of code that cuts a combined label back into its parts) that normalizes both separators (the `||` and `/` symbols written between the labels), extracts the individual references, and treats each as a valid match target for the position. Second, I made sure the fix stayed fixed: a test matrix (a checklist of inputs to try) - the clean forms, three-part variants, and malformed shapes (deliberately broken labels) like a leading `||` or a trailing `/` - checked against the case most likely to false-mismatch: only one of the pair present in the layout. That matrix went into my regression suite of fifteen real production BOMs (a "regression" is an old feature breaking because of a new code change; a "regression suite" is a saved set of test cases re-run after every change to catch that - here, 15 actual parts lists taken from production), which I ran after every parser change, so fixing one edge couldn't quietly break another. Third, the tool's debug view (a screen that shows how the tool interpreted the data at each step) shows the parsed reference after each step, including the variant split - so he could verify the fix on his own data instead of taking my word for it.

What I took from it: the dangerous failure isn't the one that crashes - a crash announces itself. It's the silent data loss, where a clean-looking report hides that the tool never looked at that line. And implementing feedback properly means generalizing past the example you were shown, then pinning it with a test.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: user-reported semantic bug (the code ran fine and simply meant the wrong thing) - the parser treated variant references (`R1||R2`, `R1/R2`) as invalid and silently dropped them; a clean report hid unchecked positions
- Customer: the manufacturing engineer running the reconciliation - false mismatches returned his manual ~20-30 min/board check (his report, not measured by me); dropped references could miss real placements
- Insight: the correction had two parts - the semantics (one position, either part by variant) and the failure class (silent drop). Implementing feedback means fixing both, not just the reported string
- Action (mine): variant splitter normalizing both separators; test matrix of clean / multi-part / malformed forms; folded into the 15-BOM regression suite run after every parser change; verification shown through the debug view on his own data
- Result: variants now match either reference; the whole notation class pinned against regression; zero false positives/negatives (false positive = a false alarm; false negative = a missed real problem) on that suite (suite-scoped claim - it covers only those 15 test files, nothing beyond)
- Learning: silent data loss is more dangerous than a crash; a proper implementation generalizes past the example and gets pinned with a test

## Follow-Up Bank

1. How is this different from the prototype feedback you've told me about? - Different event, different shape. That one was a team review listing three rough edges of a five-day demo - alignment, lighting, export. This was one user correcting the semantics of one notation in my code. Different feedback, different fix set, different lesson: that one taught me what counts as working; this one taught me how to implement a correction so it can't regress (so no later change can quietly break it again). [SAFE]
2. Was that really "critical" feedback? - Yes by consequence, not by tone. He wasn't angry - he was right. A dropped reference could hide a real placement, and the false mismatches gave back the manual check the tool removed. I took it as a code-level defect report and treated it that way. [SAFE]
3. Why did the parser drop the reference instead of erroring? - My reference pattern (the rule the parser uses to decide what counts as a valid label) only accepted the standard form, and the default skipped anything unmatched - a deliberate degradation (an intentional keep-running fallback) so unknown formats don't crash the tool on the floor. The flaw: "skip the unknown" and "lose a real part" look identical to the user. That's what his feedback exposed. [SAFE]
4. What exactly changed in the code? - The variant splitter: normalize both `||` and `/`, extract the individual references, treat each as a valid match target for the position - so `R1||R2` against one layout position matches either part. Malformed shapes like `||R1` or `R1/` were made safe at the same time, so they can't produce bogus references. [SAFE]
5. How did you verify, and how do you know nothing else broke? - A test matrix: `R1||R2`, `R1/R2`, `R1||R2||R3`, `R1/R2/R3`, plus the malformed `||R1` and `R1/`, each checked for correct extraction and for matching when only one variant is in the layout. Then it joined the 15-BOM regression suite - representative production files, run after every parser change. Zero false positives and zero false negatives - in plain words, across those 15 files the tool raised no wrong alarms and missed no planted problem - but that claim is scoped to that suite - my own harness (the testing setup I built myself), deliberately small and boring, not CI (the team-wide automated system that re-runs tests on shared infrastructure with every code change). [PARTIAL - suite-scoped, self-built]

His explanation of the intent ended the instinct: he had the manufacturing reality, I had a guess about it. I adopted his semantics completely and rewrote that part without keeping a piece of my old logic out of pride. [SAFE]

"Either reference matches" arrived as a stated requirement from him. Honest gap: no formal trade-off record. [PARTIAL]

And don't call it done until the correction is verifiable by the person who reported it - the debug view shows the parsed reference after each preprocessing step (the reading and cleaning the tool does before comparing the documents), including the split, so he can check the tool on his own data and flag a new format instead of losing it quietly. And in the tool's first week of use it caught three real mismatches the manual review had missed - three genuine part-placement errors the human check let through - same reconciliation work, engineer-reported week-one result. [SAFE - canonical, labeled]
