# Q92 - tell me about a time you used data to solve a problem

**LP:** Are Right, A Lot (primary); Dive Deep; Deliver Results.   **Story:** BGSW PCB Inspector Suite (`AMAZON_INTERVIEW_PREPARATION.md` STORY 9 + STORY 3) - the learning-curve and labeling-economics read: using data to decide when to stop collecting data and ship. Same event as Q23/Q33, distinct lens; distinct from Q63 (make-vs-buy cost call), Q27 (4-signal engine), and the pin-count rule from 20 BOMs (Q4/Q52/Q72/Q77/Q88).

## Core Answer

There was a time data solved a problem that wasn't about the product - it was about my time. It told me when to stop working.

I built a PCB defect classifier solo. A PCB is the green circuit board inside every electronic device; a "classifier" is a program that sorts photos into categories. A cropped component image goes in; it answers: good, wrong value, wrong orientation, or missing. "Labeling" means a human writing down the correct answer for each photo so the machine has examples to learn from - in my case, my own typing hours. Mine reached 94 percent on a holdout set I built myself. A "holdout set" is the batch of photos I kept back and never used in training - about 300 of them, like a final exam the model has never seen - so 94 percent means it sorted 94 of every 100 of those fresh photos correctly, and that's a measured figure, not a guess. And I hit the classic question: keep labeling, or ship?

"More data helps" is true, and useless. Of course more data helps. The only question worth answering was what the next hour of my time buys. You can't feel that, so I measured.

Cost first. I'd built a keyboard labeling tool - one key per label, auto-advance - and it came out around three seconds an image. That "about 3 seconds" counts the time to label one photo with my tool; it came from my own timing while I worked, a personal stopwatch-style measurement, not software telemetry. Cheap. But the dataset grew only as fast as I could type, and my typing was the schedule.

Then the return. I logged accuracy against how much training data went in - a learning curve, which is just a chart tracking "how right is the model" as I feed it more and more photos. The shape of that curve is a price list. It projected that doubling the dataset would buy roughly two more points - meaning about 2 more correct answers per 100 photos on that same exam - and flatten toward nothing after that. So: two points for twice my labeling hours, then a shrinking fraction of that.

The data also fixed what I was measuring. Most components on a line are good; a model that always said "good" would have scored respectably and been useless. So I weighted the rare defect classes and judged the model on per-class recall, not the headline number. "Per-class recall," in plain words: for each category of defect on its own, what share of the real defects of that kind did the model actually catch?

The decision: stop collecting, ship. The honest footnote is that more data would have helped generalization - I still think so. "Generalization" means doing well on the brand-new boards it meets on the factory floor, not just on the photos it was tested on. But the curve said the remaining effort was buying fractions, and shipping on schedule got the tool in front of the engineers who were waiting on it.

What I learned: "more data is better" is a true statement that solves nothing until you price it - hours against points. The data didn't make my model better. It told me when better wasn't worth it.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: Classifier was "good enough" with no rule for stop-vs-grind; every label cost the solo builder's typing time, so dataset growth = schedule risk.
- Customer: Manufacturing/test engineers waiting on the inspection suite; also my own labeling hours.
- Insight: "Is more data good?" is the wrong question; "what does the next hour of labeling buy?" is the solvable one - the learning curve (accuracy-vs-data chart) is a price list.
- Action (mine): Built the keyboard labeler and timed it; logged accuracy vs training-set size during training; read the projected flat point; weighted rare defect classes and switched to per-class recall (catch-rate within each defect type) over raw accuracy; set the stopping point from the curve.
- Result: Shipped at 94% on a ~300-image holdout (kept-back photos the model never trained on) with every defect class above 90% recall, on schedule, instead of grinding for a projected ~2 points.
- Learning: An unpriced truth ("more data helps") is not a decision; data told me when better wasn't worth it - and I say out loud what I gave up.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What exactly did the curve show? - 2,000 images put it at 94%; the curve projected about 96% at double the data and marginal beyond. That's a read off the plotted curve, not a trained 4,000-image model - I present it as a projection. [PARTIAL - projection, labeled]
2. What were the labeling economics, really? - Before: manual CSV entry (typing each photo's answer into a spreadsheet file), about 30 s an image. After my keyboard tool: about 3 s. The 2,000 images took roughly 100 minutes instead of an estimated 10 hours. Doubling the set  another ~100 minutes for the projected ~2 points. That's the price the curve was quoted against. [SAFE - STORY 9's own figures]
3. Was the 3 s/label measured? - My own small-sample timing while working in the tool, with the manual CSV method as the before. Personal harness, not instrumented telemetry. [SAFE - self-measured, say so]
4. How reliable is the 94%? - Held-out ~300 images, a 70/15/15 split of ~2,000, meaning of my ~2,000 labelled photos 70% taught the model, 15% tuned its settings, and the last 15% (~300) were kept back purely for the final scoring exam. Split at component level so the same component couldn't leak across train and test - one physical part never appears in both the study pile and the exam pile; ~3-point train-to-validation gap, meaning the model scored only about 3 points worse on the tuning data than on the data it learned from, so it wasn't just memorizing; every defect class above 90% recall (92 wrong-value / 96 wrong-orientation / 98 missing - on small per-class samples, so I lead with ">90"); ~45 ms per image on CPU - that's how long the program takes to judge one photo on an ordinary processor with no graphics card. [SAFE]
5. Why not just report accuracy? - "Good" components outnumbered defects roughly 5:1; always predicting "good" scores about 83% - i.e., a model that cries "defect" never once would still look 83% right, which is why the headline number misleads. I weighted defective examples 5x and made precision-recall the primary read - precision = when the model flags a defect, how often the flag is real; recall = of the real defects, how many it caught. Accuracy was the vanity metric the data warned me off. [SAFE]
6. Did you trust your own labels? - I labeled the whole set twice, a week apart, without looking at the first answers: 92% self-agreement. That counts how often my two independent passes gave the same answer for the same photo - 92 of every 100 - a check that the labels themselves, the ground truth under every other number, were stable; my own audit, not an external one. The 8% were borderline defects; I re-examined each and assigned the primary defect, so the set the model trained on was re-audited. [SAFE - same facts/numbers as Q23/Q33]
7. Was any other part of this data-decided? - Model size: bigger EfficientNet variants (larger, more parameter-heavy versions of the same family of image model - "parameters" being the internal knobs training tunes) bought accuracy I didn't need at latency I couldn't have - slower per-photo answer times - so I kept the ~21M-parameter version; the train/val gap held at ~3 points on it. [SAFE - canonical STORY 3/14 set]
8. Hardest part? - The waiting. Stopping feels wrong when more data always helps in the abstract; I had to trust a flat curve I'd read myself and ship under the projection's error bars. [SAFE - qualitative]
9. Disagreement? - No external pushback on the record for this call - I owned the labeling time and the ship decision; the engineers consumed the result, they didn't review it. I won't invent a fight; the tension was internal, grind vs ship. [GAP on external disagreement - concede]
10. Isn't this the same story as your ownership / dive-deep answers? - One event, three true faces: Q23 = making the labels trustworthy was nobody's job; Q33 = diagnosing whether the model or the data was the ceiling; here = pricing the next hour of data and deciding to stop. Numbers identical on purpose - that's the defense, not the tell. [SAFE]
11. Do differently? - Collect more up front - ~2,000 was on the low side for generalization (doing well on new, unseen boards) - and batch-label near-identical crops; duplicates of the same part at a new angle add images, not information, which makes a curve look rosier than the data. I'd still stop by the curve, not by feel. [SAFE]
12. Was 94% actually enough for them? - The defined need was a defect triage filter ahead of human verification: the model's job was to sort obvious goods from possible defects so engineers spent their eyes only on the flagged ones, with recall above 90% per class and an interactive ~45 ms CPU pass on the factory machines (fast enough that it feels instant to a person clicking through boards). Floor time saved is engineer-reported recollection, not a number I instrumented. [PARTIAL - no invented hours]

## Risk Check
1. "The ~96% - measured?" - Must stay exactly as labeled: a projection off the curve, never run on 4,000 images; the stop decision held regardless because the cost side was self-measured. Applying the BR critique: no "measured trade" phrasing. Defensible only if the word "projected" survives pressure.
2. Third telling of STORY 9's curve/economics facts (Q23/Q33) - defense is identical numbers + conceded distinct lens (follow-up 10). Any new specific here is a self-inflicted wound; keep the same-event list to Q23/Q33, not Q11's model-side telling.
3. Holdout size: earlier draft said "500 images" (STORY 3); the bank's canonical anchor is 94% on a ~300-image holdout (70/15/15 of ~2,000) - corrected here and used everywhere; also per-class recalls must go out with the small-sample softening (">90 per class," exact numbers only if pressed).
4. "Ship on schedule / it was enough" - schedule and floor-impact claims are qualitative; adoption/time-saved stays engineer-reported (~15 engineers, 2 sites, ~20 hrs/wk reported) and is never quoted as measured. Defensible as stated.

# Q93 - tell me about a time when you worked on something outside your comfort zone

**LP:** Learn and Be Curious (primary - had to reason like an attacker, a trade I don't practice); Invent and Simplify (replaced an expensive model call with a cheap deterministic pass); Ownership (personal build, the security call was mine)   **Story:** Tab Scroller - the anti-phishing tab quarantine: my first design (per-tab AI scans) was wrong on cost and defensibility, and the stretch was building a Zero-Trust heuristic risk check plus a quarantine UI from first principles of how scams actually look (background.js:1293-1307, 4370-4376; content.js:796-802, 1547-1549; progress.txt Task K); distinct from Q35 (same extension, MV3/state spine) and Q42 (same extension, JSON-contract spine)

## Core Answer

The uncomfortable part of this work wasn't a language or a framework - it was having to think like a scammer, which is not my trade. I build machine-vision and data tools. I was extending my personal Chrome extension - Tab Scroller, a searchable strip of all your open tabs - and decided it should warn about phishing tabs: pages that pretend to be your bank or a famous service to steal a sign-in. [PARTIAL - the shipped code and completion log are the evidence; "first design was AI-per-tab" is my account of the iteration recorded in the plan]

The obvious move for my skill set was to ask an AI model to score each tab. I did the math before committing and it was wrong three ways: one online call per tab change against a free allowance the extension can exhaust in seconds; a slow verdict; and an undefendable one - "the model felt sketchy" is not a reason to trust a page. Security reasoning was outside my experience, and paying a model didn't move it inside.

So I went the opposite way from my instinct: a deterministic pass - same input, same output, every line explainable - built by studying what fake pages actually look like. Three families of tells. Look-alike hostnames where digits impersonate letters - paypa1 with a one, micros0ft with a zero, the swap that fools the eye but not a string comparison. Throwaway top-level domains - the tail of an address - that scam infrastructure favors. And the tell that taught me most: mismatch between claim and location - a title asking to verify, sign in, or secure an account while naming a bank or brand, on an address that isn't that brand's. That's the attack in one line: it exploits the gap between what you read and where you are.

A flagged tab gets quarantined in the interface - visually marked, clicking never blocks but asks: "This tab looks suspicious. Are you sure you want to switch to it?" It defers to the human, because only they know their own context - a company intranet login, a test bank site.

What I kept from working outside my field: the right answer wasn't the technique I knew. For a security UI, simple, explainable, and free beat smart and expensive - because the human makes the call anyway, and my job was to hand them a reason, not a vibe.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: wanted phishing-tab warnings in my extension; comfort-zone first design (per-tab AI scan) failed on call cost, latency, and defensibility
- Customer: the extension's user - me first, personal build, no adoption claims; the "risk customer" is whoever clicks a fake sign-in page
- Insight: phishing works by a claim-vs-location mismatch, so the check can be deterministic tells, not judgment; explainability is the feature, not a bonus
- Action (mine): replaced the per-tab AI scan with a heuristic risk function (look-alike brand hosts, scam-favored TLDs, brand+auth-keyword claims on foreign hosts); on tab updates, flagged tabs get a quarantine mark; clicking asks an explicit confirm, no hard block; ran on every tab change, zero network calls
- Result: instant, free, per-line explainable screening shipped as the extension's anti-phishing task; no false-positive rate measured - bounded claim: it catches the pattern families it encodes [GAP]
- Learning: outside your field, resist importing your favorite tool; first principles (how the attack works) chose a dumber, better design than my instinct did

## Follow-Up Bank
1. Where's the code? - The risk function and its tell families sit in background.js:1293-1307; a tab-update handler runs it and broadcasts a QUARANTINE_TAB message:4370-4376; the UI tracks quarantined ids and marks the chip (content.js:1547-1549, 927), and the click-confirm dialog "This tab looks suspicious. Are you sure you want to switch to it?" is content.js:796-802. The completion log records "Task K: Zero-Trust Tab Quarantine (Anti-Phishing) completed" (progress.txt). [SAFE]
2. Why "Zero-Trust"? - Don't trust a tab's self-presentation: the risk comes from cross-checking what the page claims (its title) against where it actually lives (its address), and even a positive verdict still routes through a human confirm. It's my label for the rule design, not a certification. [SAFE - labeling honest]
3. Why replace the AI scan? - The optimization plan records the heuristic landing "to replace expensive per-tab AI phishing scans": free-tier call budgets, and a verdict you can defend line by line. Both the cost argument and the auditability argument. [SAFE]
4. False positives? - A legitimate page whose title says "verify your account" on an unusual domain will flag. The confirm click is the safety valve - it never blocks, it warns. A measured FP rate doesn't exist. [GAP]
5. Why confirm instead of block? - Personal tool: inform, don't adjudicate. Only the user knows context - a work intranet login, a test bank page, a redirect chain. Hard blocking someone's own legitimate tool is the worse bug. [SAFE - reasoning held as mine]
6. How did you learn the tell families? - From how impersonation works: character substitutions against big brands (the pattern list is in the code), throwaway TLDs that abuse reports keep naming, and the claim-vs-address gap. A hand-built pattern list, no training data. [SAFE]
7. What was genuinely outside your comfort zone? - Attacker-modeling and security UX. My background is making machines look at boards; this was making a human pause before they click. The design tools were different - patterns and friction, not accuracy. [SAFE]
8. Does it catch real phishing? - Unverified - I make no detection-rate claim. The bounded statement: it flags the pattern families it encodes, which is exactly what the tells are, and nothing more. [GAP - no evaluation set]
9. What would you do differently? - Log which tell fired so the rules can be tuned from evidence, instead of the current boolean OR of all families; and pull from a maintained blocklist source rather than only my hand-written patterns. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. "No accuracy number - so it's just regex?" - Yes, deliberately: deterministic, explainable, free; the story owns the limitation (pattern families only, FP rate unmeasured) and the design reason (security UIs need defensibility more than vibes). Defensible because no smart-sounding claim is made. PARTIAL.
2. "Personal extension - does this generalize?" - The claim is the learning path - first-principles security reasoning outside my field, shipped and completed - not enterprise security experience. Stated as personal build, no adoption figures. Defensible.
3. Sibling consistency - same extension as Q35/Q42/Q80/Q66/Q87/Q94: each keeps its own incident; no shared claims, and the extension's published performance numbers stay labeled design targets everywhere, quoted nowhere. [defensible - locked]

# Q94 - tell me about a project you recently worked on and what the... (truncated; read as "...what the impact/outcome was")

**LP:** Deliver Results; Think Big; Invent and Simplify.   **Story:** Tab Scroller - one clean STAR arc (personal project; perf figures = design targets); PCB suite appears only as a number-free one-line breadth nod.

## Core Answer

The project I'd point to is Tab Scroller, a Chrome extension - a small add-on program that runs inside the Chrome browser - I built around a problem I was living with. I keep a few hundred tabs open between work, interview prep, and paper reading, and the browser stops being usable - nothing is findable, and a research session can't be picked up a day later. Chrome won't let an extension touch the native tab bar, so everything had to live as an injected overlay - a panel the add-on draws on top of web pages, since it can't become a built-in browser part. That constraint set the architecture.

I scoped it deliberately bigger than a tab manager: an AI research workspace - you type what you want in ordinary English (an "AI command," like "snooze these tabs until tomorrow") and the tool carries it out, then turns a messy session into something reusable.

The real decision was where the model sits. My first instinct, send every command to an LLM - a large language model, the kind of AI behind chatbots - is wasteful: "close all the YouTube tabs" doesn't need a model. So I built rule-first routing - a lookup table of plain-text patterns matched on the user's own computer. Simple commands match local rules and never touch the network; the model is the last hop, not the first. For hard commands, a pre-filter narrows the tab set before any extraction - before the tool reads the pages' text - and page text gets compressed into subject-predicate-object triplets - tiny "thing -> does -> thing" summaries, far shorter than the pages - before the model sees it. I kept the UI framework-free - plain browser code (JavaScript and CSS), no third-party interface library - because a heavy framework in an injected bar is response delay that users actually feel. And I supported two backends - interchangeable AI engines - on purpose: cloud Gemini (Google's online AI service) for quality, local Ollama (software that runs open AI models on the user's own computer) so privacy-sensitive users keep everything on-machine.

Snoozing - like the alarm button on a phone: a tab is set aside and returns at a chosen time - was the reliability problem worth solving: a dismissed tab has to return even after a browser restart. So the state (which tab, when to return) lives in chrome.storage.local - the browser's own saved data on that one computer, not a server - and chrome.alarms - the browser's built-in timer service - re-arms across restarts. The timer has to be the browser's because the add-on's own background program, Chrome's so-called service worker, isn't running while the browser is closed. I wrote it against a PRD - a written product spec - and shipped in three iterations - alarm engine, message handler (the code that routes commands between the page and the AI), context-menu UI - verifying each one before moving on.

Honest status: it works, and it's a personal project - the only daily user is me. The speed numbers are design targets - figures the plan aimed for, not stopwatch readings; the documented target is simple commands back locally in under 10 milliseconds (thousandths of a second) with no API calls - no requests to any online service at all. Before it I shipped the Bosch PCB inspection suite solo, and the habit I keep reusing is the same: start from the hardest constraint and let it pick the architecture.

The miss I'd own: I shipped the AI action layer - the part that actually carries out commands - without guardrails. A wrong model call can close your tabs. A confidence gate - acting automatically only when the AI's certainty score is high enough - and transactional undo - reverting an action completely or not at all - are written in my upgrade plan but not in the build; that's the first thing I'd do next.

## Memory Anchors
- Problem: a few hundred open tabs (personal observation); Chrome can't be modified at the native tab bar -> injected-overlay constraint.
- Customer: me - this is a personal tool; no adoption claimed.
- Insight: the model should be the last hop, not the first; the hardest constraint (browser + privacy) picks the architecture.
- Action (mine): solo build vs a PRD (product spec) in three verified iterations - rule-first token-saving pipeline (pre-filter -> parallel extraction -> triplet compression), two backends (Gemini = cloud AI / Ollama = AI on the user's own machine), framework-free vanilla JS/CSS, restart-safe snooze via chrome.alarms (browser timer) + storage (saved on that computer).
- Result: working extension in my daily use; <10 ms local-match is a design target, never instrumented; memory layer turns a session into a Markdown (plain-text notes format) research brief.
- Learning: shipped the AI action layer before its guardrails - confidence gate + undo designed, not built; that's step one next time.

## Follow-Up Bank
1. What was the hardest technical decision? - Making the model the last hop instead of the first. Costs more local logic to maintain; buys latency (response speed), cost, and privacy, and it's why simple commands run offline - in plain terms, most commands never leave the computer, so they're fast, free, and private. [SAFE]
2. Why two backends instead of one? - Different users: Gemini reasons better on hard commands; Ollama lets someone who won't send tab data to a cloud still use the feature. The backend is a setting, not a rewrite. [SAFE]
3. How does snoozing survive a restart? - State lives in chrome.storage.local - the browser's own saved data on that one computer, not a server - chrome.alarms re-arms when the browser returns so the one-minute tick resumes; the tab is removed only after the storage write is confirmed. Why the browser's timer is essential: the add-on's background program - Chrome's "service worker" - stops entirely when the browser closes, so only the browser itself can promise the future wake-up. [SAFE]
4. How did you measure performance? - I didn't instrument. The figures in the implementation guide's "Expected Performance Gains" are design targets, not measurements: rule-path commands 2s -> <10 ms with zero API calls, complex 50-tab commands 8s -> 3s with 50k -> 3k tokens, extraction 5s -> 0.5s, and ~70% of commands served offline. In plain terms: 2s -> <10 ms is the time from issuing a command to it happening, for commands matched by local rules (a millisecond is a thousandth of a second); 50k -> 3k tokens is the amount of text handed to the AI (tokens  word-chunks, what AI services measure and bill by); 8s -> 3s and 5s -> 0.5s are the planned response times for complex commands and for reading page text; ~70% offline is the share of commands needing no internet. All are goals written in the design doc before building; none was timed. In my own use the rules path feels instant; that's personal observation, not telemetry. [PARTIAL - projected, not measured]
5. What does the memory layer do? - Condenses a session into a Markdown research brief - a notes file in a plain-text format - with source-referenced cross-tab Q&A (answers that cite which tab each fact came from) and evidence capture, stored in chrome.storage.local (the browser's saved data on that computer). [SAFE]
6. Biggest weakness in the build? - The action layer has no guardrails. The design exists - deterministic confidence, auto-execute above 0.75, confirm 0.4-0.74, clarify below 0.4, plus transactional undo and telemetry - but it's in the upgrade plan, not the code. In plain terms: a fixed score for how sure the AI is would decide auto-run vs. ask-the-user vs. ask-for-clarity; "transactional undo" means the action reverses completely or not at all; "telemetry" means built-in usage and error logging. None of that exists in the shipped build. [SAFE - disclosed]
7. Who else uses it? - Nobody, and I won't pretend otherwise. It started as my own workflow tool; I've made no rollout or store-listing claims. [SAFE - honest status]
8. Why no UI framework? - The bar is injected into every page; a framework tax is paid on each tab. Vanilla JS and CSS kept it light; the model call is the only heavyweight path by design. Plain terms: a third-party interface library would load extra code into every web page the user opens, slowing each one down. [SAFE]
9. Any external inputs? - Two model ecosystems (Gemini, Ollama), and watching the tab-utility category shift toward AI workspaces - that range of inputs is what set the scope. [SAFE]
10. What would you do differently? - Build the guardrails before the action layer, and instrument intent latency/failure rates from day one so "is it fast?" has a real denominator. Start from the constraint, not the feature list. In plain terms: "instrument" means build in timing and error logging so answers come from data, not feel; "intent latency" is how long a plain-English command takes to carry out. [SAFE]

## Risk Check
1. Any speed figure challenged as measured - defensible only because the core self-labels them design targets; if pressed, admit nothing was instrumented and keep the "feels instant = personal observation" line. PARTIAL.
2. "Working extension" rests on one user (me) - no external validation; defensible because the core states it up front instead of dressing a personal tool as a product. PARTIAL.
3. "Would you let an LLM close your tabs?" - rule-first routing means most destructive commands never reach the model, but undo genuinely isn't built; the disclosed miss is the answer. GAP (mitigated by honesty).

# Q95 - a time when you took a big risk and it failed

**LP:** Bias for Action (primary - the calculated single-file bet); Earn Trust (ownership of the unchecked assumption); Learn and Be Curious (the channel-verification rule)   **Story:** STORY 4 standalone build - the base64 single-file bet that broke the ~20 MB email-attachment limit. Distinct from Q14 (risk that *succeeded* - the alignment bet) and Q7 (browser-capability/IE11 failure - deliberately not retold or merged).

## Core Answer

The big risk that failed: I bet that one file could carry the whole delivery of my tool through email - and the file didn't fit the email.

The setup. I'd built a PCB inspection suite - BOM (bill of materials: the parts list every board should match) reconciliation, defect classification - running on a Flask server (a small web program: one central computer the users' machines would call over the network). The users' factory-floor machines had no internet, no installs, minimal IT. The server plan was dead. So I made the bet: one self-contained HTML file - the single-file design: the whole tool inside one double-click file, nothing kept outside it - everything embedded (packed inside), the browser libraries (ready-made code from others the tool borrows), the trained model (the AI's learned numbers), the app - with base64 encoding (a way of rewriting non-text pieces as plain-text characters so they can sit inside a text file) so nothing is fetched at runtime (the file downloads nothing when opened). No CDN (pieces hosted online for the file to pull at open time), no companion files, double-click to run. A zip would have reintroduced the failure where someone moves the HTML without its parts, so I accepted a size hit - a bigger file - on purpose. The upside was real, and I moved fast because it unblocked people.

The artifact (the thing I built - the file itself) worked. One file, roughly 25 megabytes - the size as I remember the shipped file; my account, not an instrumented measurement - opened in seconds, and the analysis matched the server build (the version that needed the central computer) on the known boards I checked. Embedding everything plus the base64 overhead - it inflates binaries by about a third (a fixed property of that text encoding: the rewritten parts come out roughly a third bigger than the originals they wrap) on top of the libraries and model weights (the learned numbers inside the AI) - is what made it that size.

The failure was the channel - the delivery route, not the tool. I distributed by email, and some mail systems cap attachments at 20 megabytes (an attachment limit: the biggest file a mail system lets ride along with a message; the 20 MB figure is the mail systems' own rule - a constraint of the pipe, not my estimate). The file was over. The one-file design that made delivery easy was the thing that couldn't fit the pipe I chose. I'd verified the file; I never verified the channel. That's on me. The cost was real: that path closed, and the file went out on USB drives (plug-in memory sticks) instead - slower, clunkier, especially for the engineers at the other site.

What I did after was bounded. USB stayed as a distribution route. The size fix - compressing (shrinking) the embedded parts more aggressively, likely bringing the file to about 15 megabytes, under the cap - I designed in reflection and never built (the 15 MB is my estimate of what that unbuilt fix would have produced: a plan, not a measurement). I'm not going to call a projection a result.

What I learned: a calculated risk includes the delivery constraint, not just the artifact. Now I check the pipe like I check the target - attachment limits, quotas, the actual channel - before I build around it. The bet itself was right; it's what got the tool onto locked-down machines. The unchecked assumption is what failed.

## Memory Anchors

- Problem: factory-floor machines were locked down (no internet, no installs, minimal IT) - the server build couldn't reach the users; delivery, not code, was the blocker
- Customer: manufacturing engineers on the floor and at the other site, receiving the tool remotely
- Insight (the bet): one embedded HTML file kills the server, the installs, and the broken-dependency failure mode - high upside, accepted size cost
- Action (mine): took the single-file architecture call solo; base64-embedded the browser libraries (OpenCV.js, TF.js, PDF.js, XLSX.js), model, and app into one double-click file (base64 = rewriting the non-text parts as text so they fit inside one file); distributed by email; after the cap failure carried distribution on USB; designed (did not build) an aggressive-compression fix projected at ~15 MB
- Result: artifact worked - ~25 MB, opens in seconds, matched the server build on known boards - but exceeded 20 MB email caps; real cost: email path closed, USB fallback carried the rollout
- Learning: risk math includes the pipe - verify delivery constraints (attachment limits, quotas) before building around them; never present an unimplemented fix as a result

## Follow-Up Bank

1. Was this really a failure, or just a trade-off? - A partial failure of a specific bet. The bet was that one embedded file (all the tool's parts inside a single double-click file) would be an easy distribution channel; the file worked, but at ~25 MB it broke the 20 MB attachment caps some email systems use (an attachment cap = the largest file size a mail system accepts on a message - a fixed rule of the mail systems, not of my file). The tool succeeded; the distribution assumption didn't, and the fallback cost - USB drives - was real. [SAFE]
2. Why was the file so big? - Embedding the browser libraries plus the model weights and the app itself pushed the single file into the tens of megabytes - I say about 25 (what it counts: the size of the delivered file; where it came from: my memory of the shipped build, not an instrumented measurement; how solid: deliberately soft, my account). On top of that, base64, the encoding that squeezes binaries into an HTML text file (it rewrites the non-text pieces as plain-text characters), adds roughly a third over what it wraps (a fixed property of the encoding - solid arithmetic; the softness is only in the parts it starts from). I'm not deriving the total from the library sizes; ~25 MB is my account of the shipped file. [SAFE - canonical phrasing, no size-chain math]
3. Why not a CDN or separate files? - A CDN (pieces hosted online for the page to download when it opens) needs internet; the floor machines don't have it. Separate files or a zip reintroduce the failure where someone moves the HTML without its dependencies and the tool breaks. The single file eliminated that - I took the size hit deliberately. I just didn't check the size against the delivery channel. [SAFE]
4. You said a fix to ~15 MB - why didn't you ship it? - Because I identified it in reflection, after distribution, and "about 15 MB" is a projection, not a measured build (what it counts: my estimate of the file's size after compressing - shrinking - the embedded parts harder; where it came from: planning on paper, never built; how solid: the weakest kind - an untested guess). The mitigations I actually implemented were USB distribution alongside email. The compression is what I'd do next, and I label it that way. [SAFE - honest boundary is the credibility of the story]
5. How is this different from the browser-compatibility failure on the same build, or a risk that worked? - Different assumption each time. That one was a capability assumption - that the fleet ran modern browsers with WebAssembly (WebAssembly = the way a browser runs compiled code quickly, which the tool's imaging libraries need; owned in a separate story, not blended here). My successful-risk story is the alignment bet - it paid. Here the bet paid on the artifact and failed on the channel. All three trace to checking the thing I built instead of the environment or pipe it ships through - which is why the lesson generalizes. [SAFE]
6. How do you know the file itself was fine? - I ran the same known boards through both builds (both builds = the single file and the server version) and compared the outputs - by hand, plus a small automated diff (a simple script that lines up the two results and flags any difference). No parity percentage; the known-board set wasn't a measured sample. [SAFE]
7. What was the actual cost - how many bounces, how much time? - None measured. The email path closed and USB drives carried distribution; it was slower and clunkier, especially for the other site. I never counted failures or lost hours, and I won't invent a number now. [GAP - concede]
8. Hardest part? Disagreement? - Hardest was admitting the failure was a half-checked assumption while the tool itself worked - it's tempting to file 25 MB under "packaging nit." No documented pushback from others: solo project, and I'd be inventing a scene to claim one. The argument was with my own default that if the artifact works, delivery works. [GAP if demanded as conflict story - stated plainly]
9. Larger scale? Do differently? - One tool, one rollout; no larger-scale instance of the new habit is documented, so I don't claim one. Differently: check delivery constraints - attachment limits, quotas, throughput (how much can move through the route at once) - before choosing the packaging, and test the compressed build early so size is a measured input to the architecture, not an after-the-fact finding. [PARTIAL]

## Risk Check

1. "You shipped a working tool - is that a failure?" - Defensible as told: a specific sub-bet (email as the channel) failed with a real cost (USB fallback); ownership is precise, the fix is labeled designed-not-done, and nothing is inflated.
2. "~25 MB - derive it." - Defensible: stated as a soft standalone account (libraries + model + app + base64 overhead -> tens of megabytes), never derived from the library sum, consistent bank-wide with the standalone stance.
3. "Where's the 15 MB compressed build?" - GAP, owned: projected in reflection, never implemented; claimed as a plan, not a result. Removing this honesty would fake an outcome.
4. "How many engineers did the broken channel hit?" - GAP: never counted; hold the line - USB fallback was used, no impact figure exists.
